US launches ‘powerful’ strikes on Iran after Jordan attack

The US has bombed multiple cities across southern Iran, including Ahvaz and Abadan, in what Central Command described as a ‘heavy wave of strikes’. Earlier, US President Donald Trump said the US would hit Iran ‘very hard’ in retaliation for an attack on US forces in Jordan.

articles.title: Trump admin invokes 30-year dormant terror court as it seeks to deport Afghan woman tied to Election Day plot
articles.excerpt: U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II details the federal charges against eight individuals involved in an alleged terror plot. The conspiracy includes providing material support to terrorists, planning...
articles.body_text:
U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II details the federal charges against eight individuals involved in an alleged terror plot. The conspiracy includes providing material support to terrorists, planning to attack a UFC event and murdering federal officials, potentially including the president and vice president. Penalties range up to life imprisonment.

The Trump administration is seeking to use a specialized federal court for the first time since Congress created it three decades ago in an effort to deport an Afghan woman accused of aiding an Islamic State-inspired terror plot in the U.S., according to court records made public on Wednesday.

Nazira Haji Zada, of Fort Worth, Texas, is the first person facing deportation through the Alien Terrorist Removal Court after her arrest earlier this week.

The court is scheduled to hold an initial hearing on Thursday in Washington, D.C., in the government’s effort to deport Haji Zada.

"The allegations in this case show the matriarch of an ISIS-sympathizing family aiding in a plot to launch a mass casualty attack on American voters on Election Day. The Department’s application in this court makes clear that terrorists have no place in the United States of America," acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

'SOMETHING BIG': FEDS REVEAL HOW RELATIVES OF SUSPECTS IN FOILED WHITE HOUSE UFC PLOT SAW WARNING SIGNS

The Trump administration is seeking to use a specialized federal court for the first time since Congress created it three decades ago in an effort to deport an Afghan woman accused of aiding an Islamic State-inspired terror plot. (ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)

According to an FBI memo dated July 15, authorities "developed information" that Haji Zada supports the Islamic State and had her children pledge their loyalty to the terrorist group.

Haji Zada "supported" a plot by family members to carry out an ISIS-inspired attack in the U.S., according to the memo.

She was identified in court filings as the mother and mother-in-law of two Afghan men who were convicted in Oklahoma in connection with a 2024 Election Day terror plot.

Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, was sentenced in November to 15 years behind bars. He previously agreed to be deported after his release from prison.

Nazira Haji Zada is the first person facing deportation through the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Haji Zada's son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, who previously worked as a security guard for a U.S. military installation in Afghanistan, pleaded guilty to conspiring and attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State. Prosecutors said he attempted to advance his attack plans by ordering AK-47 rifles, liquidating his family’s assets and purchasing one-way tickets for his wife and child to travel back to Afghanistan.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996 but never received a petition until this month, when the Justice Department filed an application attempting to deport Haji Zada.

The longtime-dormant court hears government applications seeking the removal of noncitizens alleged to qualify as "alien terrorists" under federal immigration law when the evidence supporting removal includes classified information.

FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN MOVES TO IMPEACH JUDGE WHO ORDERED CONVICTED CUBAN PLANE HIJACKER FREED FROM ICE

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996 but never received a petition until this month. (Getty Images)

"Congress created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court three decades ago to remove from the United States alien terrorists who never should have been here in the first place," Blanche said.

The court is made up of five federal judges from various districts across the country who are appointed by the Supreme Court's chief justice.

For the time being, the court says all proceedings will take place at the E. Barrett Prettyman U.S. Courthouse in Washington.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Evo Morales defiant after new Bolivia arrest warrant
articles.excerpt:
A court in Bolivia has issued an arrest warrant for former President Evo Morales.

The Santa Cruz district prosecutor’s office said Morales is being investigated for “armed uprising against the securi...
articles.body_text:
A court in Bolivia has issued an arrest warrant for former President Evo Morales.

The Santa Cruz district prosecutor’s office said Morales is being investigated for “armed uprising against the security and sovereignty of the state, terrorism and attacks on the safety of means of transport”.

Morales backed protests in June by farmers and truckers against an economic crisis, rising living costs and conservative President Rodrigo Paz’s austerity plans.

“They will not intimidate us,” he responded to the charges in a post on X.

Morales said the government was going after him “to conceal the true drama Bolivia is experiencing: a deep economic and social crisis…a model that has abandoned the people and protects corruption”.

Morales, Bolivia’s first Indigenous president, rose from poverty to serve three terms as president, one of Latin America’s longest-serving leaders.

He was in office from 2006 until his fraught 2019 ouster, when he was forced to resign after elections tainted by claims of fraud.

Initially refusing to leave power, he eventually had to go, casting a shadow over nearly 14 years of economic progress and poverty reduction mixed with accusations of political heavy-handedness.

He went into exile in Mexico and later, Argentina, returning a year later after his political ally Luis Arce won the presidency.

In late 2024, allegations surfaced against him of trafficking a minor and statutory rape of a 15-year-old girl who became pregnant.

By early 2025, Morales’s supporters cut off roads and paralysed the country in protest against the charges, which he rejected. He has also refused to appear at court hearings.

As the unrest over Bolivia’s economic crisis was brewing in May, Morales was found in contempt of court, and a renewed warrant for his arrest on the rape charges was issued.

His supporters threatened to “throw the country into turmoil” if he was arrested, at a time when protests had shut down roads and forced the government to airlift food to some areas.

After Paz declared a state of emergency in June and the protests slowed, the latest investigation began, triggered by a criminal complaint over Morales’s involvement with the demonstrations.

The complaint, filed by the civic group Comit pro Santa Cruz and later picked up by the Interior Ministry, alleges that Morales’s supporters “caused a shortage of food, fuel and medicine” by blocking transport in the country for 53 days.

The charges filed on Wednesday were outlined in a document published by local media, according to German wire service DPA.

The order instructs police to detain Morales and bring him to the special anticorruption unit.

“We will continue fighting alongside the people, as we have always done, with the conviction that Bolivia deserves a different path: one of dignity, sovereignty, social justice, and the recovery of hope for all,” said Morales responding to the latest charges.

articles.title: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
articles.excerpt:
The US military says it launched "heavy" strikes against Iran on Wednesday in retaliation for attempted Iranian ballistic missile attacks on American forces.

Centcom said it hit "dozens" of Islamic R...
articles.body_text:
The US military says it launched "heavy" strikes against Iran on Wednesday in retaliation for attempted Iranian ballistic missile attacks on American forces.

Centcom said it hit "dozens" of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in response to Tuesday's firing by Iran on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

The latest hostilities came a day after the conflict expanded, with the first publicly announced joint US-Saudi strikes targeting Iranian proxies in Iraq.

When the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February, President Donald Trump said the war would last only a few weeks, but it has gone on for five months with no end in sight.

On Wednesday, Axios reported, citing an unnamed US official, that Trump had met with Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, who had conveyed that Saudi Arabia wants to de-escalate tensions. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

The conflict has reignited after several days of relative calm.

For days, both sides halted strikes as talks apparently restarted in hopes of some type of diplomatic solution. Trump called them "very friendly negotiations", though Tehran denied any discussions were happening.

The strikes on Wednesday started at 20:00 ET (01:00 BST on Thursday) and lasted about an hour, with Centcom calling them a "powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East". All of Iran's missiles were intercepted, Centcom said.

The attack by the US targeted "military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities," Centcom wrote once the strikes were complete.

Hours before the announced strikes, Trump vowed to retaliate against Iran for their attempted attack on US troops a day earlier.

The US president told reporters at the White House: "We're going to be hitting them very hard because it's our turn to hit them.

"They know it's coming. They asked us not to do it."

The IRGC said it had targeted a US air base and a command centre in Jordan "in response to the acts of aggression of the American child-killing army".

It also said naval forces had struck three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they "ignored warnings" and sailed along what it described as an "unsafe and illegal route" through the vital Gulf waterway.

Last Friday, Trump suspended an intensive bombing campaign that had lasted for 13 consecutive nights. The US said it had targeted Iranian weapons and military sites. Scores of people were reported to have died.

On Tuesday, Centcom said the joint US-Saudi strikes hit "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours".

Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which is dominated by Iran-backed Shia militias, said at least 20 of its members had been killed in US-Saudi strikes on its bases.

The Iraqi presidency said it denounced the bombing of the PMF bases, calling it "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty".

But Trump told Fox News the strikes had been "co-ordinated with the Iraqi government".

Saudi Arabia, which sees itself as the leading Sunni Muslim power, and Iran, the largest Shia Muslim country, have been locked in a struggle for regional dominance for decades.

articles.title: Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling charged with assaulting NT administrator
articles.excerpt:
Member for Solomon has previously denied alleged incident with administrator David Connolly

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news...
articles.body_text:
Member for Solomon has previously denied alleged incident with administrator David Connolly

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Luke Gosling, the federal Labor member for Solomon, has been charged over an alleged assault on the Northern Territory’s administrator earlier this month, NT police have said.

“The Northern Territory police force has charged the 54-year-old federal member for Solomon, Luke Gosling, in relation to an alleged assault on the administrator of the Northern Territory,” police said in a statement on Thursday.

The incident involving the administrator, David Connolly, whose position is similar to that of a state governor, is alleged to have occurred at a cultural festival in Darwin on 18 July.

Police arrested Gosling on Thursday morning. They subsequently said he had been “charged with two counts of assault on the administrator” and had been bailed to appear before Darwin local court on 1 September.

Gosling, a former military officer, is the federal special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia. He was first elected to the parliament in 2016.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, declined to comment on Thursday’s arrest.

“There is a legal process under way. It would be inappropriate to comment further,” a spokesperson for the PM said.

Gosling had previously denied having any altercation with Connolly, and NT media reported Gosling previously called the claims “ridiculous allegations that I categorically deny”.

Gosling’s lawyer, Marty Aust, on Thursday said the charges were “completely and utterly denied and will be contested”.

“It’s particularly concerning that the police resorted to the power of arrest when they could have dealt with the matter by way of summons or notice to appear,” Aust told reporters.

A spokesperson for Connolly said they could not comment as it was a police matter.

Liberal senator James Paterson, the shadow minister for defence, called on Albanese to stand Gosling down from his envoy role.

“The allegations facing the special envoy for defence and veterans, Luke Gosling, are incredibly serious. While everyone is entitled to the presumption of innocence, an arrest for assault requires him to immediately stand down from his duties,” Paterson wrote on social media. “The PM must act today.”

The Liberal senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, who represents the NT, said in a statement that Gosling’s arrest was “a deeply concerning development”. She called for him to be stood down.

“It is troubling that one of our community’s elected leaders has been arrested in relation to an alleged assault on the King’s representative in the territory,” she said.

“It would be wrong to prejudge the investigation or any future proceedings. All parties must cooperate fully with police, and the investigation must be allowed to proceed without fear, favour or political interference.”

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: US launches ‘heavy waves of strikes’ on Iran after days-long pause in attacks
articles.excerpt:
US says attacks on Thursday morning hit dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets while experts say earlier strikes by both sides increase risk of return to all-out war

US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push regi...
articles.body_text:
US says attacks on Thursday morning hit dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets while experts say earlier strikes by both sides increase risk of return to all-out war

US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warn

The US military is saying is has finished its “heavy wave of strikes” against Iran.

Central Command said in a statement posted on X that it struck “dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran, including military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities”.

It said the two hours of strikes were in response to Iran’s attempted missile attacks on US forces in the region and “aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries”.

Centcom also recapped that IRGC forces had launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran in “an attempted surprise attack” on US forces on Tuesday, US time, adding: “All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted.”

The fresh US strikes after the days-long lull in its direct attacks on Iran were launched hours after Donald Trump vowed to hit the country “very hard” after it targeted a base in Jordan hosting US forces.

Iranian state media said two people were injured in attacks on the island of Qeshm in the strait of Hormuz and explosions were also reported in the western province of Khuzestan.

The renewed hostilities sent oil prices spiking, with Brent crude – the international standard – jumping 7.3% past $88 a barrel.

There’s more in our new full report here:

Donald Trump has been considering a US commander’s plan for a punishing air campaign against Iran that could take up to two weeks, the Wall Street Journal has reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

It says the plan drawn up by Adm Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, involved 10 to 14 days of intensive airstrikes intended to cripple Iran’s missile capability, despite warnings that the US is running low on air-defensive munitions.

Or Trump could opt for a more limited military strike in hopes diplomacy could be pursued, said the report, published shortly before the US launched a fresh round of strikes on Iran.

double quotation markThe idea behind Cooper’s high-end option is to go beyond the tit-for-tat airstrikes that have done little to deter Tehran from threatening ships in the Strait of Hormuz and lobbing missiles at American forces in the region by sharply escalating the war, according to people familiar with his thinking.

If the U.S. wants military action to be effective, Cooper has said, the U.S. must step up its air attacks, significantly blunting Iran’s missile threat, to try to break the stalemate. This “go big” approach, which is among a series of options he has developed, would reduce the need for the U.S. to use defensive munitions because Iran would have less capability to attack.

The US military is saying is has finished its “heavy wave of strikes” against Iran.

Central Command said in a statement posted on X that it struck “dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran, including military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities”.

It said the two hours of strikes were in response to Iran’s attempted missile attacks on US forces in the region and “aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries”.

Centcom also recapped that IRGC forces had launched multiple ballistic missiles from Iran in “an attempted surprise attack” on US forces on Tuesday, US time, adding: “All Iranian missiles were successfully intercepted.”

Before this new round of American strikes against Iran, Saudi Arabia joined the US in hitting an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq – a move that has pushed the Middle East region into “uncharted territory”, analysts are warning.

Riyadh’s decision to publicly join the US in striking sites associated with Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces – killing at least 20 fighters – has added another complicating dimension to a war being seen as increasingly unpredictable and in danger of widening.

While Saudi Arabia has reportedly been involved in a handful of secretive strikes on Iran as part of the war, Riyadh’s overt involvement marks a new turning point in the conflict, reports Peter Beaumont.

Wednesday’s flare-up in fighting followed days in which Tehran and its proxies have targeted bases and facilities of the US and its allies, including in Saudi Arabia, despite the brief US pause in attack on Iran.

The sense of growing chaos in the Middle East was summed up by Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and north Africa programme at the Chatham House thinktank, who said:

double quotation markEveryone is trying make sense of something that is increasingly senseless. One view is that the informal [US] pause in direct strikes on Iran saw a shift from Tehran to its proxies to maintain pressure [on Washington]. But there is no longer any plausible deniability because everyone knows how the relationships are intertwined.

The US military has hit the south-western Iranian city of Abadan as well as Qeshm Island, Iranian media is saying, citing regional authorities.

The US attacked “a point near Qeshm” at 4am local time (0030 GMT), the deputy governor of the southern Hormozgan province said, according to the Mehr news agency.

The deputy governor of Khuzestan province said US missiles attacked “points around Abadan city”, the Fars news agency said.

State TV said several loud explosions were also heard in Ahwaz, Khuzestan.

A missile strike has hit a residential area of Qeshm island, Iran’s Tasnim is now also saying.

The US military earlier said its new strikes against Iran began at 8pm Eastern Time (midnight Thursday GMT).

Three explosions have been heard on Iran’s Qeshm island, Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency is saying.

The Gulf island near the strait of Hormuz is a storage location for Iranian attack craft, drones, sea mines and other materials used to disrupt shipping through the vital energy route.

Before Wednesday’s flare-up of hostilities, mediators had expressed optimism about bringing the US and Iran back to the negotiating table following the collapse of an interim agreement amid renewed fighting over the strait of Hormuz.

A regional official quoted by the AP said mediators were “still trying with both sides” to restore calm and get the ceasefire back on track. He gave no details on whether progress was being made.

Another official said regional countries would continue to push to de-escalate the situation, but that prospects for successful mediation were slim as both sides continued to attack each other and shown no inclination to stop.

“We’re in a very bad place right now,” the unnamed official said.

Welcome to our live coverage of the continuing crisis in the Middle East.

The ​US has said it is conducting ​airstrikes ‌in ‌Iran, after a lull of several days in direct US attacks on targets in Iran.

Donald Trump said America would strike Iran hard, telling reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “We’re going to be hitting them very hard, because it’s our turn to hit them. They know it’s coming.”

The US military said its attacks were a “powerful response to yesterday’s attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East”.

On Wednesday Iran launched a barrage of missiles at American military installations in Jordan – its first attack in the region since the pause in fighting – meanwhile the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers.

Elsewhere, drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta, according to Ambrey, a British maritime security firm. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a US-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker. No injuries were reported.

A strike on Egypt by Iran or its allies, if confirmed, would mark a significant widening of the conflict. Asked during an Oval Office event if Iran was responsible for the strikes, Trump responded: “It’s a little more of the same.”

The flare-up on multiple fronts after several days of relative calm raised the risk of a return to all-out war. It also underscored the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict.

The US-Saudi strikes came hours after Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, departed his first meeting with Trump since they launched the war against Iran on 28 February.

The renewed hostilities sent oil prices spiking. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 7.3% to $88 a barrel.

The office of the Iraqi president, Nizar Amidi, called the US-Saudi airstrikes on multiple logistics and weapons sites in eastern Iraq “a blatant violation of Iraq’s sovereignty”.

An oil refinery in Jazan, on the Red Sea coast, had temporarily shut down due to “relatively significant” damage from a Houthi attack on Saturday, a Saudi official told the Associated Press.

Saudi Arabia is seeking to build an international coalition to protect ⁠shipping in the ⁠Red ​Sea from Houthi attacks, Reuters quoted two people familiar with the deliberations as saying.

articles.title: Deadly strikes on Ukrainian cities after Zelenskyy warns of ‘massive’ Russian attack
articles.excerpt:
Six dead in Kryvi Rih including two children and fires in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, after wave of ballistic missile launches

A Russian missile strike killed at least six people in central Ukraine,...
articles.body_text:
Six dead in Kryvi Rih including two children and fires in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, after wave of ballistic missile launches

A Russian missile strike killed at least six people in central Ukraine, including two girls, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s military administration said, while at least one person died in Kyiv, after the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned the country hours in advance of Moscow launching another massive attack.

“In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults,” said Oleksandr Vilkul, adding that a further eight people were wounded and that the death toll may rise.

In Kyiv, “sadly, one death has been confirmed” the military administration for the capital city announced. The Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reported fires in several districts. Earlier, he posted: “The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!”

Elsewhere, residential buildings ⁠in ⁠the western city ​of Lviv ⁠were damaged ⁠by ​Russian ‌air ‌attacks, ‌mayor Andriy Sadovyi said on ‌Telegram, citing ​preliminary reports and ⁠asking people ​to seek ​shelter.

Late on Wednesday, Zelenskyy had posted: “The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago, and there is a high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight … Please, in all regions of Ukraine, pay attention to air raid alerts today and stay safe.”

As the attacks took place, Poland, which shares a border with Ukraine, protectively scrambled fighter ​jets to protect ​its airspace, its armed forces said.

“Fighter aircraft and ​an early warning ‌aircraft have ​begun operations while ​ground-based air defence systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness.”

Zelenskyy also repeated his request to Ukraine’s allies to supply Kyiv with the missiles its air defence system lacks. “It is important that our partners fully ​understand what is happening and that the protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence missiles.”

Meanwhile in Russia, a ⁠warehouse of ⁠online ⁠retailer Wildberries in ​the western ⁠city of ⁠Penza ​caught ‌fire from a Ukrainian ‌drone attack, ‌said the regional governor, Oleg Melnichenko. One person was ​injured and around ⁠200 people ​were evacuated from ​the ​site, he ​added.

articles.title: US launches fresh strikes on Iran after days-long pause, amid fears the war is widening
articles.excerpt:
Trump vowed to hit Iran ‘very hard’ after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, a day after joint US-Saudi strikes on militants in Iraq

The US military has launched strikes on Iranian ta...
articles.body_text:
Trump vowed to hit Iran ‘very hard’ after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, a day after joint US-Saudi strikes on militants in Iraq

The US military has launched strikes on Iranian targets in response to Tehran’s attack on American forces in Jordan on Wednesday, raising the risk of a return to all-out-war in the region.

The new strikes were launched hours after president Donald Trump vowed to hit Iran “very hard” after it targeted a base in Jordan that hosts US troops, and comes after a days-long pause in violence between the two sides.

Iranian state media said two people were injured in attacks on the island of Qeshm in the strait of Hormuz and that explosions were also reported in Khuzestan province to the north-west.

US central command said in a social media post that over the span of two hours they struck “dozens” of targets belonging to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp, including military command centres as well as missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defence sites.

The barrage came after the US partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Iran-backed militias in neighbouring Iraq on Wednesday, killing at least 20 fighters and six Iranian advisers.

Elsewhere, drone strikes ignited fires on two natural gas vessels at the Egyptian port of Damietta, according to British maritime security firm Ambrey. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes on a US-owned floating storage facility and a Greek-owned tanker. No injuries were reported.

Asked during an Oval Office event if Iran was responsible for the strikes on the natural gas vessels, Trump responded: “It’s a little more of the same.”

“In the meantime, we’re going to be hitting them very hard because it’s our turn to hit them,” he added.

Analysts said the flare-ups on multiple fronts after several days of relative calm pushed the region into “uncharted territory”. It also underscored the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict that has jolted the world economy and which remains unpopular among Americans.

The fighting was also likely to add to concerns that the US is further drawing down already diminished stockpiles of sophisticated munitions needed to defend its bases and allies.

Wednesday’s joint US-Saudi strikes on Iraq came after Riyadh had accused Iraqi militias of firing drones against its oil facilities. An umbrella group of Iraqi militias initially denied the allegations.

The Popular Mobilization Forces, a coalition of primarily Shiite Iranian-backed armed groups that is officially under the command of the Iraqi military, said at least 20 fighters were killed and 32 wounded in the overnight strikes.

Iran’s deputy governor for political, security and social affairs in Markazi province told Iranian state media that four advisers from Tehran were also killed.

The coalition joined the fight against the Islamic State group after it seized large sections of Iraq in 2014. The Iraqi government later designated the coalition as an “independent military formation” within the armed forces, but the militias have significant autonomy and some have attacked US facilities.

Before the latest eruption, mediators had expressed optimism about bringing the US and Iran back to the negotiating table. An interim agreement collapsed in recent weeks over renewed fighting in the strait of Hormuz.

A regional official said mediators are “still trying with both sides” to restore calm and get the ceasefire back on track. He gave no details on whether progress was being made and spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door diplomacy.

The renewed hostilities sent oil prices spiking. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 7.3% to over $88 a barrel.

Saudi Arabia is also locked in a renewed conflict with the Houthis. The Iran-backed militants have declared a blockade of Saudi shipping that could choke off another crucial Middle East trade route, the Bab el-Mandeb strait from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden.

On Monday, the Houthis said they had launched drones targeting oil facilities used to transport oil across Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, a key bypass for Saudi exports blocked by Iran’s chokehold on the strait of Hormuz.

The rebels said the attack was in response to a Saudi drone they said had breached Yemen’s airspace.

articles.title: Matthew Stafford, Josh Allen headline 'Madden NFL 27' ratings as 99 Club members
articles.excerpt:
Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams will aim to avoid the "Madden Curse" in a pivotal third NFL season after being tabbed as the video game's cover athlete.

NFL training camps are opening across...
articles.body_text:
Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams will aim to avoid the "Madden Curse" in a pivotal third NFL season after being tabbed as the video game's cover athlete.

NFL training camps are opening across the league, and the countdown to the latest edition of "Madden NFL" is officially underway.

"Madden NFL 27" is still a little more than two weeks from release, but the ratings debate will likely start now. EA Sports unveiled its latest player ratings Wednesday, releasing the top 10 players at quarterback, running back and wide receiver.

Reigning league MVP Matthew Stafford and Buffalo Bills signal caller Josh Allen led the quarterback group ratings and earned a spot in the coveted 99 Club.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) throws a pass against the Carolina Panthers during the second quarter of an NFC wild-card playoff game at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Jan. 10, 2026. (Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Stafford and Allen tied for the top quarterback rating, but the Los Angeles Rams signal caller was listed ahead of the Buffalo Bills star in the category.

Joe Burrow was third with a 97, followed by Baltimore Ravens standout Lamar Jackson. Patrick Mahomes received a 93 rating and was slotted fifth, while Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff rounded out the group's top 10 with an 88.

The other 99 Club members were wide receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Jaxon Smith-Njigba, defensive end Myles Garrett and tight end Trey McBride.

CALEB WILLIAMS LANDS 'MADDEN NFL 27' COVER, BUT INFAMOUS CURSE LOOMS OVER PIVOTAL THIRD SEASON

After winning the franchise’s second Super Bowl title in February, the Seattle Seahawks reached an agreement on a four-year contract extension with Smith-Njigba that made him the highest-paid receiver in NFL history. Chase has eclipsed the 1,000-yard receiving mark in every season since entering the league in 2021.

Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja’Marr Chase (1) reacts after picking up a first down against the Arizona Cardinals during the first quarter at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio, on Dec. 28, 2025. (Ben Jackson/Getty Images)

After Chase and Smith-Njigba, Puka Nacua, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Justin Jefferson rounded out the top five wide receivers. Mike Evans, who left the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for the San Francisco 49ers this offseason, came in at No. 10.

Detroit Lions star Jahmyr Gibbs led all running backs with a 98 overall rating. Christian McCaffrey followed at 97 after a bounce-back season, with Jonathan Taylor third and Bijan Robinson fourth at 95. Rams standout Kyren Williams rounded out the top 10.

Caleb Williams may be the face of "Madden NFL 27," but the Chicago Bears quarterback is still eyeing a higher rating. Earlier this week, he said his goal is to climb into the 99 Club before the end of the year.

A detailed view of NFL Madden 2026 items at Moscone Center in San Francisco, California, on Feb. 4, 2026, before Super Bowl LX. (Ishika Samant/Getty Images)

"If I get my completion percentage up, I'll be a 99," Williams told "Up & Adams" on Monday. "That's how everybody feels about it. I don't throw picks, I'm not a pick guy, never been a pick guy. Throw a few more touchdowns, keep the picks down and then just get the completion up."

"Madden NFL 27" is scheduled to launch worldwide Aug. 13, with MVP+ members receiving early access up to seven days ahead of release.

On the team side, the Rams earned the game’s top rating with a 93 overall.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Why did Anthony Fauci invoke the Fifth Amendment? Senate hearing explained
articles.excerpt:
Dr Anthony Fauci pleads the Fifth at Covid hearing

Dr Anthony Fauci, a former top United States public health official, has declined to answer questions at a Republican-led Senate committee hearing i...
articles.body_text:
Dr Anthony Fauci pleads the Fifth at Covid hearing

Dr Anthony Fauci, a former top United States public health official, has declined to answer questions at a Republican-led Senate committee hearing into the origins of COVID-19 and the handling of the pandemic.

The former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination on Wednesday.

Fauci was called to testify by Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who accuses him of misleading Congress and questions whether US-funded research in China played a role in the pandemic, allegations Fauci denies.

Although former President Joe Biden granted Fauci a preemptive pardon in 2025, Republicans claim it does not protect him from any alleged crimes committed after it was issued, such as perjuring himself at a Senate hearing.

Fauci’s lawyers advised him not to testify, arguing that anything he said under oath could expose him to new legal risks.

Fauci, 85, is a physician and immunologist who led the US NIAID for 38 years, advising seven presidents, both Republican and Democratic.

He became the public face of the US response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, after helping lead the country’s response to health crises including HIV/AIDS, Ebola and the 2001 anthrax attacks.

He became a target of conservative criticism over pandemic policies, including mask recommendations, vaccines and school closures.

During his last year in government, Fauci was also chief medical adviser to Biden until he retired in 2022.

During the pandemic, between 2019 and 2022, he kept more than 1,000 pages of diary entries documenting his work advising the White House and responding to the pandemic.

The notes chronicle his interactions with senior officials and the media.

He was subpoenaed to testify over his handling of the pandemic and its origins before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

The hearing, led by Paul, focused on several issues:

The tense hearing lasted about three hours.

After a brief opening statement, Fauci repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and declined to answer more than 100 questions.

He accused committee chairman Paul of having an “obsession” with prosecuting him.

The hearing included several tense moments:

Closing the hearing, Paul asked rhetorically: “Did [Fauci’s] actions lead to the largest man-made plague in history?”

Fauci said he invoked the Fifth Amendment on the advice of his lawyers because he believed his answers could expose him to new legal risks.

He argued that Paul was trying to build a criminal case against him rather than conduct legitimate congressional oversight.

Although Biden’s pardon protects Fauci from prosecution for actions before January 2025, Republicans say any false statements made under oath during this hearing could still expose him to perjury charges.

The Fifth Amendment protects people from being forced to give evidence that could incriminate them in a criminal case. Invoking it is a constitutional right and does not imply guilt.

Most scientists believe COVID-19 likely spread naturally from animals to humans, known as zoonotic spillover, pointing to a wildlife market in Wuhan as the most likely place where it first spread.

Fauci has consistently said he believes that scientific evidence points to a natural origin, while remaining open to other possibilities.

Notes from his diary detail a January 2020 call with 11 top virologists and evolutionary biologists – only two were convinced the virus had a natural origin, while the rest debated whether it could have been engineered.

Today, most scientists favour a natural origin, while the US intelligence community is divided.

The FBI said in 2023 that a laboratory-related incident is the most likely origin of the pandemic. The CIA reached the same conclusion in 2025, but with low confidence. Other agencies and the National Intelligence Council continue to favour a natural origin or remain undecided.

Yes, but only what happened before the pardon was issued.

On January 19, 2025, Biden granted Fauci a full and unconditional pardon covering any federal offences he may have committed since 2014, saying the move aimed to protect Fauci from “politically motivated prosecutions”.

The pardon does not cover actions taken after it was issued. Fauci could face legal consequences if he were accused of committing a new crime, such as making false statements under oath during Wednesday’s Senate hearing.

Paul and other Republicans also argue that because Biden’s pardon shields Fauci from criminal liability for his past actions, he can no longer claim that his testimony about those actions would incriminate him and should not be able to invoke his Fifth Amendment.

The legal standing of this argument is not clear, and Paul has acknowledged that it is a novel “legal question that the courts may have to decide”.

Potentially, but it remains unclear whether either will happen.

Paul said the Senate committee will vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer more than 100 questions.

Being held in contempt means lawmakers believe a witness has refused to cooperate with a lawful investigation. It does not automatically lead to criminal charges, but can trigger further legal action.

If the committee approves the measure, it could refer the case to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution, ask a federal court to pursue a civil action, or, in the rarest case, ask the Senate to use its powers to detain a witness through the Senate sergeant-at-arms.

Paul has not said which option, if any, he plans to pursue.

articles.title: Australia takes Telegram to court over alleged failure to remove 'pro-terror' material
articles.excerpt:
Julie Inman Grant has launched legal action against social media platform Telegram

Australia is taking Telegram to court over its alleged failure to remove "pro-terror" material, including video of t...
articles.body_text:
Julie Inman Grant has launched legal action against social media platform Telegram

Australia is taking Telegram to court over its alleged failure to remove "pro-terror" material, including video of the Christchurch shootings, the country's eSafety commissioner has said.

Julie Inman-Grant, who last year led Australia's world-first ban on social media for under-16s, said the platform faced a fine of up to to A$54.6m (£28m, US$38m) for failing to comply with its safety obligations under the Online Safety Act.

The platform had left content "linked to some of the most notorious acts of known extremist violence in recent history" online long after it had been put on notice, she alleged.

"This should concern all of us," she said, adding "no platform is above the law".

The announcement comes a day after Russia charged Telegram's founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorism, based on allegations that the messenger app had been used for recruitment by Ukrainian secret services.

Durov was also arrested and placed under formal investigation in France in 2024 for his alleged failure to properly moderate the app to reduce criminality. He was allowed to go home months later, while the investigation continues.

Inman-Grant said her agency had begun inquiring what Telegram was doing to combat terrorist and extremist material in March 2024, and had endured "five very difficult months of unresponsiveness".

Though the platform later started engaging, she said it had retained a "permissive environment" for hosting extremist content that was "very easy to find".

"This only serves to desensitise, to normalise and to sometimes radicalise" users, she said. She also alleged that the platform was "sometimes used to plan attacks".

A Telegram spokesperson said the platform's "extensive" anti-terrorism efforts were "well documented", adding: "We reject these allegations and will contest them in court."

Extremist content that was allegedly accessible on Telegram included video of the 2019 Christchurch mosque and Buffalo shooting in New York in May 2022, as well as videos of terrorist executions, according to Inman-Grant.

With the "painful aftermath" of the attack that targeted a Jewish festival in Bondi in December fresh in Australians' minds, it "is more important than ever that digital platforms meet their obligations to protect the community", she said.

Inman-Grant noted that Australia does not issue licences for platforms like Telegram, but said "we could apply to the federal court and ask that the service be ceased".

"We've never used those powers," she said. "We'll see how this all plays out and whether that kind of action is warranted."

The eSafety regulator also fined Telegram A$1m in February 2025 for failing to respond on time to questions about how it was tackling child abuse and extremist material on the platform.

articles.title: Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 23 as aftershock and heat complicate rescue efforts
articles.excerpt:
Soldiers and emergency workers are combing through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors

The death toll from the major earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday ...
articles.body_text:
Soldiers and emergency workers are combing through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors

The death toll from the major earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday rose to at least 23 as the search for trapped survivors inside a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses in the country’s south-west continued.

The magnitude 6.8 earthquake that struck the Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu has injured at least 62, the prefectural government said. That number has steadily grown, fanning fears it will rise.

Almost 5,000 Self-Defence Forces personnel deployed to the region will be challenged by temperatures rising to 35C on Thursday, officials said, and a significant magnitude 5.8 aftershock hit overnight to further complicate recovery efforts.

About 170 rescue workers are searching the Aeon mall shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake happened.

The company said about 3,000 customers were evacuated to a parking lot before a gas explosion happened in another part of the mall, where some people were still working. Eight people have been pulled from the rubble of ​the mall. Of them, three have died.

Japanese media footage of the mall showed that part of the ceiling had caved in, and metal pieces and other debris were scattered about as helmeted and masked rescue workers searched the area.

In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at a factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government.

Nearly 34,900 homes were still without electricity and 15,000 homes without running water, Kumamoto officials said. More than 8,800 people left their homes to stay in over 400 shelters, where power sources were being added to provide air conditioning.

Aerial police footage showed some homes in residential areas were completely flattened, including a few that crumbled into a nearby river.

“There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time,” the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.”

A government spokesperson said on Wednesday more than 9,000 people had sought refuge in 506 shelters in three regions of Kyushu island.

Some stunned locals said the quake was the biggest they had felt in their lifetimes, measuring at the top of Japan’s seven-level shindo scale.

“It was the strongest quake I ever experienced,” Kanzo Matsumoto, 73, the operator of a luxury onsen hot spring inn in Yatsushiro, told Agence France-Presse.

Japan’s Geospatial Information Authority said some ground surfaces were displaced by as much as 87 centimetres in the quake.

Takaichi said the region had suffered extensive damage, including collapsed buildings, fires and damage to roads.

Some auto and ​chip manufacturers with plants in Kyushu halted production on Wednesday.

Toyota said it would halt operations at three plants in the region through Friday as it weighed the quake’s impact on suppliers and ⁠logistics.

Kyushu is ‌a key base for Japan’s automotive and semiconductor industries, which account for roughly two-fifths of regional industrial output.

Analysts said factory shutdowns at automakers and chip manufacturers appeared to be driven largely by precautions for workers, rather than by damage to production facilities.

Japan is one of the world’s most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific “ring of fire”.

Kumamoto was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016, which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.

The archipelago, home to about 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18 percent of the world’s earthquakes.

With Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Singapore fines French teen $465 for viral straw-licking stunt
articles.excerpt:
Didier Gaspard Owen Maximilien is 'truly sorry' for causing trouble, his lawyer says

A Singapore court has fined a French student S$600 ($465; £348) for licking a straw from an orange juice vending m...
articles.body_text:
Didier Gaspard Owen Maximilien is 'truly sorry' for causing trouble, his lawyer says

A Singapore court has fined a French student S$600 ($465; £348) for licking a straw from an orange juice vending machine and putting it back into its dispenser.

Didier Gaspard Owen Maximilien, 19, pleaded guilty to one count of public nuisance.

Maximilien, who is studying in Singapore, posted the video of himself licking the straw on Instagram with the caption "city is not safe".

Many online reacted with disgust to his video, which was reposted on a community page and picked up by local news outlets.

The company that owns the vending machine, iJooz, said it replaced all 500 straws in the machine dispenser after Maximilien's stunt.

Public nuisance offenders in Singapore face up to a S$2,000 fine, three months in jail, or both.

Both the prosecution and the defence sought a fine for Maximilien.

Maximilien is "truly sorry for having caused all this trouble and he realises that what appeared to him at that time as something perhaps playful has turned out to be something very consequential," a defence lawyer was quoted as saying by The Straits Times.

Serving freshly-squeezed orange juice at S$2 per cup, iJooz vending machines are a common sight in shopping districts, train stations and housing blocks in Singapore.

Maximilien licked the straw from an iJooz machine in Goldhill Centre on 12 March, in one of the city-state's more affluent neighbourhoods, after a boxing workout, Channel News Asia reported.

articles.title: Malik Nabers 'looked good' in surprising full practice as Giants kick off training camp in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: The NFL season is only 6 weeks away, and Danny Parkins, Greg Jennings, and Eric Mangini discuss the biggest stories from training camp. They ask if the New York Giants are playoff contenders under Joh...
articles.body_text:
The NFL season is only 6 weeks away, and Danny Parkins, Greg Jennings, and Eric Mangini discuss the biggest stories from training camp. They ask if the New York Giants are playoff contenders under John Harbaugh, if the Denver Broncos can repeat their success from last season, and if the Detroit Lions can protect Jared Goff with their new offensive line.

New York Giants fans were enthralled to see one player in particular participating in practice on Wednesday.

Malik Nabers, who suffered a serious knee injury in Week 4 of last season, "looked good," according to his new head coach John Harbaugh, as he went through a full practice much to the delight of everyone involved with the organization.

While there is no commitment on a timeline for the 2024 first-rounder, seeing Nabers out on the field was quite the surprise for many.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers practices during NFL training camp Wednesday, July 29, 2026, in White Sulphur Springs, W.Va. (AP Photo/Chris Carlson)

Nabers’ injury wasn’t a simple knee tear, as he had to wait for swelling to go down before undergoing surgery. Then, in the spring, Nabers had to get scar tissue removed from the same knee, while eliminating stiffness he felt.

After undergoing two surgeries and remaining sidelined, Nabers' status for Week 1, or the first few weeks of the season, was up in the air.

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION PLAXICO BURRESS COMPARES PLAYING FOR JETS TO HIS TIME IN PRISON: 'A F–KING LOSER'

But general manager Joe Schoen also enjoyed seeing him running around at The Greenbrier in West Virginia to start off camp.

"We've got a really good plan for him," Schoen said. "The medical staff has a really good plan for him, and we're going to always say listen to the patients. So, we're going to see how he reacts. We got a good plan in place, so as long as everything goes as planned, we'll listen to Malik and his body. And, again, hopefully he'll be ready and we'll see how it plays out. But no predictions right now, just because we have a long way to go. Still a lot of camp."

New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers (1) catches a pass as Dallas Cowboys cornerback Kaiir Elam (20) defends in the second half of an NFL football game Sunday, Sept. 14, 2025, in Arlington, Texas. (AP Photo/Jerome Miron)

Nabers tore his ACL and suffered a full meniscus tear after jumping for a pass in quarterback Jaxson Dart’s first career start. He immediately clutched his knee, silencing the MetLife Stadium crowd as fans feared the worst while he was carted off the field.

Nabers remained in New Jersey this summer, though, working alongside the Giants’ medical team on his recovery. The injury occurring early in the season gave the team hope he would be back healthy for Week 1, and after not being put on the physically unable to perform list to start training camp, Nabers was on the right track.

"It was great. You saw him. He looked good," Harbaugh said after watching Nabers. "He's got a process going. Thought he looked good."

New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers looks on before the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sept. 21, 2025. (Vincent Carchietta/Imagn Images)

Dart, who said happy birthday to his top receiver on Instagram as Nabers turned 23, loved being able to throw to him on day one.

"He definitely has a presence about him," Dart said of Nabers. "There's an aura that he has on the field that is exhilarating. It makes me happy. It makes everybody happy just to see him out there. I think for him, he's had a lot of positives. We're just going to continue to get him in slowly. He's doing a great job with how he's attacking his recovery. I've got all the confidence in the world in him and his approach to the game, how much he's missed being out there with the guys. I think it's definitely, for him — I don't want to speak for him too much, but I just think it's a really good feeling for him to just be out there with the team and to be involved."

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Queensland MP pens ‘White Men Can Sprint’ social media post after Lachlan Kennedy takes silver in Glasgow
articles.excerpt:
LNP member Llew O’Brien says ‘there is nothing wrong with being proud of your heritage’, leading Angus Taylor to state: ‘I congratulate all Australians’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest...
articles.body_text:
LNP member Llew O’Brien says ‘there is nothing wrong with being proud of your heritage’, leading Angus Taylor to state: ‘I congratulate all Australians’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Federal Coalition MP Llew O’Brien has declared it’s “encouraging to see a White Australian” win a sprinting medal at the Commonwealth Games, after Lachlan Kennedy took silver when setting a new national record in Glasgow.

O’Brien, the member for Wide Bay in Queensland, wrote on social media on Wednesday: “White Men Can Sprint!”

“Lachlan Kennedy’s performance in the 100 metres final at the Commonwealth Games was absolutely outstanding,” the LNP MP said.

“Although he narrowly missed gold by just two hundredths of a second, his brilliant 9.85 seconds not only broke the long-standing Australian record held by sprinting great Patrick Johnson, it also announced Australia as a genuine force in world sprinting.

“It was also encouraging to see a White Australian compete at this level in one of the world’s premier sprint events.”

O’Brien went on to write that his “observation isn’t intended to diminish the extraordinary achievements of Black athletes, who have dominated elite sprinting for many years”.

“It’s simply an acknowledgement that Australians of every background can take pride in seeing someone who reflects their own heritage succeed at the highest level,” he wrote on Facebook.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, downplayed the comments from his backbencher, who has previously hosed down speculation he was considering a switch to One Nation.

Taylor, asked about O’Brien’s comments on Thursday, praised the achievements of all Australian athletes.

“I don’t care what their background is,” Taylor told reporters.

“I congratulate all Australians who are competing for Australia and doing well. We want it. We love Australians winning medals. We love Australians succeeding. We always have.”

Kennedy took silver in the 100m final behind Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme, who won the gold in a Commonwealth Games record time of 9.83 seconds. Bronze was won by Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi, who ran 9.90.

“There is nothing wrong with being proud of your heritage,” O’Brien said in his social media post.

“Whether you’re Black or White, pride in who you are is good when it doesn’t come at the expense of respect for others. Congratulations to Lachlan, and well done to every athlete who represented Australia in green and gold at the Commonwealth Games.”

O’Brien has a reputation as being somewhat of a maverick. In 2020, he moved a spill motion against then-leader and deputy prime minister Michael McCormack, in a bid to allow Barnaby Joyce to contest the leadership.

That motion failed, and O’Brien temporarily split from the Nationals party room.

O’Brien later accepted a nomination from the Labor opposition to serve as the parliament’s deputy speaker, which had been proposed in an attempt to deny the government’s endorsed candidate, the Victorian MP Damian Drum.

There had previously been speculation that O’Brien could follow Joyce and leave the Nationals to join One Nation amid the rise of Pauline Hanson’s party in Queensland and Nationals-held areas of the country.

But O’Brien said in May that he would remain a Nationals member “until I either choose to retire or when the people choose to retire me”.

articles.title: WNBA yanks Paige Bueckers, Angel Reese betting post after fans blast league hypocrisy online
articles.excerpt: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert continues to face intense scrutiny for her leadership missteps, especially surrounding Indiana Fever superstar Caitlin Clark. But despite mounting criticism, some in ...
articles.body_text:
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert continues to face intense scrutiny for her leadership missteps, especially surrounding Indiana Fever superstar Caitlin Clark. But despite mounting criticism, some in the media are rushing to shield her.

Leave it to the WNBA to turn a friendly $400 wager it promoted into a gambling controversy.

So when Paige Bueckers of the Dallas Wings and Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream sat together during All-Star Weekend and agreed to a friendly $400 wager on their upcoming matchup, nobody in the room batted an eye. It was harmless banter.

EX-FORDHAM BASKETBALL PLAYERS PERMANENTLY BANNED BY NCAA OVER ALLEGED GAME MANIPULATION BETTING SCHEME

Paige Bueckers of the Dallas Wings and Angel Reese of the Chicago Sky react during the 2025 AT&T WNBA All-Star practice sessions at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on July 18, 2025. (Getty Images)

To two young stars whose endorsement deals dwarf their league salaries, $400 is probably couch-cushion change.

Naturally, the league's social media team couldn't resist. It clipped the exchange, posted it across the WNBA's official channels and quoted Bueckers explaining the $400 bet ahead of Wednesday night's Wings-Dream matchup.

The social media team appeared to overlook Section 5(c) of the league's own Collective Bargaining Agreement.

Under Section 5(c), any player found guilty of wagering money or anything of value on the outcome, score, or aspect of a WNBA competition is subject to fines, suspensions, or outright disqualification.

In its rush to chase clicks, the league publicly showcased a wager that appeared to raise obvious questions under its own CBA.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The post disappeared quickly, but on the internet, deleting something rarely makes it disappear.

Within minutes, deleting the post only made more people want to see it.

The timing couldn't have been worse. The WNBA has spent years embracing legalized sports betting, integrating odds into broadcasts and signing lucrative sportsbook partnerships.

Paige Bueckers #5 of Team Coop reacts against Team Spoon during the second half of the 2026 AT&T WNBA All-Star Game at United Center in Chicago, Ill., on July 25, 2026. (Getty Images)

Now, Commissioner Cathy Engelbert faces an awkward predicament. Does she punish two of the league's brightest young stars over a clip her own staff promoted? Or does she look the other way and invite questions about whether the rulebook is optional?

The real misstep belonged to the league, not the players.

Plus, it's also safe to say Caitlin Clark probably wouldn't have made this kind of mistake.

Dallas Wings guard Paige Bueckers (5) drives to the basket against Atlanta Dream guard Te-Hina Paopao (2) during the second half at College Park Center on June 24, 2025. (Chris Jones-Imagn Images)

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking ...
articles.body_text:
New Victorian premier also considering ‘sensible changes’ to laws that would enshrine right to work from home two days a week

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victoria’s new premier has not ruled out redirecting billions of dollars earmarked for the controversial Suburban Rail Loop to other projects, saying he’s seeking to pursue the “greatest value for Victorians”.

Ben Carroll also used his second day in the top job to flag “sensible changes” to nation-leading laws that would enshrine the right to work from home two days a week, as he tries to distance himself from predecessors Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews.

Speaking at the Essendon tram depot on Thursday, Carroll did not dispute reports that he would order a review into the costly 90km public transport project, which would also consider whether billions of dollars worth of construction contracts already signed could be redirected.

“I’ve got no announcements to make today,” he said.

“What I can say is that every dollar of my government will be invested where it delivers the greatest value for Victorians – and it will be invested responsibly, transparently and respectfully.”

Carroll, who spoke to Anthony Albanese for the first time as premier on Wednesday, said he did not discuss with the prime minister the prospect of diverting federal funds into other projects.

Speaking on ABC News Breakfast on Thursday morning, Albanese said he would work constructively with the Victorian government “to make sure that the interests of Victorians are looked after”.

Albanese said that under the former federal Coalition government, Victoria’s share of federal infrastructure funding dropped to 8%.

“They weren’t getting their fair share,” he said.

The federal government has allocated $6bn to the SRL, which Albanese has previously described as “a gamechanger”, including  $3.8bn in May’s federal budget.

The state government has also committed about $11.8bn for the first stage of the loop, known as SRL East – a 26km stretch of tunnels between Cheltenham and Box Hill – and signed $14.5bn worth of contracts.

Two tunnel-boring machines are in the ground in Burwood, expected to begin tunnelling to Glen Waverley in four to six weeks.

The state opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has said if the Coalition is elected in November, she will pause and review the project.

Last year, however, the opposition’s transport infrastructure spokesperson, Matthew Guy, said once the “holes in the ground and the boring machines have started” it would likely have to proceed.

The SRL was first promised by Andrews ahead of the 2018 election, and has been credited with securing a number of eastern seats for Labor. Allan also championed the project, first as SRL minister and then as premier

But it has been the subject of repeated criticism in the years since, including over its origins, the veracity of its business case and the total cost.

The independent Parliamentary Budget Office released a costing on Thursday, commissioned by Libertarian MP David Limbrick, showing that cancelling the project now would improve the state’s budget position by $21bn over the decade, though the government would have to spend $1.8bn in contract termination fees.

“Nobody in my electorate is pining for a train trip from Cheltenham to Box Hill,” said Limbrick, who represents the south-east electorate where the SRL begins.

“These figures show that it is absolutely not too late for Mr Carroll to take a new direction with the SRL. Continuing it for this reason amounts to a sunk-cost fallacy,” he said.

Carroll also shifted away from another signature policy of Allan’s on Thursday by flagging “sensible changes” to her bill that legislates the right to work from home two days a week for those who can “reasonably” do so.

The bill is expected to pass the lower house by the end of today before moving to the upper house, where it will be debated during the next parliamentary sitting week beginning 11 August.

articles.title: Ted Cruz demands Fauci face jail time, labels him as America's 'most damaging bureaucrat'
articles.excerpt: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, blasts former COVID-19 adviser Anthony Fauci, backing efforts to hold him in contempt and arguing he should face jail time for misleading the American people about the virus. (...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, blasts former COVID-19 adviser Anthony Fauci, backing efforts to hold him in contempt and arguing he should face jail time for misleading the American people about the virus. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, is calling for Anthony Fauci to be held in contempt, prosecuted for perjury and sent to jail after the former White House COVID-19 adviser pled his Fifth Amendment right more than 100 times during a Senate hearing Wednesday.

"Years from now they'll look back and say, ‘What collective madness overtook this country?’" Cruz told Fox News Digital.

"I think Anthony Fauci has had contempt for Congress and contempt for the American people for decades," he said. "His diary shows that he deliberately lied to the American people over and over and over again."

FAUCI PLEADS FIFTH WITH 'ZERO LEGAL JUSTIFICATION' AS CRITICS ERUPT AND DEMAND CONTEMPT CHARGES

Anthony Fauci, the former Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and medical advisor to several U.S. presidents, testifies under subpoena about his role in the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a U.S. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 29, 2026. (REUTERS/Nathan Howard)

Cruz’s comments come after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul announced that he will seek contempt charges against Fauci after he dodged self-incrimination by refusing to answer any questions throughout the entirety of the hearing.

"Dr. Fauci ought to think about what it says about the end of his career, that what he will be remembered for the most is pleading the fifth more than 100 times," Cruz said.

"He's been the most damaging bureaucrat in the history of America."

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas., is calling for Anthony Fauci to be held in contempt and sent to jail after his Senate hearing on Wednesday, for his alleged dishonesty about COVID-19 to both Congress and the American people. (Nicholas Ballasy/Fox News Digital)

Cruz and Fauci have had a longstanding feud, similar to his relationships with other GOP senators like Paul, over Fauci’s handling of the outbreak and claims he was dishonest about the origins of COVID-19 to both Congress and the American people.

"In his diary, he wrote early on that it was clear that the COVID virus did not come from the wet market in Wuhan and then he turned around and said exactly the opposite thing on national television," Cruz said.

The released private diaries expose that Fauci considered possibilities about how the virus originated that he later downplayed to the public. He wrote that scientists considered the possibility of a deliberately inserted laboratory origin worthy of further expert review, while his later statements suggested the opposite to the public.

LEGACY MEDIA IGNORES MASSIVE ANTHONY FAUCI DOCUMENT RELEASE ALLEGING HE MISLED CONGRESS ON COVID ORIGINS

The Texas senator also accused Fauci of pushing for lockdown of schools — which Fauci wrote in his diary that he convinced both New York and California government officials to lock down their state’s school systems. This was, again, contradictory from what he said publicly, where he claimed multiple times in interviews and testified to the House Oversight Committee that he "did not close the schools."

"In his diary, he brags about convincing Democrats in New York and California to shut schools down and yet he goes on TV and says, ‘Oh, I wasn't for shutdowns,’" Cruz said.

"The school shutdowns, which Fauci bragged that he was responsible for, may well be the single most destructive public policy step we've seen in decades. That learning loss will stick with those kids the rest of their lives when they're 90 years old."

He continued, "They will still be suffering the consequences of Anthony Fauci's corrupt and dishonest shutdowns."

"The fact that he knew he was lying to the American people — he should be held in contempt, he should be prosecuted for perjury and he should go to jail."

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.
