Katie Lee Biegel addressed ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Billy Joel's ex-wife has called out Chevy Chase for being "not-so-nice" during an old-school keg party.

Katie Lee Biegel addressed the incident on a recent episode of her podcast, "All on the Table." She explained that the incident with Chase happened while she was married to Joel. The former couple tied the knot in 2004 before divorcing in 2009.

"My celebrity run-in that was not so nice was Chevy Chase," Biegel began.

Billy Joel's ex-wife, Katie Lee Biegel, claimed Chevy Chase wasn't "nice" to her on a recent podcast episode. (Getty Images)

"So, I was having a party with my ex-husband. It was a keg party. I wanted to have like an old-school keg party. We had a house that we were going to tear down. And it was like this little — we called it ‘The Sugar Shack,’ and had a very fun summer there, staying with friends," Biegel said.

JOEL MCHALE DISLOCATED CHEVY CHASE'S SHOULDER WHILE FILMING 'COMMUNITY'

She continued, "But then at the end of the summer, we decided to have a kind of like, ‘Tear the House Down' party, a keg party, and I had jello shots, kegs. It was a very star-studded party."

Chevy Chase reportedly mistook Biegel for a member of the party staff. (Gerardo Mora)

Biegel went on to explain the moment Chase mistook her for a member of the staff and "shooed" her away.

"And my ex-husband was standing talking to Chevy Chase and his wife. And I had a tray of jello shots. And I went up with the tray of jello shots and said, you know, ‘Do you guys want a shot?’ and Chevy thought that I was the staff at the party, and he took his hand and shooed me away," she said.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He just did this," she said, making a shooing motion with her hand.

Billy Joel and Katie Lee Biegel were married from 2004 until 2009. (WireImage)

Chase has long had a reputation in Hollywood for being difficult to work with, with multiple former co-stars and collaborators alleging abrasive, confrontational and inappropriate behavior over the years.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

His most public controversies stem from his time on "Community," where he clashed with creator Dan Harmon and several cast members before leaving the show in 2012 after reportedly using racially insensitive language on set.

Chevy Chase has long had a reputation for being difficult. (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images; Photo by Gerardo Mora/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to Chase for comment.

Janelle Ash is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital covering Hollywood, celebrity culture and breaking entertainment news through exclusive reporting, interviews and in-depth storytelling.

articles.title: Lindsey Graham funeral service under way, with Trump expected to deliver eulogy – live
articles.excerpt:
The Republican senator died earlier this month; his funeral is expected to be attended by members of Congress as well as Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy

Donald Trump’s motorcade has left t...
articles.body_text:
The Republican senator died earlier this month; his funeral is expected to be attended by members of Congress as well as Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy

Donald Trump’s motorcade has left the White House and is en route to the funeral service for Lindsey Graham at Washington National Cathedral. The president is due to deliver a eulogy at 2pm ET.

With Lindsey Graham’s funeral now underway, here is Guardian reporter Aram Roston’s dispatch from just a few moments earlier: 
 I’m outside the National Cathedral where the Lindsay Graham funeral is to take place. It’s a very quiet scene with few people around. Wisconsin Avenue is completely closed to traffic. there’s about two dozen metropolitan police cars and an extensive Secret Service presence. This is obviously being considered a very high profile security threat and they’ve locked it down. They are searching the buses bringing guests.

There very few protesters. At edge of the security site, a handful of local residents are waving an American flag, a Ukrainian flag and a NATO flag. One woman was wearing a “childless cat ladies against fascism” T-shirt said she doesn’t remember security anywhere near as extensive as this at previous funerals. “This is insane. We’ve never seen it like this,” she said.

Another said: “We’re here in support of democracy.”

At the north end of the security fence, about a dozen silent protesters held Palestinian flags. One of the protesters, who gave her first name as Sumer, said they were at the funeral because “[Benjamin] Netanyahu should not be here.” Graham, she said was a war criminal because of his support of Israel’s operations. “He’s not someone who deserves an honorary funeral,” she added.

The funeral service for Lindsey Graham is now underway at the Washington National Catheral.

In attendance are several high profile White House officials including Donald Trump, JD Vance, defense secretary Pete Hegseth, treasury secretary Scott Bessent, interior secretary Doug Burgum, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, among others.

Donald Trump’s motorcade has left the White House and is en route to the funeral service for Lindsey Graham at Washington National Cathedral. The president is due to deliver a eulogy at 2pm ET.

Kentucky’s governor Andy Beshear yesterday called on ailing GOP senator Mitch McConnell to either “directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky” with “proof of your capacity to serve” in the Senate or to resign from Congress.

McConnell, 84, continues to recover at home from a fall that left him hospitalized over a month ago. According to a statement from his office yesterday, McConnell said he’s “still working hard to get back to my full schedule of work in the Senate and in Kentucky.” A note from the attending physician said he had undergone “strenuous” physical therapy and rehabilitation, but added: “He is not yet medically cleared to leave the rehab facility and return to the office.”

“It has now been 43 days since news of your hospitalization,” Beshear wrote in a letter addressed to McConnell and his staff. “During that time you have cast zero votes, engaged in no official activities, and aside from two photos and corresponding statements, have made no effort to communicate with your Kentucky constituents or the nation.”

“I understand anyone’s desire for privacy, but when you run for office and serve as one of a state’s two US senators, you willingly abdicate much of your personal privacy,” he went on. “That’s the deal, and we all know it when we run.”

Beshear added: “President Trump is stuck in a war of his own making and has greatly strengthened the very country he claims is a threat. Prices continue to rise, crushing Americans who are working hard but not getting ahead. Americans’ voting rights are being eliminated by the Supreme Court and threatened by congressional action. All while you are absent and refuse to communicate clearly and directly to the people you serve.”

double quotation markAs Governor of the state you serve, I am calling on you to directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.

The governor noted that a Senate vacancy occurs when a senator dies, resigns or is expelled by a vote in the upper chamber.

Beshear said he was also writing to Senate majority leader John Thune to urge him to investigate McConnell’s condition “if you are unwilling to voluntarily show that you still have the capacity to serve”. “If Senator McConnell is unwilling to voluntarily show that he still has the capacity to serve, I will insist that you as the Majority Leader of the Senate fully investigate his condition, report to the American people, and begin the process if warranted,” he wrote to Thune.

“All of this speculation and even this letter could have been avoided with a minimal amount of transparency,” Beshear wrote to McConnell. “Kentuckians are just asking you to be honest.”

McConnell is due to retire when his terms ends in January.

Trump’s closed-door meeting with Netanyahu has now ended. It lasted nearly an hour and a half and was “positive and productive”, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on X. We’ll bring you any more details as we get them.

As we’ve been reporting, Benjamin Netanyahu arrived to the White House today to meet with Donald Trump for the first time since they launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February, with the Israeli PM reportedly anxious to smooth out strains in their relationship.

It comes as both face growing pressures at home. Netanyahu, who is up for a tough re-election fight, is embattled in part because of his deteriorating relationship with Trump and his want to carry on fighting against Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon, which left him sidelined as Trump sought a deal with Tehran. Indeed, the US president is under pressure to end an unpopular war that has wreaked economic havoc and driven up prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Trump revealed some tension with Netanyahu ahead of their meeting this morning, complaining about reports that the Israeli leader plans to discuss intelligence on Iranian activities at Pickaxe Mountain, a potential nuclear site that Trump has threatened repeatedly to bomb.

“I know exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe,” Trump told Fox and Friends. He insisted that whatever Iran is doing is “not a big problem” and that “Bibi’s telling me that because he wants me to stay involved”.

“Why do you have to announce to the world?” Trump added, signaling his frustrations with his ally.

Near the White House where the public was able to gather near fencing, protesters chanted, “Netanyahu, you’re a tyrant” and “Bibi, you’re not welcome here.”

The two leaders also planned to discuss the framework agreement the US and Israel signed with Lebanon over the Israel-Hezbollah war and the expansion of the Abraham Accords, a White House official told the Associated Press.

“We have a little difference,” Trump said yesterday when asked by reporters if he and Netanyahu were on the same page on Iran. “But pretty close, yeah.”

But even as Netanyahu sees an opportunity, he also needs to persuade Trump that he won’t play spoiler to US diplomatic and reconstruction efforts in Gaza and in Lebanon, where the president has previously complained that “too many people are being killed” by Israeli strikes.

It all comes as Israel has lost a significant amount of bipartisan support in the United States, particularly over its conduct in Gaza where it stands accused of committing genocide.

In June, US vice-president JD Vance warned Israeli officials that Trump was their only friend among world leaders. Vance is expected to be in attendance at the meeting with Netanyahu, a person familiar with the plan told the Associated Press.

An AP-NORC poll published earlier this month found a dramatic erosion of support among American adults for Israel.

For more on that, my colleague Matthew Cassel traveled to New York City – the heart of Jewish-American life – to explore how Israel’s wars across multiple fronts has seen so many American Jews turn away from Israel.

And now we have this statement from the Ukrainian president on his meeting with Trump and a tribute to Lindsey Graham, whom he called “a true friend of Ukraine”.

double quotation markA good meeting with President Trump @POTUS at the Oval Office. Thank you for everything we do together to protect the lives of Ukrainians and advance peace. First and foremost, I offered President Trump our condolences on the passing of Lindsey Graham. He was a true friend of Ukraine. The President and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help. We also spoke about diplomacy – it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated. Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has now left the White House after his meeting with Trump, and Benjamin Netanyahu arrived about 15 minutes later.

The ceremony was the first of two major Washington services today for Lindsey Graham, who died on 9 July.

Donald Trump is expected to deliver a tribute to the late senator at a 2pm ET funeral at Washington National Cathedral.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy are also due to attend, reflecting Graham’s role as one of Washington’s most outspoken advocates for both countries.

The two leaders scheduled separate White House meetings with Trump during visits that coincided with pivotal moments in the wars involving Iran and Ukraine.

Zelensky was also due to meet senators later today ahead of a preliminary vote on tougher sanctions against Russia, legislation Graham had worked on for more than a year before his sudden death.

Graham was one of Congress’s most consistent advocates of an assertive US military role abroad, supporting intervention against Iran and strong backing for Israel and Ukraine.

As reported earlier, Trump acknowledged that reputation this morning, telling Fox News that Graham was “very strong on the military”.

double quotation markLindsey liked war. He’s never seen a war that he didn’t like.

Vice-president JD Vance also delivered remarks, telling mourners that Lindsey Graham was an affable, gregarious politician who would slap Senate colleagues on the back and had a passion for engaging opponents in “swashbuckling” debate.

“Lindsey Graham loved people from all walks of life,” said Vance, who served two years in the Senate. “I think in part because of the way that he grew up, because the fact that he wasn’t handed everything, he was fascinated in everybody.”

He also credited Graham with the successful confirmation of Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court. “I believe that he saved that nomination,” Vance said.

Vance said he remembered Graham as someone “who could disagree with you without being disagreeable”.

double quotation markI choose to remember Lindsey Graham as a person who could fight with you on one issue, but fight for you on another issue. I remember Lindsey Graham as a man who loved people, and because he loved people, he was willing to reason with them, to respect them and ultimately to persuade them.

Speaking at the brief ceremony in the Capitol rotunda, Senate majority leader John Thune credited the late Lindsey Graham for his leadership on foreign affairs, calling him “a towering figure” in Congress and on the international stage.

He called the late senator a “fierce defender of Ukraine” and hailed him “as a powerful voice for the [anti-abortion] movement” and lauding his efforts to pass tax cut legislation.

“I look forward to the days when you make us all laugh again,” Thune said, visibly emotional as he concluded his tribute.

Lindsey Graham’s casket was brought into the Capitol rotunda short while ago by military service members as the two days of ceremonies and funeral services began at 10am ET.

Trump’s meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is under way. We’ll be looking out for a sense of US support for Ukraine and signs of changed posture from the Trump administration on Ukraine-Russia.

articles.title: Anthony Fauci diary entries set social media ablaze as critics mock, condemn behavior
articles.excerpt:
Laura Ingraham criticizes Dr. Anthony Fauci, suggesting his refusal to be questioned stems from insecurity.

Once-private diary entries written by Dr. Anthony Fauci have set social media ablaze with c...
articles.body_text:
Laura Ingraham criticizes Dr. Anthony Fauci, suggesting his refusal to be questioned stems from insecurity.

Once-private diary entries written by Dr. Anthony Fauci have set social media ablaze with critics mocking the former White House COVID advisor’s fixation on emerging from the global pandemic as a celebrity and condemning his behavior.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, while detailing his media appearances and personal observations.

While much of the mainstream media initially ignored the shocking diary entries, there was no shortage of backlash on X. Outkick founder Clay Travis urged his followers to read the diary, calling Fauci "one of the true villains of American history."

ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN AND MS NOW IGNORE FAUCI DIARY ENTRIES THAT REVEAL FIXATION ON FAME DURING COVID

Diary entries written by Dr. Anthony Fauci shocked social media over the weekend.  (Getty Images)

Grabien Media founder Tom Elliott, who spent hours digging into the diary, found that the word "award" was mentioned 80 times, "hero" appeared 49 times, "press" appeared a staggering 641 times and Fauci never wrote anything about "peer review," "meta-analysis," "risk-benefit," "learning loss" or "mental health."

Dana Loesch was stunned, calling the diary "one of the most infuriating things I’ve ever read."

Piers Morgan added, "These diaries are very damning. Fauci comes across as a fame-hungry narcissist who regularly said different things in private about Covid to what he told the world publicly."

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Dr. Anthony Fauci wrote about newfound fame and celebrity status that he found during the COVID pandemic.  (CBS)

Others put a spotlight on Fauci's apparent love for the TV camera.

XX-XY founder Jennifer Sey unearthed an old Politico appearance in which Fauci simply read flattering tweets about himself.

"Hard hitting stuff here," Sey snarked. "Could you kiss his butt anymore?"

FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES

CNN anchor Jake Tapper became fast friends with Dr. Anthony Fauci during the COVID pandemic, according to the former White House COVID advisor's diary.  (Scott Kowalchyk/CBS via Getty Images)

Many comments were focused on Fauci's relationship with CNN anchor Jake Tapper, who appeared to be the doctor's closest media ally.

The diary release came days before Fauci is scheduled to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Paul, who also took to X to lampoon the diary. The senator shared an AI-generated image of Fauci sitting on a bed while writing in a diary. In the background are posters and toys in a humorous attempt to suggest the doctor was like a self-obsessed teenager. Next to the image, Paul wrote: "What Anthony Fauci looked like every night when he wrote about how great he is in his diary."

Fox News Digital reached out to Dr. Fauci and CNN for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News Digital’s Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

Brian Flood is a media editor/reporter for FOX News Digital. Story tips can be sent to brian.flood@fox.com and on Twitter: @briansflood.

articles.title: Uganda declares end to Ebola outbreak
articles.excerpt:
Authorities in Uganda have declared the country free of Ebola, as infections from the viral haemorrhagic disease continue to surge in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Ugandan Heal...
articles.body_text:
Authorities in Uganda have declared the country free of Ebola, as infections from the viral haemorrhagic disease continue to surge in neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Ugandan Health ⁠Minister Chris Baryomunsi on Tuesday announced the “successful completion ⁠of the mandatory 42-day monitoring period which begun after the discharge of the last Ugandan national, a locally transmitted patient, on the 16 of June, 2026”.

“Throughout this ⁠period the Ministry of Health maintained intensive surveillance nationwide, and no new Ebola cases have been detected,” Baryomunsi said.

In a later statement on social media, Baryomunsi urged Ugandans “to remain alert” and continue observing public health measures.

Of the 20 confirmed ⁠cases, 18 were discharged while two died from the viral haemorrhagic disease, both of whom ⁠were from the DRC, where a much larger outbreak has been under way since mid-May.

According to the Congolese Ministry of Health, there have been at least 3,262 infections in the DRC, with 1,437 people killed. This is nearly the same as the 2018-2020 outbreak that is the largest ever recorded in the country.

The World Health Organization says the latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest spreading ever recorded, and that its true scale could be two to four times larger than reported data.

The virus strain spreading in the DRC is Bundibugyo, which is the rarest of the four variants of Ebola known to affect humans and currently has no approved vaccines or treatments.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic disease that can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and internal bleeding. It spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of people who are sick with the virus or who have died from it.

articles.title: Patriots receiver Mack Hollins’ barefoot escapades reach a new plateau in second New England season
articles.excerpt:
New England Patriots Super Bowl hero spoke to Fox News Digital about the dietary rules he followed as he got later into his NFL career.

Mack Hollins has turned the proverbial corner as a New England ...
articles.body_text:
New England Patriots Super Bowl hero spoke to Fox News Digital about the dietary rules he followed as he got later into his NFL career.

Mack Hollins has turned the proverbial corner as a New England Patriots wide receiver, but not in the ordinary way one might think, like his speed is improved or he reads defenders better now. This is more about his feet.

Hollins reports that in his second year on the Patriots roster, his life habit of walking everywhere in his bare feet has gained acceptance locally. He knows this because restaurants are welcoming him in and allowing him to dine – sans shoes.

MACK HOLLINS ENTERS STADIUM WITH NO SHOES OR SHIRT

New England Patriots wide receiver Mack Hollins (13) runs with the ball against Cleveland Browns cornerback Denzel Ward (21) during the fourth quarter at Gillette Stadium on Oct. 26, 2025. (Brian Fluharty/Imagn Images)

"I love it," Hollins told reporters at Patriots training camp during an interview session conducted barefoot. "It's really great because now they're kind of letting me slide being barefoot in restaurants and stuff because they know who I am.

"At first, it was like, some homeless guy coming in here, but now it's like the mechanic homeless guy so it's all right. So yeah, it's been great."

If you're pretty much disgusted by somebody else's bare feet on display anywhere but a beach, you're not going to be a fan. If you're thinking this is an attention-seeking move, well, maybe. Hollins has been known to stand out and not shy from attention.

ROB GRONKOWSKI OFFERS ADVICE FOR PATRIOTS TO SILENCE NOISE AROUND MIKE VRABEL CONTROVERSY AHEAD OF 2026 SEASON

Mack Hollins (13) of the New England Patriots arrives prior to Super Bowl LX against the Seattle Seahawks at Levi's Stadium on Feb. 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Kathryn Riley/Getty Images)

But if you're a Patriots' fan and watched last season when Hollins unexpectedly started 13 regular-season games and two postseason games, and scored the team's only touchdown on a 35-yard reception in the Super Bowl LX, you might be more accepting of the guy's eccentricities.

He doesn't, for example, use forks or spoons or chopsticks or any other eating utensils. He uses his hands to eat because, he says, it helps him correctly gauge the temperature of the food which prepares his mouth for what's coming.

So, these New England restaurants are showing love to the barefoot guy who eats with his hands.

"Every team I've been on, you ask them who's the weirdest guy they're going to say Mack," Hollins once admitted.

New England Patriots offensive tackle Will Campbell (66) and wide receiver Mack Hollins (13) walk to the practice fields for training camp at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, on July 23, 2025. (Eric Canha/Imagn Images)

"Yeah, yeah, it's not like a bad weird," Hollins said.

It's weird like Hollins showing up to NFL games in Buffalo's frigid temperatures shirtless. Also barefoot, of course, despite the ice and snow on the ground.

It's weird like him arriving to the 2025 AFC Championship game between the Bills and Kansas City Chiefs wearing an Animal Muppet character — you know, the red thing that plays drums — mask.

All that aside, shoeless Mack Hollins is gaining traction in New England. And he has an explanation why he prefers to do without footgear when he's not actually in a game.

"I think shoes are a tool and people have made them a part of their body," Hollins once said. "I wouldn't walk around with a hammer just because I might need a hammer sometimes."

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Lindsey Graham ‘almost cried’ tears of joy over war on Iran, footage shows
articles.excerpt: Senator Lindsey Graham credited himself with persuading United States President Donald Trump to join Israel in going to war against Iran, “almost cried” with joy when the conflict began, and offered t...
articles.body_text:
Senator Lindsey Graham credited himself with persuading United States President Donald Trump to join Israel in going to war against Iran, “almost cried” with joy when the conflict began, and offered to lobby Trump on behalf of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to attack Lebanon too, newly released footage has shown.

Graham, who died on July 11 aged 71, was a close confidant of Trump and Netanyahu, both of whom are attending his funeral on Tuesday.

British filmmaker Alex Holder and his team, who were granted extraordinary access to shadow the hawkish Republican senator over the past three years for a planned documentary, gave the Wall Street Journal some recent excerpts from more than 400 hours of footage they had accumulated.

One excerpt shows Graham chatting with the documentary crew shortly after watching Trump on television answering questions from reporters on March 3 for the first time since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, which killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and started the war.

Graham, laughing and clearly delighted, exclaimed: “How long have we been pushing this?”

“Look what we’ve done here. I almost cried,” Graham said. “I talked to Trump this morning. Oh, he’s jacked! He said ‘best thing I’ve ever done’. He loves blowing stuff up.”

Graham said he had successfully persuaded Trump to launch the war despite many people in the president’s circle being opposed to it, and compared the alliance of Trump and Netanyahu to the World War II partnership of President Franklin D Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill.

“So, you know, there are a lot of people inside [who] didn’t want to do it, so I’ve had my challenges. But President Trump, when he gets into the zone, he listens, he asks good questions, you know, no tweeting,” Graham said.

“He hasn’t tweeted much at all. No drama. He’s been a great wartime president,” Graham continued. “I said last night that Trump and Bibi are like Roosevelt and Churchill. I mean, they’re the right two guys to confront this evil.”

Another section of the footage shows part of a telephone conversation between Graham and Netanyahu on March 4, two days after Hezbollah resumed rocket attacks on Israel in support of Iran.

“Hey Bibi, Lindsey,” Graham began, using Netanyahu’s nickname.

“I’m just so impressed, glad to be your friend,” he continued, in his distinctive South Carolina drawl.

“Glad you are my friend,” Netanyahu replied.

Graham told Netanyahu he planned to try to persuade Trump to join Israel in bombing Hezbollah targets in Lebanon: “I’m going to meet with the president this weekend … I’m gonna try to get him to join with y’all in Lebanon, to maybe fly some with you, would you like that?”

“I think you have a point,” Netanyahu said, before telling Graham to hold off.

“We’re concentrating right now on Iran,” Netanyahu said. “If we tell Hezbollah that we’re going all the way, we threaten them, but if we actually do it, then they have no reason not to go all the way against us. And right now, that’s not our interest. We can do it later.”

The Wall Street Journal said some of the footage showed Graham’s occasional frustration with Trump.

In the final interview for the documentary, at a bagel shop in Columbia, South Carolina, in June, Graham was concerned about the preliminary ceasefire agreement Trump had signed with Iran, according to the newspaper.

“He’s letting this thing slip away,” Graham said. “I got to go talk to him.”

articles.title: Joe Biden appears to discuss sensitive information on tape with ghostwriter
articles.excerpt:
In recordings made in 2016 and 2017 former president also appears to describe possessing classified information

Former US president Joe Biden appeared to discuss sensitive information and describe po...
articles.body_text:
In recordings made in 2016 and 2017 former president also appears to describe possessing classified information

Former US president Joe Biden appeared to discuss sensitive information and describe possessing classified documents in audio recordings released on Monday by the Oversight Project, a conservative activist group.

The heavily redacted transcripts and recordings were made in 2016 and 2017, while Biden was working with a ghostwriter on his 2017 memoir, Promise Me, Dad: A Year of Hope, Hardship, and Purpose. No classified material was ever alleged to have appeared in the book.

Biden, at times, seems to struggle to remember certain details or dates regarding events and topics in the transcripts and recordings, prompting the Oversight Project – as well as some conservative media outlets – to allege that he was “already demonstrating significant cognitive decline” in the years before he ran for president.

In a recording dated October 2016, near the end of Biden’s second term as vice- president under former president Barack Obama, Biden can be heard discussing notes he says he kept from his time in office.

“There was a lot of stuff going on at the same time in foreign policy,” Biden said. “You didn’t want to go into it, but I have extensive notes … over this period of time.”

“Oh, that’s in – oh, you actually have those here,” the writer responds. To which Biden says, “yeah, now, there’s a lot of other notes too”, and goes on to say: “These – this is my – they didn’t even know I had this.”

“Some of this stuff, I’m not, you know, going to – um so I go back, you know what I mean?” Biden continues. “I have stuff on, you know, five – here we go, I mean, it’s like … I have stuff on all the way up to 5/19.”

A representative for Biden didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on Tuesday about the recordings. But a spokesperson for Biden told CBS News: “President Biden’s conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way.”

“Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DoJ for political retribution,” they added. “It’s wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today’s decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy.”

Classified materials were also found at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club after he left office following his first term. In 2024, a federal judge dismissed the case, ruling that the special counsel who brought the prosecution had been improperly appointed.

The tapes of Biden appear to align with the findings in former special counsel Robert Hur’s 2024 report on his handling of classified documents. That report concluded that Biden had “willfully” kept and shared classified information “after his vice presidency when he was a private citizen” including “classified documents about military and foreign policy in Afghanistan” and handwritten notes about national security and foreign policy “implicating sensitive intelligence sources and methods”.

The report also stated that Biden, during his eight years as vice-president, “regularly wrote notes by hand in notebooks” and that some of those notes “related to classified subjects” and that “some of the notes are themselves classified”.

It also said that Biden “shared information, including some classified information, from those notebooks with his ghostwriter”.

Hur described Biden as a “sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory”, prompting a furious response from the then president and his officials, and claimed that Biden’s “memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017, and in his interview with our office in 2023”.

But Hur ultimately determined that no criminal charges were warranted, in part because he said it would be hard to convince a jury that “a former president well into his 80s” was guilty of a felony that “requires a mental state of willfulness”.

The Oversight Project, a branch of the Heritage Foundation, sued for the tapes, which had been handed over to the justice department during its investigation into Biden’s handling of the records. House judiciary committee Republicans also sought the tapes. Biden had fought the release, but recently withdrew his legal challenge after a federal appeals court rejected his effort.

In another recording dated 3 November 2016, Biden tells the writer: “And, and then – and then the next thing I have here is – this is classified. It’s all – it goes through the 17th.” The context of this clip is not clear.

In a separate recording dated 16 February 2017, about a month after Biden left office, Biden tells the ghostwriter: “After that diary entry, the next one, between that and the 7th of July” was a “was a long meeting on the Security Council on – and part of it’s classified”.

Later in that recording, Biden says: “So this was – I, early on, in ’09 – I just found all of the classified stuff downstairs. I wrote the President a handwritten 40-page memorandum arguing against deploying additional troops to Iraq – I mean, to Afghanistan – on the grounds that it wouldn’t matter, that the day we left would be like the day before we arrived.”

In a statement on Monday, the Oversight Project said that since 2024, it and the Heritage Foundation “fought tooth and nail to bring these tapes to light”.

articles.title: What a fourth-generation fishing captain has learned from nearly 100 years on the Gulf
articles.excerpt: Marine Veteran Matt Moore, owner of Hellbender Outfitters, builds custom fishing rods for Gold Star families and veterans in Eastern Tennessee. Moore shares his personal journey, revealing how nature ...
articles.body_text:
Marine Veteran Matt Moore, owner of Hellbender Outfitters, builds custom fishing rods for Gold Star families and veterans in Eastern Tennessee. Moore shares his personal journey, revealing how nature provided healing after military service. He emphasizes the importance of passing down durable fishing rods that tell a story, connecting individuals with the outdoors to support mental well-being and honor fallen heroes' families.

For Dylan Hubbard, fishing is the easy part.

The harder part is carrying nearly 100 years of family history on his shoulders while figuring out how to keep the operation alive through hurricanes, federal regulators and a rapidly changing Florida tourism industry.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

Hubbard is the fourth generation of his family to run Hubbard's Marina in Madeira Beach, Fla. The business traces its roots to 1928, when his grandfather started with five rowboats and 40 cane poles.

Today, John's Pass in Madeira Beach is a popular tourist destination for water recreation, shopping and dining. (Photo courtesy of Dylan Hubbard / Hubbard's Marina)

Today, Hubbard is vice president of the company and has begun the process of purchasing it from his father. But stepping into the family business was never as simple as inheriting a title.

"Oh, you have no idea," Hubbard told OutKick Outdoors when asked whether he had to earn his place before calling himself captain.

His grandfather, Wilson, originally ran the operation before leaving to serve during World War II. Hubbard's great-grandfather stepped in during that time, which is why the family considers it a fourth-generation business. His father later purchased the company from the family in 2004. Now, Dylan is preparing to carry it forward.

"It's also really cool to have that layer of: it's a family business. I'm fourth generation," Hubbard said. "Not only am I working, but also it's that legacy. So it's just an added layer of maybe responsibility or honor or blessing — whatever you want to call it — that really makes it even that much more special."

Watch Dylan Hubbard's full interview with OutKick Outdoors here:

That responsibility means knowing when to hold onto tradition and when to embrace change.

Hubbard's Marina began in Pass-a-Grille, back when Florida's barrier islands looked very different. But as new bridges changed traffic patterns and Pass-a-Grille became increasingly residential, Hubbard's grandfather recognized that the business needed a new home. Even though he was nearing 70 years old, he uprooted the operation and moved it north to John's Pass.

"He saw the writing on the wall," Hubbard said.

Captain Wilson Hubbard (Dylan's grandfather) circa 1960. (Photo courtesy of Dylan Hubbard / Hubbard's Marina)

It was the kind of decision that probably felt risky at the time but proved essential in the decades that followed. John's Pass eventually developed into a major tourism destination, and Hubbard's grandfather also worked with the city to establish the boardwalk that now runs through the area.

That willingness to adapt has remained necessary — especially when nature delivered its worst, twice in less than two weeks.

In September 2024, Hurricane Helene brought nine feet of water into Hubbard's Marina. The main office was completely submerged, the main dock was destroyed, and the business lost infrastructure, inventory and equipment. Before the water had even fully receded, Hurricane Milton was bearing down as a Category 5, forcing the family to brace for a second direct hit while still standing in the wreckage of the first.

"It was pretty numbing," Hubbard said, "just a wild situation to go through."

Still, the boats survived. More importantly, so did the people.

Before official rescue crews could even reach the barrier islands, Hubbard and several crew members set out before daylight to assess the damage at John's Pass. What began as a trip to inspect the business quickly became something else entirely.

"We were the first boat out there," Hubbard said. "No one was out there — no fire, no EMS, no emergency folks. It was just us."

President Joe Biden walks with Pinellas County Emergency Director Cathie Perkins and Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Deanne Criswell during a tour of Hurricane Milton damage in St. Pete Beach, Fla., on Oct. 13, 2024. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

As they navigated through the damaged area, residents stood along seawalls crying, waving and begging for help. Some had stayed behind during the storm, become trapped, and then emerged to find they had lost everything.

"So what was supposed to be a search and find out what we needed to do and what got damaged turned into a rescue mission," Hubbard said.

Other members of the fishing community soon joined in, deploying their own boats to move people and supplies to and from the barrier islands — even as police tried, unsuccessfully, to keep boaters off the water given the debris and damage.

"We were essentially pirates for a week," he said.

For Hubbard, reopening quickly was never primarily about preserving the business's reputation or getting tourists back on boats. It was about his employees. At the time, the company had 84 staff members. Fifteen had lost everything in the storm.

"If I had just sat there and waited and not got to work, those people would not only have lost their homes and their vehicles and everything they owned, they would have also lost their jobs and not had income," Hubbard said. "So to me, it was imperative to open up as quickly as humanly possible."

The team rebuilt the dock in two days and had trips running again five days after Helene — faster than the barrier islands themselves officially reopened. The community later raised nearly $75,000 to help affected staff members.

In the year that followed, Hubbard's kept growing rather than pulling back: the company acquired a pirate ship, a dolphin tour boat and a shark tour operation in November 2025, adding to a portfolio that already includes a seafood market, a fuel dock and a boat-building operation. A new ghost tour just launched, and a Tampa Bay ferry service is next.

Capt. Hubbard may prefer being offshore, but much of his job now happens behind a desk, in meetings, or fighting battles that never make it onto a dock report.

Hubbard is heavily involved in fisheries management, serving as president of the Florida Guides Association and sitting on Gulf Council advisory panels covering reef fish, data collection and outreach.

A few years ago, that involvement got personal. After Hubbard publicly criticized weak enforcement against illegal charter operations at a federal meeting, NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement took a closer look at his own business — and told him the way Hubbard's Marina operated was against federal regulation.

It took him roughly 85 days to get the regulation itself changed, preserving his business model in the process.

"If you're not in the room, you're on the menu," Hubbard said of why he keeps showing up to meetings most people would find, in his words, "mind-numbing and boring."

CHARTER CAPTAIN JONATHAN MOSS EXPLAINS HOW TO GET KIDS HOOKED ON FISHING FROM AN EARLY AGE

It's not the only wild thing nearly 100 years on the Gulf has produced. Ask Hubbard for his strangest moment on the water and the answer comes without hesitation: "We've found dead bodies. We've come across boats on fire. We've saved people." His grandfather ran across great white sharks; his father, orcas; Hubbard himself has crossed paths with pilot whales, a right whale and one of the largest leatherback turtles he's ever seen.

"People always ask me, 'Do you still get to go fishing?'" Hubbard said. "I do, and I make time for it, and I definitely get out on the water as much as I can."

But he also understands that spending all his time fishing wouldn't necessarily serve the larger operation.

"If I spent my time offshore, that's definitely where I would rather be and enjoy a lot more," he said. "But I definitely wouldn't be in the position we are today if I did that all the time."

Captain Dylan Hubbard shows off his catches of the day. (Photo courtesy of Dylan Hubbard / Hubbard's Marina)

Hubbard hopes his grandfather would approve of where the family business stands today.

"I hope he would be happy," Hubbard said.

The pirate ship, the ferry, the federal meetings — none of that existed when Wilson Hubbard started with five rowboats. But the motto he built the business on hasn't changed.

"If you're too busy to go fishing, you're just too darn busy."

Love all things fishing and outdoors? Follow OutKick Outdoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: ESPN’s favorite insider accidentally explained why most Americans don’t trust the media
articles.excerpt:
Dan Zaksheske believes that Ryan Calrk became too much of a headache for ESPN to retain during layoffs.

"Write what you know, not what you think."

Andrew Marchand offered that lesson to other report...
articles.body_text:
Dan Zaksheske believes that Ryan Calrk became too much of a headache for ESPN to retain during layoffs.

"Write what you know, not what you think."

Andrew Marchand offered that lesson to other reporters while discussing ESPN’s decision to part ways with NFL analyst Ryan Clark. The sports-media columnist for The Athletic, a New York Times-owned outlet, was responding to what he described as inaccurate opinions circulating online about Clark’s dismissal.

He thought he was explaining the difference between responsible journalism and uninformed speculation. Instead, Marchand accidentally explained why so many Americans distrust the press.

ESPN PARTING WAYS WITH NFL ANALYST RYAN CLARK AHEAD OF NETWORK'S FIRST SUPER BOWL BROADCAST

To be clear, his advice was perfectly sound. The problem came when Marchand revealed what he knew, how long he had known it and why he had not told his readers.

Andrew Marchand's defense of withholding the Ryan Clark story accidentally exposed how access journalism lets powerful people control the news cycle. (Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

On his own podcast, Marchand claimed he had anticipated Clark’s departure since February. He went so far as to assert that he had "a story prepared in February" and received a "very strong indication" roughly one week before ESPN let Clark go.

"Like others, you want to allow ESPN to tell him first," Marchand explained. He said he eventually reported that Clark was expected to be dismissed because the scoop became "competitive."

In other words, Marchand says he knew ESPN was preparing to part ways with Clark but he withheld the information while ESPN followed its preferred timetable. Then another outlet threatened to make the information public, and he published.

Marchand apparently believed that account enhanced his reputation as a responsible journalist.

It actually exposed the access-journalism game.

Before going further, it's important to make clear that the point is not Marchand personally, or who published one Ryan Clark story first.

Legendary sports radio host Dan Patrick recently brought up another situation that exposed why access-journalism serves the people involved, but often not the public at large.

Dan Patrick questioned whether modern insider reporting serves the public or simply lets powerful institutions decide when news can be released. (Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)

After the San Francisco 49ers disclosed that head coach Kyle Shanahan had suffered serious injuries in a car accident 11 days earlier, ESPN’s Adam Schefter posted the news one minute later. ESPN quickly followed with a detailed report.

Patrick wondered whether ESPN and Schefter already knew what had happened but waited until the 49ers authorized its release.

"This isn’t journalism. Not really reporting," Patrick said. "They’re giving you the information" and then effectively saying, "Okay, now you can tell everybody."

Patrick didn't prove ESPN had been sitting on the story. But he identified the central problem with the modern insider economy: What is the public value of privately knowing something if the institution involved decides when the public may know it?

That's not journalism. It's public relations.

And while we don't know exactly what happened between Schefter, Kyle Shanahan, ESPN, the NFL and the San Francisco 49ers, we do know exactly how the Marchand-Clark situation played out and it illustrates Patrick's point.

As I detailed last week, my colleague Bobby Burack and I developed separate lines of reporting that ESPN was preparing to part ways with Clark. Four sources in total confirmed the information.

We contacted ESPN at 4 p.m. ET on Monday and gave the network until 5 to respond. ESPN asked us to delay publication until 5:45 while it was "trying to chase this down." We declined but offered to add anything the network provided.

Clark then disappeared from "NFL Live," ESPN unexpectedly told us at 4:49 that we could "stick to" our original timeline, and Marchand published a two-paragraph report 14 minutes later. OutKick’s more detailed story followed one minute after that.

That looks damning because it appears Marchand rushed out a short and incomplete story just to beat OutKick to the news.

Marchand has now explained his side, and his explanation makes the sequence harder to defend.

Recall that Marchand claimed he had "a story prepared in February." But his initial report didn't resemble a completed article that had been waiting since February. It consisted of two hurried paragraphs and included a typo.

Whatever "prepared" meant, his comments in a separate interview with Puck’s John Ourand established the more important point: Marchand had the information, intentionally waited on ESPN and published only after OutKick’s reporting forced the company to act.

"ESPN knew, I knew," Marchand told Ourand, explaining that the network had been trying to keep the Clark decision "close to the vest."

Then, Marchand said, "another entity called up" with the information and informed ESPN that it intended to publish. According to Marchand, ESPN became concerned and decided to tell Clark immediately rather than risk having him learn about the decision online.

CNN PANELIST BLAMES 'CULTURE WAR' RETRIBUTION AS REASON FOR RYAN CLARK'S ESPN DEPARTURE

Marchand didn't identify the other outlet, but he was describing precisely what OutKick had done. Our inquiry didn't merely make the story abstractly "competitive." By Marchand’s own account, it forced ESPN to accelerate its timetable.

Once ESPN had informed Clark, Marchand rushed out his two-paragraph report and made sure to note afterward that he had "reported it first," while the other outlet published "a little bit after."

Marchand didn't explain who alerted him that OutKick was preparing to publish or who told him Clark had been informed. Nor does his account prove ESPN asked us to wait specifically to help another reporter publish first.

And there is nothing inherently improper about giving a company a brief opportunity to notify an employee before he learns online that he has been let go. Reporters should consider the human consequences of publication.

But Marchand didn't describe granting ESPN a few minutes of courtesy. He said he possessed strong information for roughly a week and waited until competition threatened the arrangement.

Marchand went further in his interview with Ourand. He described himself as "being respectful" by waiting for ESPN and said he tries to wait "as long as you can" before publishing layoff news.

He then suggested that being a good reporter and being a good person "go hand-in-hand."

Marchand isn't simply admitting that he honored ESPN’s timetable. He is presenting that deference as evidence of his moral and journalistic superiority.

Andrew Marchand accidentally exposed the access journalism game while defending his handling of ESPN's decision to part ways with NFL analyst Ryan Clark. (Ric Tapia/Getty Images)

But OutKick didn't recklessly publish unconfirmed information or deny ESPN an opportunity to respond. We independently confirmed the story through four sources, contacted the company and gave it a firm deadline.

Marchand’s definition of responsible journalism appears to require something more: allowing the corporation at the center of the story to determine when the reporting may become public.

Responsible journalism means giving the subject of a story an opportunity to respond, as OutKick did when we offered ESPN one hour to comment.

But it does not mean giving the subject control over when the story becomes public. And it especially doesn't mean allowing the subject to dictate the framing of the news.

That's the difference between responsible journalism and access journalism. It seems that Marchand and many other insiders confuse the two quite frequently.

Access reporters receive strategically selected information from powerful sources, honor the source’s preferred timetable and publish when the institution decides the information can be released.

The reporter receives exclusives and status. The institution receives a predictable messenger.

Marchand demonstrated that predictability during the interview with Ourand.

Although he called ESPN’s execution "horrendous," he repeatedly insisted the company was "trying to do the right thing" and that its "hearts were in the right place."

ESPN put Clark on live television despite planning to part ways with him, removed him only after an outside outlet threatened to publish and created the humiliating spectacle Marchand was discussing.

Yet even while criticizing the result, a reporter who benefits from staying in ESPN’s good graces rushed to defend management’s intentions. The execution was bad, Marchand conceded, but ESPN’s motives, in his view, remained pure.

That instinct points to the second half of the access bargain. It's not only about allowing a source to control the timing of information. It's also about how aggressively a reporter is willing to scrutinize the people providing it.

A reporter who depends on one corporation for a steady stream of scoops has a powerful incentive not to challenge that corporation too aggressively. The next exclusive depends on the same executives and communications officials continuing to take his calls.

Marchand does criticize people associated with ESPN. But notice who draws his criticism and when they draw it.

His most sustained criticism has focused on Pat McAfee, an independently powerful personality whom ESPN does not fully control and who has repeatedly clashed with people inside the network. One Marchand report contained several petty and embarrassing details about McAfee that clearly came from ESPN insiders. Sports Illustrated described it as a "pretty brutal inside job."

Pat McAfee’s clashes with ESPN insiders show how access reporting can become a weapon for one faction of a network against another. (Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos)

That was technically reporting critical of an ESPN personality. It also demonstrated how an insider can serve one faction of a corporation against another.

Marchand criticized Ryan Clark after ESPN had decided to fire him. He wrote that "Around the Horn" had lost its way during the show’s final week, months after ESPN publicly announced its cancellation.

Even Marchand and Katie Strang’s substantial investigation into former ESPN executive Lee Fitting arrived after ESPN had let him go, when scrutinizing Fitting no longer threatened his standing inside the network. The report documented conduct that employees said went unchecked for years, but its target was already outside the building.

The discarded executive received scrutiny. The executives who still controlled access received credit.

That doesn't prove a formal quid pro quo. But it doesn't need to.

The institution supplies information. The reporter supplies predictability and favorable coverage.

The same arrangement becomes far more consequential when the subject is not a sports network but a government official helping shape national policy.

Newly released diary entries from Dr. Anthony Fauci showed just how cozy relationships between powerful officials and the journalists covering them can become.

Fauci wrote that he was building a friendship with CNN’s Jake Tapper and documented dinners at each other’s homes. He wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" another health official during a CNN interview.

Dr. Anthony Fauci’s newly released diary entries offer another example of how access can blur the line between journalism and public relations. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Dana Bash sent Fauci an encouraging message after a confrontation with a Republican lawmaker. George Stephanopoulos praised Fauci privately after an interview, while Andrea Mitchell called to apologize for failing to book him.

Reporters need sources, and friendly relationships can produce important information. None of those described interactions is a problem in a vacuum.

The problem arises when access, ideological sympathy and personal friendship erase the necessary distance between reporter and subject.

During a historic public-health crisis, the press was supposed to scrutinize one of the most powerful and influential officials in the country. Fauci’s diaries raise a different possibility: that some journalists covering him had begun to view him less as a subject requiring skepticism and more as an ally whose access and approval they valued.

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

The Marchand-ESPN sequence shows the access bargain in sports media. The Fauci diaries show what happens when that same bargain reaches national policy.

That's the access bargain in its most dangerous form.

The information can be accurate and still function as PR. It can be selectively leaked, strategically timed and framed to benefit the institution or official providing it.

That's why many insider scoops provide limited public value. Firings, trades, contract extensions and television assignments generally become public anyway. The insider’s product is often not discovery, it's speed.

And in today's social media world, how much value does that even hold?

The Founding Fathers didn't enshrine freedom of the press in the First Amendment so reporters could distribute corporate announcements a few minutes early or launder government messaging from powerful officials.

The First Amendment protects a free press so reporters can challenge concentrated power, not simply carry messages from it.

They protected it because a free press was supposed to stand between the public and concentrated power.

That freedom carries a purpose: expose what powerful institutions want concealed, demand answers they would rather avoid and publish truths they would prefer remain buried.

When reporters instead allow corporations and government officials to control the timing, framing and scrutiny of the news, they are not fulfilling that founding role.

My own career has often involved seeking access where I was not wanted. Nike stonewalled questions about a study on "transgender" youth athletes, the WNBA denied game credentials several times because they didn't want me asking questions and reporting on a Michigan high-school volleyball controversy led to harassment and required me to have a personal security detail at several games.

OUTKICK REPORTER HARASSED COVERING GIRLS VOLLEYBALL, TRANS PLAYER, AS PRINCIPAL DOES NOTHING

That resistance didn't make all of my conclusions correct, but it established that the subjects weren't controlling the reporting process. Quite the opposite, in fact.

Only 28% of Americans told Gallup last year that they trusted newspapers, television and radio to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, the lowest figure Gallup has recorded.

Media organizations often blame polarization, misinformation, social media and politicians for that collapse.

They should also examine the system they created.

Marchand thought he was establishing his superiority over reporters who lacked his access. He knew earlier, had better sources, supposedly had a story ready months before and then simply waited because that was the "responsible" thing to do.

Instead, his defense revealed the unspoken arrangement.

A powerful institution gives information to a favored reporter. The reporter protects the institution’s timeline and rarely makes himself a threat to the people providing access. When an outside outlet disrupts the arrangement, the insider rushes out the news, preserves his reputation and continues receiving information from the same sources.

Then he lectures everyone else to "write what you know, not what you think."

Marchand should add the unofficial second half of that rule: Write what you know... as long as the corporation that told you says it is okay.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Andrew Marchand accidentally showed the entire process in action.

articles.title: House committee passes Foreign Funding Transparency Act to expose foreign donations to nonprofits
articles.excerpt: Gordon Chang, a senior fellow at Gatestone Institute and author of 'Plan Red,' joins 'The Big Weekend Show' to discuss Marxist millionaire Neville Roy Singham. Chang exposes Singham's alleged $591 mil...
articles.body_text:
Gordon Chang, a senior fellow at Gatestone Institute and author of 'Plan Red,' joins 'The Big Weekend Show' to discuss Marxist millionaire Neville Roy Singham. Chang exposes Singham's alleged $591 million dark money network funding far-left nonprofits and influencing anti-U.S. activities, potentially with ties to the Chinese Communist Party. The House Ways and Means Committee issued subpoenas in its investigation.

Lawmakers are seeking to expose foreign nationals who may be funneling money and donations through tax-exempt organizations to political committees as the House Ways and Means Committee passed a bill that would revise reporting requirements for tax-exempt groups.

The Foreign Funding Transparency Act, which passed 23-18 in the committee last Wednesday, would require tax-exempt organizations to collect and report to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) donations received from foreign nationals.

"For far too long, foreign influence and interference have plagued our tax-exempt sector," committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., said in a statement. "Foreign donations have no place in American politics, particularly when the sole goal is to manipulate our public discourse, promote propaganda and support violence."

Smith noted that many of the protests and demonstrations that take place across the U.S. appear to be grassroots but are actually well-organized and well-funded, often by groups within what he described as "shadowy networks."

"As the Ways and Means Committee conducted its investigation into the nation’s tax-exempt sector, it became clear that shadowy networks of well-funded organizations have been enjoying lucrative tax benefits for decades, while simultaneously accepting donations and direction from foreign nationals," Smith added. "From the outside, it looks like a movement, but once you see how the money flows, it becomes clear that this is a machine," he added.

The bill’s passage came just a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for global cooperation at a summit in Washington to combat far-left political terrorism.

SHANGHAI SABOTAGE: INSIDE SINGHAM'S SECRET STRATEGY TO DEMONIZE AMERICA

"For far too long, however, our counterterrorism doctrine has had a blind spot – a blind spot when it comes to extremist violence from the political left," Rubio said. "Even today, the very idea that far-left terrorism could be a serious threat is treated as a right-wing fever dream, or worse, as a dangerous fascist conspiracy."

While Rubio didn’t mention any organizations or individuals by name, the House Ways and Means Committee noted Marxist Neville Roy Singham in a statement about the bill’s passage.

Singham, a 72-year-old American now based in Shanghai and who sold his tech company for $785 million in 2017, is known to fund pro-Chinese Communist Party groups operating in the U.S. He has funneled $278 million into the broad network of nonprofits since 2017, according to a Fox News Digital investigation.

The funneling of funds through nonprofit networks has been a key point of concern for lawmakers and the Trump administration. Major contributors, including Singham, often have dispersed funds through shell 501(c)(3) nonprofits, which subsequently contributed to various tax-exempt organizations.

RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS

During his address to more than 60 countries earlier this month, Rubio noted that networks have been coordinating across multiple countries, providing training instructions and using encrypted communication to facilitate unrest. He said international cooperation was critical to disrupting the financing of dangerous organizations, some of which were working with hostile foreign states.

Singham did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Preston Mizell is a writer with Fox News Digital covering breaking news.

articles.title: Secret Service agent and two others arrested for ‘prolonged’ hazing in Miami
articles.excerpt:
Three men were arrested for ‘repeated beatings with canes and paddles’ causing near-fatal injuries to two pledges

A US Secret Service agent and two others have been arrested after Florida state inves...
articles.body_text:
Three men were arrested for ‘repeated beatings with canes and paddles’ causing near-fatal injuries to two pledges

A US Secret Service agent and two others have been arrested after Florida state investigators uncovered evidence of “alleged hazing incidents involving prolonged and repeated beatings with canes and paddles” in Miami.

Investigators arrested Marquez Christopher Pinder, 29, on Sunday. Two other men – Jared Lamar James, 26, and Elijah Delano Dyous, 29 – were also arrested for allegedly helping to orchestrate the beatings, purportedly as part of a fraternity hazing ritual in April that left two people hospitalized with severe injuries.

Court documents said that a University of Miami graduate student and another young man had injuries that could have been fatal had they not been treated. One of the victims required skin grafts to his backside and suffered kidney damage, while the other had a tube placed in his windpipe to help him breathe.

Charges against Pinder, James, and Dyous include felony counts of hazing with a deadly weapon, aggravated battery with great bodily harm and attempted manslaughter.

“In Florida, hazing is abuse and it is a crime,” Katherine Fernandez Rundle, a Miami-Dade county state attorney, said in a statement. “It’s victims too often lie in their graves and in hospital beds.”

According to the Miami Herald, the accused men conducted the beatings after the victims failed to correctly answer questions relating to initiation into the Miami chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi, a historically Black fraternity where Pinder served as a “dean of pledges”.

Miami prosecutors said the alleged hazing began on 1 April at an apartment in the Sweetwater district close to Florida International University. However, the graduate student victim was not affiliated with FIU.

The hazing allegedly continued for two days at the Sweetwater location before moving to another residence for a fourth day.

The beatings stopped on the fourth night when one of the victims had blood seeping through the seat of his pants, according to a warrant in the case – and the fraternity leaders ordered the victims to strip off their clothes and place them in garbage bags.

The warrant said that injuries to one of the alleged victims “would have resulted in renal failure leading to death” while the second denied being paddled – but acknowledged receiving emergency medical care.

Medical records show he had been hospitalized with injuries to his backside and “was intubated during his stay in the hospital to prevent further physical deterioration and death”.

Pinder, James and Dyous each face multiple felony charges, including attempted manslaughter with a deadly weapon, aggravated battery with a deadly weapon or causing great bodily harm and hazing with a deadly weapon.

Rundle’s statements referred to Chad Meredith, a University of Miami baseball recruit, who died in 2001 while pledging the Kappa Sigma fraternity. He had been induced to swim across Lake Osceola in the middle of the night and drowned.

A decade later, Robert Chapman died after being pummeled by fellow members of Florida A&M University’s Marching 100 band during a ritual known as “crossing Bus C”. A third student, Andrew Coffey, died after pledging for the Florida State University chapter of Pi Kappa Phi, after being assigned to drink a bottle of bourbon.

“Among some, fraternity hazing might be seen as a tradition creating a sense of belonging and brotherhood, but since 2001, hazing in Florida has killed Chad Meredith, Robert Champion and Andrew Coffey while seriously injuring others,” Rundle said.

“This case, with the victims requiring hospitalization, provides clear-cut examples of hazing’s danger.”

Pinder, the man accused of orchestrating the latest hazing case, is a 2021 Florida International University graduate assigned to the US Secret Service’s Miami field office. He was first employed by the service in 2023, according to his LinkedIn page.

Pinder’s attorney, Justin Beckham, described that the case pending against his client was “grossly overcharged”.

A spokesman for the Secret Service agency said “any misconduct will be addressed swiftly and appropriately upon completion of the investigative and judicial process”.

The US Secret Service is best known for protecting the country’s presidents as well as other national leaders, and its other duties include investigating cases of fraud.

Days before Pinder’s arrest, in a separate and unrelated case, a Secret Service spokesperson publicly said that an agent assigned to vice-president JD Vance’s protective detail had become “the subject of an administrative investigation, and potential criminal inquiry, involving allegations of compromising operational and information security”.

CNN, citing a source, reported that the agent came under suspicion after allegedly providing information that appeared in an MS Now report about Vance’s planned Marine Corps helicopter trip with his son to a golf lesson.

The Associated Press contributed reporting
