On a spring day last year, James Desborough marche...
articles.body_text:
Man already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman

On a spring day last year, James Desborough marched up to Cornwall’s county hall in Truro and began bombarding the offices with dozens of eggs stolen from a supermarket.

It was a drug and drink-addled protest at his plight – homeless, jobless and generally angry at the world. He expected to be arrested and messaged a friend: “If I’m going to get nicked, might as well round the charges up.”

He certainly did that. In the weeks and months after the egg incident, Desborough committed three murders.

He killed two vulnerable friends, Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, whose dismembered and burnt bodies were found in woodland close to a shack where he sometimes lived off-grid in south Cornwall.

Then while awaiting trial, he murdered Steven Kempster, his cellmate in Exeter prison, strangling him to death because he was annoyed with some of his habits.

Desborough, 40, is already serving a life sentence for the prison killing. After a jury at Winchester crown court convicted him of murdering his two friends, he may never be released, putting him on a par with serial killers such as Rose West who are expected to spend the rest of their lives behind bars.

Acquaintances have said Desborough was a control freak with a terrible temper – he has an old conviction for GBH – and was furious at what he saw as his bad luck in life. A civil engineer by profession and a father, he had fallen on hard times.

Quite what tipped him over into an explosion of violence is unclear. He used Aquilino’s and Coleman’s bank cards after he killed them, but police do not believe it was a simple matter of theft.

The prosecutor in his trial, Ahmed Hossain KC, put it to Desborough that he might have killed them because he considered them worthless, deserving to die because of their troubled lifestyle and because they were “dinlos” – a local slang term for fools. Had he simply got annoyed with them and snapped? “I thought they were OK,” he replied in court. “They were good friends.”

The trial has certainly put the focus on a different Cornwall to the one most holidaymakers to the county love.

It highlighted not surfing beaches and historic landscapes, but the deep-rooted social issues that make life for many in the far south-west of England difficult. There are pockets of serious deprivation in Cornwall where people experience homelessness and addiction problems.

Desborough, Aquilino and Coleman were among those who – in the words of the defence barrister, Sean Brunton KC – had slipped through the cracks in society.

The three got to know each other when they lived in a hostel for homeless people in the seaside resort of Newquay.

In the months before he died, Aquilino, 57, was taking hard drugs, suffering from depression and subjected to “cuckooing”, in which dealers take over the home of a vulnerable person.

Coleman, 43, abused alcohol and had cirrhosis. He had been kidnapped and stabbed at the age of 13, leaving him with post traumatic stress disorder.

The police were first called in after Coleman was reported missing. He had last been seen on 3 June 2025, drinking with Desborough.

Police thought they had solved the case quickly when they found a body in woodland between Truro and the village of Probus.

It turned out not be Coleman though, or Aquilino, but a third man, Lee Hockey, who had vanished from Truro. Police believe he too may have been murdered, but have not linked his death to Desborough.

Attention began to focus on Paramoor Woods, near Sticker, once a mining settlement now popular with people who work in the town of St Austell.

Desborough had inherited land there from his grandfather and built a shack, though, to his frustration, he did not have the correct planning permission and had been told by the council that he was not allowed to live there permanently.

He would let homeless friends camp there, grew cannabis and had a “stash tree” where he hid class A drugs in a hollow. Machetes, knives and saws were also scattered around the property.

Police searched the woods for five months, eventually finding the remains of Coleman and Aquilino. The latter had last been seen alive on 18 April 2025, also drinking with Desborough.

Codenamed Operation Honeyfall, the search was extraordinary. More than 700 officers and scientists were involved, with Devon and Cornwall police drawing on resources from five other forces. Dog teams, soil experts and anthropologists were brought in.

The weather was very hot and the nature of the terrain jungle-like and boggy. Officers sometimes had to wade through water up to their chests as they searched.

In excess of 1,900 burnt bone fragments – Aquilino’s remains – were discovered in a stream, while Coleman’s charred body parts were found in a shallow grave. A hatchet hung on a nearby tree.

Another unusual feature was that Desborough kept a beady eye on the search. Before there was enough evidence to remand him in custody, he hung around, at one point telling a forensic biologist that he liked the dismemberment scenes in the serial killer show Dexter.

Sometimes officers smelled burning and at other times heard digging, perhaps as Desborough tried to destroy evidence.

As well as discovering the victims’ remains, police came upon notes and plans Desborough had made that suggested he may have been planning to change his appearance through plastic surgery after the murders and flee the UK, perhaps to south-east Asia.

Detectives also discovered he had used his victims’ bank cards to buy goods and services, including a roast beef dinner soon after cutting up Coleman’s body.

He was eventually charged with the two murders and held in Exeter prison sharing a cell with Kempster, who had been jailed for drunkenly suffocating his 91-year-old father in north Devon.

Desborough’s appearance in the witness box was remarkable. He was considered so dangerous that he was handcuffed to an officer when he was moved from the dock to the main area of the court.

He was articulate when speaking about his time as a civil engineer and building regulations concerning his cabin, but he was less certain when he told the story of finding the bodies of Aquilino and Coleman.

He claimed he had come upon one hanging in a tree, the other naked in a stream. It was, in his words, a “series of unfortunate circumstances”.

Desborough repeatedly denying killing the pair, but accepted burning and hiding their bodies while high on ketamine and drinking tequila.

During the trial there was a suggestion that Desborough might have carried on killing, murdering members of his circle who could have implicated him in the deaths of his friends or who simply annoyed him.

In one note, he had written: “I’m a killer and ready to execute any predators.” In another, headed “bug out” – military slang for a retreat – he set out what appeared to be escape plans but added: “Take out the remaining muppets.”

articles.title: NFL legend praises Sophie Cunningham for saying 'what's true' about transgender athletes in girls sports
articles.excerpt:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher praises Sophie Cunningham for her stance against transgender athletes participating in girls' and women's sports.

Brian Urlacher is hardly a WNBA fan, but th...
articles.body_text:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Brian Urlacher praises Sophie Cunningham for her stance against transgender athletes participating in girls' and women's sports.

Brian Urlacher is hardly a WNBA fan, but the NFL legend cannot help but watch Sophie Cunningham.

"She’s great. Bro, she’s so fun to watch... It’s unbelievable. She’s so aggressive. She’s fun to watch. I follow her on Instagram. She’s got great stuff out there," the former Chicago Bears linebacker told Fox News Digital in a recent interview.

But now, Urlacher is an even bigger fan of the Indiana Fever guard.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham brings the ball up court against the Connecticut Sun on July 22, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Urlacher told Fox News Digital last month that he follows the transgender-athlete issue "closely," so when Cunningham said "young girls...shouldn't have to go against biological men" in sports, Urlacher was ecstatic.

"She just says what’s true. She says common-sense things, and she gets so much backlash. She’s like, 'Men should not be playing in women’s sports.' Why is that so controversial? I don’t get it. I don’t understand it," Urlacher said.

The Hall of Famer also praised Cunningham for continuing to stand by her sentiments.

"It’s a simple statement. She stood by it. That’s what I love about when people say things: Don’t back down. If you say something, stand by it. And she said it. She backed it up. She’s not backing down, no matter how much heat she gets from certain people," Urlacher said.

"It’s an 80-20 issue. Eighty percent of the country thinks it’s true. The 20% is crushing her. Let them. Who cares? But I love that she didn’t back down. I love everything she stands for. She plays hard. She’s good. Like I said, I don’t watch the WNBA, but I like those two girls (Cunningham and Caitlin Clark) right there."

Indiana Fever superstars Sophie Cunningham and Caitlin Clark are arguably the two most popular players in the WNBA. (NBAE via Getty Images)

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS' SPORTS

Urlacher also noted that Cunningham probably took a risk in expressing her opinion, given that her peers are largely liberal or part of the gay community.

"It’s a liberal and mostly gay league, which is fine. I have no problem. My daughter is gay. No problem. I’ve got no problem with that... But man, what do you do, right? She said what she said. I cannot disagree with her," he said.

Since her comments surfaced, Cunningham has received support online from various Republican lawmakers and advocates for women's sports, including Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Eric Schmitt, R-Mo.

"I'll always believe in that. It's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category," Cunningham said last week.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham reacts after scoring during the second half of a WNBA game against the Seattle Storm on Sunday, May 17, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"I'm not a very political person, but I do have beliefs. I have morals, and I'll always stand on those."

OutKick's Alejandro Avila contributed to this report.

articles.title: Black people’s risk factors for stroke ‘rising faster than for white people’
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean people

Stroke risk factors including high blood pressure and diabetes are risi...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: King’s College London analysis finds diabetes and hypertension are more common in Black African and Caribbean people

Stroke risk factors including high blood pressure and diabetes are rising faster among people from Black African and Caribbean backgrounds compared with their white counterparts, according to analysis.

Researchers at King’s College London analysed data from more than 8,500 adults over a 30-year period from the South London Stroke Register, one of the longest-running population-based stroke registers in the world.

The study found that while the prevalence of stroke risk factors, including diabetes and hypertension, were increasing faster among Black people, people from Black African backgrounds were also twice as likely to experience stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis than white people, at a rate of 12% compared with 6%. About one in six people across the UK will have a stroke in their lifetime.

Diabetes was about twice as common in Black Caribbean and Black Africans on the stroke register compared with white participants, and high blood pressure was 29% more prevalent in Black Caribbean and 47% more prevalent in Black African people. Although diabetes rates increased for all ethnic groups over the 30-year study period, they increased most rapidly among Black African participants, rising from 21% between 1995 and 2004 to 41% between 2015 and 2024.

Dr Eva Emmett, a research fellow at King’s College London and the lead author of the study, said: “Our study shows that the prevalence of pre-stroke hypertension and diabetes is higher and increasing faster in ethnic minority and lower socioeconomic groups. Together with Black people’s younger age at stroke and higher likelihood of having a stroke without a prior risk factor diagnosis, these findings call for targeted and earlier primary prevention efforts.

“NHS health checks, which screen for hypertension and diabetes, begin at the age of 40. However, this may be too late for higher-risk groups who often experience stroke at a younger age.”

She called for “universal improvements in cardiovascular risk detection” as well as more targeted prevention strategies, such as younger screening age for those most at risk.

The data also revealed socioeconomic disparities among the study’s participants. The prevalence of diabetes was 23% higher in participants with manual occupations, such as bus drivers, security guards and plumbers, compared with those in non-manual employment such as teachers and nurses. Diabetes prevalence was also 21% higher in those with lower education levels.

While diabetes diagnoses increased in all socioeconomic groups over time, the greatest increases were seen in those with routine and manual jobs and with lower education levels. Similarly, high blood pressure rates increased the most in those with lower socioeconomic status.

Dr Maëva May, the director of policy at the Stroke Association, said the findings were a stark reminder that “the benefits of prevention are not being felt equally”.

“Too many people from Black African and Black Caribbean communities, and those living in more deprived circumstances, are developing stroke risk factors earlier and are experiencing stroke before those risks have even been identified,” May said.

“Stroke is not inevitable. Many strokes can be prevented by finding and treating conditions like high blood pressure and diabetes early, but that only works if people can access the right care at the right time. Preventing stroke means preventing inequalities in who gets the opportunity to stay well.”

articles.title: Young people ‘expected’ to engage with new work support, says McFadden
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he unveils funds to stop families in England losing benefits

Young people will be expected to engage with new support to seek work, Pat M...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he unveils funds to stop families in England losing benefits

Young people will be expected to engage with new support to seek work, Pat McFadden has said, as he unveiled funds to stop families losing benefits when teenagers take up apprenticeships.

Speaking to the Guardian, the work and pensions secretary echoed the comments of Andy Burnham when he suggested that access to support would be conditional on young people properly participating in the support that would be provided.

“We have an obligation to put good support in place,” he said. “And then there is an expectation that people engage with the support.”

McFadden – one of the few ministers to keep his job in the reshuffle when Burnham became prime minister – said the new bursary would compensate for a quirk in the system that could mean families lose some benefits if a teenager took up an apprenticeship.

The penalty – where the family loses the child component of universal credit – is most likely to affect single parents or disabled teenagers under 18.

The policy is the second key announcement from Burnham as he seeks to address the crisis of mounting unemployment among young people – after stating on Tuesday morning he would seek fundamental changes in the education system to emphasise technical and vocational skills, especially those relevant to local businesses.

Both Burnham and McFadden have said they are also determined to reform the welfare system, especially by providing more opportunities for young people on long-term sickness benefits to return to the workforce.

The prime minister also said on Monday he wanted to change the nature of the support and make some of it “conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them … So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits”.

McFadden said the bursary was part of removing those unintended barriers on young people taking up work – £30m funded through the current departmental budget – but added it was crucial that young people responded to the support on offer.

“The key to it is to remove this barrier to opportunity really,” he said. “And to stop people being trapped in the benefit system when they would otherwise take up an opportunity which is in their interest, which would put them on to the next step of a career path.

“These cliff edges are never created by design, they’re just in a big complex system, they are just there and I’m very grateful to the charities and campaigners who drew this to our attention.”

Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts to benefits to get the welfare bill down … Often that just pushes people into even more crisis and then even more public spending in another part of the system.”

McFadden said there would be a significant system redesign when the second stage report from social security minister, Stephen Timms, and disability campaigners reports back in the autumn. An interim has already found that the criteria for personal independence payments was not fit for purpose.

“We’ll need a whole government response, not just a [Department for Work and Pensions] response, because the issues affecting young people go way beyond the boundaries of the DWP, if you take mental health issues among young people, that’s obviously going way beyond the DWP,” he said.

The government is also expected to receive the second part of Alan Milburn’s review this autumn – looking at growing youth unemployment and lack of engagement with education and training.

McFadden said that welfare reform would mean both “opportunities and expectations”. He said: “We are trying to get the system to ask: ‘How do we help you live your fullest life? How do we maximise your opportunities?’

“One of the things that struck me about the benefits system is how sticky it is, how when people get on to these long-term benefits they tend to stay in them for a long time.”

The new bursaries of about £4,500 will be offered to families – particularly single parents with a disabled child – where they could otherwise lose approximately £80 a week because the apprenticeship salary is lower than the lost benefits.

Charities have welcomed plans for the new bursary but warned that young people needed to be directly made aware of its existence by potential employers.

Enver Solomon, the CEO of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “If more young people are to take up apprenticeships, it is vital their family isn’t worse off so introducing a new bursary is a welcome step towards narrowing the income gap.

“As the new scheme is rolled out, the government must ensure it is as easy as possible for young people to apply, and that nobody loses out because they were not directed towards support.

“We know in families where wages should outweigh benefit payments there can still be real difficulty as payments shift from parents to young people who have to take on the responsibility of contributing to overall household income.”

articles.title: Guardian Essential poll: Angus Taylor’s approval rating crashes and One Nation support plateaus
articles.excerpt:
Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost of living crisis

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation’s primary...
articles.body_text:
Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost of living crisis

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation’s primary vote has plateaued and Angus Taylor’s approval rating has crashed, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll.

But it is not all smooth sailing for Labor with Australians rubbishing the government’s handling of the inflation and cost of living crisis.

Australians have also shown their reluctance to embrace new AI datacentres, with less than a third saying they’d be happy to have a facility in their local area and sharing concerns about energy demands, water supply, environmental impacts and noise.

The Guardian Essential poll, of 1,060 voters last week, found One Nation’s popularity was continuing to level off, attracting a 25% primary vote, down one point from June’s poll. Meanwhile while Labor’s indicative primary vote ticked up one point to 31% and the Coalition’s vote dropped further, down another point to 22%.

All those movements are within the poll’s margin of error, but it is the second consecutive Essential poll where One Nation’s primary vote has dropped since reaching a high of 28% in May. The populist right-wing party has dipped back to where it was in April. It comes after weeks of scrutiny over Pauline Hanson’s European trip, her interview with Tommy Robinson, and comments about domestic violence and immigration policy.

Struggling for political oxygen and attention amidst One Nation’s rise, the opposition leader has seen his own approval ratings plummet in the last month. In June, 36% of people approved of Taylor’s job performance and 37% disapproved, for a net approval of minus-1; but this month’s poll has seen his approvals drop three points and his disapprovals increase by seven points, for a new net approval of minus-12.

Taylor’s approval rating has crashed 16 points among men and four points among women, as well as by 20 points among people aged 35-54 and 13 points among those aged 18-34.

Anthony Albanese’s approval rating ticked up one point to minus-14, with 38% approving and 52% disapproving of his performance as prime minister. It’s the fourth straight month in which more than half of voters have disapproved of his performance.

Respondents to the poll also rejected Labor’s handling of the inflation and cost of living crisis, with a decisive 64% rating the government’s performance as poor; while just 16% of Australians rated it as good.

Nearly 80% of voters said cost of living and inflation was one of the most important issues to them, far and away the most-cited issue among respondents. Next most-cited was Medicare and health (50%), crime (42%) and immigration (35%).

But only 39% of voters rated the Labor government’s performance on Medicare and health as good, with 30% saying poor; on crime, 22% rated Labor as good and 50% as poor, while 24% rated Labor as good on immigration and another 50% as poor.

“Cost of living remains the stand-out issue for voters and the government’s handling of inflation is being rated down,” the executive director of Essential Media, Peter Lewis, said.

On managing technology and AI, the subject of a major speech by Albanese earlier this month, 29% rated Labor’s performance as good and 30% as poor.

The Essential report found only 28% of voters would support a new datacentre being built in their area, with 37% against. Men (34% support and 34% oppose) were far more supportive of new datacentres than women (22% support and 39% oppose).

Asked about their reservations about datacentre development, 61% raised concerns about impact on energy demand and power prices, and another 44% were worried about water supply.

Environmental impacts and noise were raised by 41% of voters, while 39% had general concerns about the growth of AI generally.

Albanese this month announced plans to more strongly regulate datacentres and AI, particularly setting rules for power and water use, and building social license for the construction of facilities.

articles.title: Royal commission into Victorian construction sector could boost Labor’s chances at state election, expert says
articles.excerpt:
Commission promised by new premier would be an ‘important signal’ for voters that the government was acting on alleged corruption

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victoria...
articles.body_text:
Commission promised by new premier would be an ‘important signal’ for voters that the government was acting on alleged corruption

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victorian voters heading to the polls will probably get a taste of the evidence heard by a royal commission – including how taxpayer funds were used on Big Build projects – but it could actually help Labor’s standing, an integrity expert says.

William Partlett, an associate professor of law and a fellow at the Centre for Public Integrity, said the commission promised by the new premier, Ben Carroll, would be an “important signal” for voters that the government was taking action.

Shortly after being sworn in on Tuesday, Carroll said the creation of a royal commission into the construction sector would be his “first action” as premier. This follows sustained pressure to investigate alleged corruption on the government’s Big Build infrastructure projects.

Carroll said the commission’s terms of reference would be “exhaustive”, and it would be established “as soon as possible”, suggesting it could hold hearings before November’s state election.

“Whether it’s the top-tier companies, whether it’s subcontractors, whether it’s businesses or unions, these terms of reference will be thorough,” the premier said.

Carroll also said a special prosecutor would be appointed to work in parallel to the royal commission, and that the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission will be bolstered with follow-the-money powers.

It comes after his predecessor, Jacinta Allan, had resisted calls for a royal commission into allegations that organised crime figures and bikie gangs infiltrated major infrastructure projects, including the Big Build.

Partlett told Guardian Australia the decision to hold a royal commission was not surprising, given the pressure the former premier was under from the Labor caucus over the issue.

“In some ways it was probably the downfall of [Allan] in her failure to call that because it did seem that many wanted that to be called,” Partlett said.

The Big Build is the state’s infrastructure program that has, since 2015, given about $109bn in public money for more than 180 projects, including the Metro Tunnel, level crossing removals and the Suburban Rail Loop.

Many of the projects had suffered cost blowouts, which Allan had previously said was due to inflation, supply chain disruptions and rising labour costs. Her claims came in response to reporting by the Age that money from the projects was being paid to gangland figures, and alleged union corruption was adding premiums of up to 30% to major project budgets.

Allan later acknowledged there had been criminality in the projects but said it was best for police to investigate any allegations of wrongdoing.

A report by the Centre for Public Integrity’s director, Geoffrey Watson SC, tabled during a Queensland inquiry into the CFMEU, found that “the flood of government money” had made the Big Build “ripe for corruption”.

That included “ad hoc corruption on the part of former organisers and delegates” as well as “a more organised or systemic corruption involving collaboration by some elements in the CFMEU with outlaw motorcycle gangs and other crime outfits,” Watson wrote.

The report stated a labourer’s job on the Big Build was so lucrative that a market was allegedly created where corrupt organisers and delegates bought and sold the jobs, and alleged the government “knew and had a duty to know” about wrongdoing but chose to do “nothing about it”.

Partlett said the terms of reference for the commission need to be “as broad as they can be” to include private organisations, the unions, institutions and government officials. The commission should also use its coercive powers to get to the bottom of the allegations in an open and transparent way, he said.

He said it was important that the commission begin sooner rather than later, and would have some potential impact on the election.

“The fact that the Labor party now is showing that it has interest in tackling these issues is an important signal … they are willing to accept something has gone wrong.”

Partlett said Labor getting in before the election allows them to set the terms of reference, and no one in the integrity sector would like to see it turn into “a demonisation of unions”.

“They can make it an inquiry into the construction sector that is done in a responsible way. It doesn’t demonise the unions, but then at the same time tries to understand what went wrong here.”

articles.title: Anger at Labor as Rex Patrick faces potential six-figure legal fee if he loses Aukus documents battle
articles.excerpt:
Australian government insists legal costs should be paid by former senator as FoI fight escalates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The government will insist Rex Patrick p...
articles.body_text:
Australian government insists legal costs should be paid by former senator as FoI fight escalates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The government will insist Rex Patrick pays up to $150,000 to cover its legal costs if he loses a fight to access documents about the Aukus agreement, escalating a battle in which several crossbench MPs have swung behind the former senator.

The transparency campaigner has used freedom of information laws to seek details on where nuclear waste from the submarine fleet will be stored, and won an administrative appeal on the matter in May.

But the Department of Industry, Science and Resources has appealed the matter to the federal court, seeking the decision be overturned and an order for Patrick to pay the government’s legal costs if he loses.

Politicians including Jacqui Lambie and Pauline Hanson have lashed the decision, warning it is a breach of rules requiring the government to act as a model litigant.

They, along with unions and transparency groups, have made appeals to the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, but have been rebuffed.

According to documents seen by Guardian Australia, Rowland last week said the government could rightly insist on Patrick being required to pay costs if he loses, acting “firmly and properly” to protect its interests.

Rowland wrote to a group of crossbenchers – including independents Helen Haines, David Pocock and the Greens’ David Shoebridge – saying the industry department was responsible for conduct of the case.

The department does not accept the model litigant rules prevent it from seeking costs from Patrick. Previous legal fights have seen fees of much as $150,000.

Lambie has accused Rowland of “behaving like a Labor stooge”.

“The government is sending a very clear message to people: stop when we say you can’t have information under FoI, or we’ll take you to court and you could lose all your savings … and maybe your house,” she said.

“I cannot believe the attorney general has handballed what is a whole-of-government principle issue to the secretary of a single department. The attorney is behaving like a Labor stooge, and either doesn’t have any leadership within her or doesn’t care. So which one is it?

“This issue is not going to just go away.”

Organisations including the Media Entertainment & Arts Alliance, the Grata Fund, the Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom and Australian Democracy Network have all called on the government to stop the legal challenge.

Tosca Lloyd, a Whistleblower Justice Fund campaigner, said the risk of a six-figure legal bill would limit ordinary use of FoI rules.

“This chilling effect is neither hypothetical nor unintentional,” she said.

“Public interest journalism depends on the FoI system. Investigative reporters – especially those at smaller and independent outlets – use it constantly to uncover stories the public has a right to know.

“If the cost of challenging a bad government decision is federal court litigation, most newsrooms simply won’t take that risk. The stories then won’t get told. That’s a loss for all of us.”

Bill Browne, the Australia Institute’s Democracy & Accountability program director, said departments and ministers should not fight FoI applicants.

“The Albanese government already tried to restrict Australians’ right to access government information, and was rebuffed by the Senate. This looks like another attempt to raise the cost of scrutinising the government.”

Patrick said legal precedent dating back to a 1912 high court decision showed a “standard of fair play” should be observed by governments.

“I have some experience in courtrooms and have asked the court to ensure fairness from government and that these laws will be decided with competent barristers arguing different sides of the secrecy/transparency questions before it,” he said.

“I can just hope that the courts will address the misguided sense of fairness and proper process exhibited by the attorney general.”

A spokesperson for Rowland declined to comment, referring questions to the department.

articles.title: The professor facing prison in ‘antifa’ case: ‘They want to scare all who oppose ICE’
articles.excerpt:
Erik Davis is accused by the government of a ‘conspiracy’ to obstruct ICE – experts say it’s part of a pattern to criminalize lawful organizing and ruin activists’ lives

Erik Davis was driving to a m...
articles.body_text:
Erik Davis is accused by the government of a ‘conspiracy’ to obstruct ICE – experts say it’s part of a pattern to criminalize lawful organizing and ruin activists’ lives

Erik Davis was driving to a medical appointment in St Paul, Minnesota, on 16 June when federal agents surrounded his car.

“They hauled me out … and put me in a belly chain,” recalled the 53-year-old. He was arrested on the spot on charges of being part of a “conspiracy” to “impede or injure” Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

Davis, a college professor and father of two, was one of thousands of Minnesotans who had rallied earlier this year when the Trump administration launched an aggressive crackdown on immigrants in the Twin Cities.

Now the government alleged that he and 14 others used “force, intimidation, and threats” to prevent officers from carrying out their duties.

In its 94-page indictment, the government has argued that Direct Action Minnesota, the loose coalition of organizers that Davis was connected with, conspired to obstruct federal law enforcement and had “ties” to “antifa”. The prosecution follows a pattern seen in other cases against demonstrators this year, with the government highlighting the comments and actions of some activists in the coalition to paint all 15 defendants as agitators pursuing violence against ICE.

One such case in Chicago spectacularly collapsed last month. Demonstrators in Texas were recently convicted of terrorism charges and sentenced to decades behind bars, though in that case one protester shot and injured an officer. Prosecutors have not alleged any specific injuries to officers in Minnesota.

Civil rights advocates have said these prosecutions, even when unsuccessful, are part of an effort to criminalize lawful community organizing, weaken movements opposing deportations and turn the lives of activists upside down.

Davis, the government says, has attended and facilitated meetings about protests and discussed his “anti-authoritarian” ideology with other activists. He is not accused of violent acts, taking any specific actions at protests nor having any encounters with ICE agents.

“It’s petty revenge,” Davis said. “They’re trying to portray being part of a community as an illegal conspiratorial act.”

Davis, and other defendants interviewed by the Guardian, are confident that the case against them will collapse. But the government is trying to send a signal, he said: “This isn’t just about us. It’s about trying to scare everybody who opposes ICE.”

Davis is a Buddhist studies scholar at Macalester College in St Paul and has long been part of labor organizing and activism against police violence in the region. When federal agents flooded the Twin Cities in January in a massive effort to round up immigrants, he felt compelled to step up, he said: “It was a federal invasion and terror campaign on our streets. The behavior of these masked thugs was horrific … they were ripping human beings out of families.”

Outrage and local organizing efforts swelled following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. There were rapid response and mutual aid networks, groups documenting ICE sightings, know-your-rights training sessions, food donations for immigrant families trapped at home. And many joined Signal groups with strangers to get plugged in.

“It was astonishing. The overwhelming sense was that almost everybody was opposed and angry and scared, and almost everybody wanted to do something,” said Davis, who joined hyper-local group chats with neighbors.

The indictment does not describe Davis orchestrating any specific protest plans, giving detailed directions to other activists or conducting any violence. It does allege that on 11 January, four days after Good’s killing, Davis helped facilitate an “emergency meeting” for residents interested in “resistance to ICE” that featured discussions of protest tactics, like civil disobedience, marches and “blockades” to stop ICE officers.

Prosecutors also cite a post by Davis in a Signal group six days later in which he shared information about upcoming protests and encouraged people to be at a federal immigration building. The indictment further notes Davis suggested people delete the group while on the ground during demonstrations, and that he participated in two additional meetings and a rally.

The indictment accuses other defendants of more serious offenses: eight of the other defendants are said to have participated in an action at a federal building on 1 March where demonstrators held shields and blocked vehicles from entering or leaving a federal building. Prosecutors say “individuals threw projectiles” at local sheriffs during the protest, but did not specify if any defendants were involved in that.

Four defendants face charges for separate incidents. One is accused of telling people to get guns in January. One is accused of following an agent in May to Wisconsin, just across the state border. And one is accused of assault and destruction of government property after allegedly knocking paperwork out of an agent’s hand and kicking an officer’s car in May. The indictment doesn’t allege Davis was involved in any of the incidents in March or May.

Across the indictment, there are no allegations of injuries to specific ICE officers, or charges of serious violence like there were in the recent federal prosecution of protesters in Prairieland, Texas, in which one protester shot and injured an officer.

Daniel Rosen, the Minnesota US attorney, said whether the Minneapolis protesters caused physical harm was not the measure of criminality in this case.

The broader suggestion of the indictment is that Davis’s statements in Signal chats and meetings, alongside the statements and actions of others, show the groups collectively were conspiring to oppose the US government’s authority and interfere with ICE – and that they were connected to “Antifa groups” that “blend anarchist and communist views”.

At a press conference announcing the charges, Rosen said the prosecution supported the mission of Donald Trump’s executive order last year that designated “antifa” a “domestic terrorist organization” responsible for “riots” against ICE. Antifa is not a formal entity, but an umbrella term for a wide array of anti-fascist activism.

To support the alleged “antifa” connection, the Department of Justice (DoJ) has highlighted a photo showing one of the defendants wearing an “I’m Antifa!” sweatshirt. Prosecutors also quoted another defendant’s post on Facebook: “YOU WILL NEVER WIN WITH NON-VIOLENCE ALONE.”

The indictment does not cite any comments by Davis about antifa. The charges don’t define the relationships of the protesters to one another, nor does it provide evidence that defendants like Davis endorsed the more radical statements or actions of others facing charges.

Authorities say Davis referred to his ideologies as “anarchist”, “broadly anti-authoritarian” and “broadly anti-capitalist” and praised the “revolutionary potential of our organizations” and “militancy” in a Signal message.

Spokespeople for the DoJ in Minnesota declined to comment. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson declined to answer questions about the case, pointing to an earlier statement saying people who “lay a hand on law enforcement … will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law”.

Davis said his own political beliefs are focused on expanding equality and people’s freedoms and opposing state violence and authoritarianism – far removed, he said, from the stereotype of a violent “anarchist” extremist.

Davis said the meeting he helped facilitate involved more than a hundred participants with a wide range of ideologies – a space for people to come together after Good’s killing. “I’m not sure I’m described as doing anything illegal, which makes sense, because I didn’t.” He noted it was common for people to delete Signal chats at protests due to concerns about officers accessing phones during arrests.

“It’s bewildering. It seemed weird and laughable,” Davis said of the indictment. “It felt like the length of the indictment was a cover for how thin it actually was. I’m a professor. I’ve seen people pad out papers when they’ve got nothing to say.”

Among the Minnesota protesters facing the most severe charges is Natasha Rakotz.

Rakotz, a 45-year-old home health aide, said it took her a while to get involved in organizing efforts after ICE arrived in the city. She said she wasn’t connected to any activist groups and didn’t know where to start. But she felt morally obligated: “People say, if it was 1935 Germany, what would I do? I couldn’t do nothing. I couldn’t sit by and wait for them to kill somebody else. I couldn’t sit in my privileged white existence and allow the government to absolutely ravage people that need protecting … It felt like nobody was going to save us.”

Rakotz eventually linked up with groups monitoring ICE and threw herself into the work. Like Davis, Rakotz faces conspiracy charges. The government says she participated in a Signal chat focused on observing ICE vehicles, talking about what times she would be observing and how she takes photos of license plates. She asked others what they had observed and said she was interested in learning more about civil disobedience.

But in addition, the DoJ says that on 18 May, Rakotz followed a federal immigration officer’s vehicle, “brake checked” and “side swiped” the car, “causing a collision”. The indictment does not provide further details.

Rakotz has denied the allegation. State records show local officers called to the scene of the collision cited her for a misdemeanor of allegedly violating her “duty to drive with due care”, a minor offense. A court report said she told an officer she was not following the federal agent and the collision was an accident. She was not arrested at that time.

Eventually, state prosecutors dropped the misdemeanor, saying federal prosecutors were filing charges covering the incident. The US attorney’s office has since accused Rakotz of assault on an officer, with a charge alleging “physical contact” and “injury”, though the indictment doesn’t identify a victim nor specify the injuries the collision may have caused, and it doesn’t detail any damage to the government’s car. That charge could carry a 20-year sentence on top of six years for conspiracy.

“I really believe these charges are going to get dropped because they’re unfounded and ridiculous,” said Rakotz. “But I feel like the process is the punishment.”

A trial date has not been set and complicated cases like this can drag on for months.

In the meantime, the consequences of the case have been far-reaching for the defendants. “They are trying to ruin our lives … I try not to remind myself all the time that the consequence of this bureaucracy is my freedom,” said Davis.

Davis worries about impacts on his career. He said he has long strived to keep his academic work and activism separate, but now thrust into the spotlight as an alleged “conspirator”, he wonders if his scholarship could be affected moving forward.

He has struggled to sleep, and the case has taken a toll on his personal relationships, he said. The 15 defendants are under a strict “no contact” order with each other, which has meant he has been cut off from several close friends, who are also defendants in the case.

He has worked hard to not dwell on the possibility of being locked up for six years: “I suspect I’m going to be afraid at some point and will have to process that … but I’ve been able to be unafraid because of the support and solidarity we’ve received.”

Both Davis and Rakotz said they didn’t want the case to discourage others from organizing against ICE and hoped people would stay focused on immigrant communities subjected to ICE enforcement and violence.

“Far more important than anything that happens to us is continuing to organize against the armed masked people in our streets,” Davis said.

Rakotz said she, too, has tried not to think about what a conviction would mean. “I am free right now and I refuse to let this stop me from enjoying life and doing what I can to positively impact the community.”

She paused. “And if I have to go to prison because I did what I could for the greater good, I’m ready and willing to do that.”

articles.title: Angus Taylor has inadvertently taken centre stage in an Icac hearing – and the fallout could be profound
articles.excerpt:
If the opposition leader was funding one side of a vicious factional war, it would be hard for many in the party to stomach

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Independent Co...
articles.body_text:
If the opposition leader was funding one side of a vicious factional war, it would be hard for many in the party to stomach

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Independent Commission against Corruption inquiries have an uncanny tendency to sprawl in unexpected directions.

Just ask former New South Wales premier, Gladys Berejiklian, who was caught on tape with her secret boyfriend, former NSW MP Daryl Maguire, during an investigation into his dealings with developers. Or former premier Barry O’Farrell, who was tripped up over a bottle of Penfolds Grange during an inquiry into state water contracts.

In the Icac hearing on Tuesday into allegations of corruption against people associated with the NSW Liberal party, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, took centre stage – even though he was hundreds of kilometres away in Rockhampton. He is not accused of wrongdoing.

The bombshell came in a group chat of young Liberal power brokers known as “Reformers” who are at the centre of Icac’s Operation Rosny, an investigation into alleged breaches of the NSW Electoral Funding Act.

The secretive Reformers group were a sub-faction of the right of the NSW Liberals who were intent on restoring conservative values to the party. The Icac is looking at alleged undisclosed donations made by the fugitive developer Jean Nassif and others that were used to fund the Reformers’ efforts to recruit members and take over branches.

Taylor surfaced in a message from Dallas McInerney, head of the Catholic Schools Association NSW and supporter of the Reformers, which was shared with the group in March 2021. In the message McInerney allegedly said he planned to “to shake down Angus for $10,000” while at a meeting in Canberra.

On Tuesday, a former NSW Liberal parliamentary staffer and associate of the Reformers, Dylan Whitelaw, who is not named in Icac’s allegations, gave evidence. He was shown a message sent to the group in which he allegedly wrote “Dallas has told me he got the commitment from Angus the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation!” Whitelaw said he did not recall sending the message, nor did he recall Taylor making a financial contribution to the Reformers.

We don’t know whether Taylor actually made the payments – and even if he did, there’s a question over whether they were covered by NSW’s political donations laws. A statement issued after Taylor was named at Icac did not deny the payments or address them directly.

“The Leader is not a party to the matters before the commission, nor has he been approached,” a spokesperson for Taylor said in a statement. “Donations and fundraising activities are declared in accordance with the rules and are a matter for the Party.”

The implications, if these payments were made, though, could be profound.

For a start, there is a question as to whether these are undeclared political donations or in breach of the donation caps in NSW’s Electoral Funding Act.

This would be serious for the leader of a major political party.

But there is also the internal political fallout. The Reformers were set up to demolish the Centre Right faction and wrest control of the NSW party from the Moderates.

If it was proven that their leader was funding one side of a vicious factional war, it would be hard for many in the party to stomach.

Taylor does not appear as a donor on the NSW donation disclosure register in 2020-2021, 2021-22 or 2022-23. He is listed on the federal donations register as having made only one $1,500 donation in 2010 – to Malcolm Turnbull’s campaign.

Icac is also investigating other alleged donors to the Reformers, including Nassif, former hotelier Michael O’Hara, and Catholic Schools NSW. McInerney has stood down as Catholic Schools NSW CEO and is expected to give evidence later in the inquiry.

Nassif allegedly paid a total of $2m to Reformers members Christian Ellis, Charles Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood. O’Hara paid $165,000 and Catholic Schools NSW donated over $250,000.

Some of these funds were allegedly paid under sham arrangements to public relations firms controlled by Ellis and Greenwood.

Most of Tuesday was spent hearing evidence from Whitelaw, who joined the Liberals when he left school and who was vice-president of the Mittagong branch of the Liberal party. He soon fell into the orbit of the conservative Reformers.

In 2019 he went to work for Catholic Schools NSW and later for Ellis’s public relations firm, Beckington, again on Reformer work.

His evidence revealed how Catholic Schools NSW, a registered charity, was used to employ young men in the Reformers.

The organisation is responsible for funding Catholic schools in NSW and administers nearly $4bn in state and federal grants for the sector.

The allegations will now turn attention to whether there are breaches of charities laws and politicisation of a major education funding body.

Whitelaw was employed by Catholic Schools NSW as a data processor, a junior role, but told the commission he spent much of his time on Reformers work, which included organising events and recruiting like-minded conservative members in the Wollondilly area.

Robert Assaf, a key member of the Reformers, was also employed at Catholic Schools. Cecile Piat, Ellis’ wife, was employed as a secretary.

“Rob did very little Catholic Schools work,” Whitelaw said. “It was a running joke between me and Rob,” he said, adding that his “guess” was Assaf spent 60% of his time on Reformer work and 40% on “his real job.”

There is a live issue, still to be addressed by Icac, as to whether the contributions to the Reformers were caught by the NSW political donations laws.

The group was doing political work – it was recruiting conservatives to branches, trying to take control of the Liberal party administrative structure and attempting to influence policy, but it had no formal status within the Liberal party.

O’Hara, the hotelier and former business partner of right power broker and MP Damien Tudehope, took issue with whether the payments he made to the Reformers were political donations.

The Reformers were not registered as a political party, or a third-party entity, raising questions about how far the Electoral Funding Act reaches to require disclosure of donations to entities outside the formal party structure.

Counsel assisting the inquiry, Peggy Dwyer SC spent considerable time seeking to establish that O’Hara knew the Reformers were recruiting conservatives to branches, and that the objective was to take over branches from the Moderates.

But O’Hara became disillusioned by 2022 and pulled his funding. In his last conversation with the Reformers, he told Jean Claude Perrottet he would only pay the most recent invoices, adding: “I may as well support the Greens or Teals, as Dominic [Perrottet] was rolled on so many issues instead of prosecuting the principles I believed he stood for.”

articles.title: Captain Chris ‘Hunter-Killer’ Philp takes on French navy single-handed
articles.excerpt:
Shots fired in the Channel are all in a day’s work for the intrepid shadow home secretary

C’est magnifique, mais ce n’est pas la guerre. Captain Chris ‘Hunter-Killer’ Philp had been on patrol since f...
articles.body_text:
Shots fired in the Channel are all in a day’s work for the intrepid shadow home secretary

C’est magnifique, mais ce n’est pas la guerre. Captain Chris ‘Hunter-Killer’ Philp had been on patrol since first light in the English Channel. While the rest of the country was still asleep, the Philpster was scanning the horizon for rubber dinghies full of illegal immigrants. Something he had never done in his previous life as immigration minister. Back then he had sought to rehouse new arrivals in hotels. Now he wanted to send them to a watery grave.

It had been a quiet morning. Too quiet. Just the one sighting of a child with a rubber ring paddling off the beach in Boulogne. But Hunter-Killer was taking no chances. All it takes is one child and before long there will be hundreds of thousands making the crossing with swimming aids bought from the local Carrefour. So the Philpster had called in the RAF. Minutes later, a Typhoon FGR4 had blasted the kid out of the water. Job done. Pour encourager les autres.

Half an hour later, all hell broke loose. A French warship had appeared to starboard. The next thing Hunter-Killer heard was the sound of 17 indistinct pops in the distance. “Get down,” he shouted to his crew. “We’re under attack.” Weirdly, no one on board the Philpster’s MTB disguised as a fishing vessel seemed remotely worried. How come they were so slow to sense danger? There again, few had the finely tuned antennae of the Philpster. Those years of training with the Special Boat Service had paid off.

Hunter-Killer threw himself on the floor of the wheelhouse, waiting for the gunshots to stop. “I think it’s safe now,” a deckhand said. “It was just some French sailor firing some shots from a handgun away from us into the sea. It wasn’t as if he was aiming at us or anything. He was probably just test-firing. It’s no big deal.”

“You don’t understand,” squeaked Captain Philpster. “This was a definite attempt by the French to intimidate me. Typical of Johnny Foreigner to send out a warship to track the shadow home secretary. They don’t like it up ’em. They’ve probably got special guns that fire round corners. So you think they’re shooting in a harmless direction but the bullets turn 90 degrees in flight. I came within a whisker of being hit. Not that anyone gets to intimidate Hunter-Killer. Help! Help!”

The crew looked rather nonplussed. Most of them hadn’t even heard the shots – “he was probably using a silencer,” said the Philpster – let alone had any idea they had come under serious attack. But Hunter-Killer was adamant. The Frenchies had been out to eliminate him. He had got too close to stopping the small boat crossings and Macron would never stand for that. So he was prepared to stop at nothing. Even risk starting a global conflict. Well, it had ended badly for Napoleon and it would end badly for Macron. Nor should the French forget that it had been the English who saved them in the second world war. Well, we wouldn’t make that mistake again.

“Sacré bleu!” said one member of Border Force. “There are often exercises at sea involving the Royal or the French navy, and shots are occasionally fired, usually using blanks. This may be nothing at all.”

The Philpster ordered him to keep quiet. The last thing he wanted was any collaborators speaking in French. Careless talk costs vies. He pulled the burner phone out of his pocket and speed-dialled Kemi. “I’m under attack,” he gasped. “Even though the French aren’t shooting at me, they are definitely shooting at me. They don’t want me to stop any small boats crossing the Channel, even though I haven’t yet seen any small boats. We need to be on our guard. The smuggling gangs must now be using invisible dinghies.”

Kemi’s eyes lit up. If only she was prime minister, she would be able to launch a tactical first nuclear strike on Calais. OK, there might be some collateral damage in Kent but it would still be worth it. Instead, she had to order the Philpster to disengage with the enemy.

“I can’t do that,” said Hunter-Killer. “While most politicians run from danger, I am trained to run towards it. So what I will do is film a clip of me being extraordinarily brave by doing nothing and then phone the French embassy to complain. If only they put as much effort into intimidating the people smugglers as they put into intimidating me. Not that I was intimidated. But it would be good to see the French navy also firing shots in the opposite direction to the dinghies.”

articles.title: FIFA World Cup: For India, qualification is still just a distant dream
articles.excerpt: As the FIFA World Cup 2026 reached its final week, Gourav Roy, an Indian software engineer living in San Francisco, drove more than 9,650 kilometres (6,000 miles) across the United States to attend bo...
articles.body_text:
As the FIFA World Cup 2026 reached its final week, Gourav Roy, an Indian software engineer living in San Francisco, drove more than 9,650 kilometres (6,000 miles) across the United States to attend both the semifinals and the final.

For Roy, it was the next best thing to what he had grown up dreaming of: seeing India play in the World Cup.

But the possibility of that dream coming true is looking ever more distant as deep-rooted systemic issues and the failure to implement reforms have left the country of 1.45 billion ranked a lowly 138th in the world, failing to even qualify for the 2027 Asian Cup.

“I’ve learned to love without expectation. That’s the burden of the Indian football fan,” said Roy.

While countries with tiny populations like Curacao and Cape Verde qualified for the 2026 World Cup, India remains a prime example of wasted potential in the planet’s most popular sport.

Those working in Indian football say the problems range from poor youth development systems, a lack of popularity, and a national federation (the All India Football Federation) struggling to implement a uniform vision with a loose patchwork of state associations.

“If you ask me, to clean up the system and reorganise it will take a full cycle of four years,” Ravi Puskur, the CEO of Indian Super League (ISL) club FC Goa, told Reuters.

“Then it’s another 20-25 years to get us to the World Cup.”

In cricket-mad India, football remains popular only in a handful of states like West Bengal, Goa, Kerala, Mizoram and Manipur.

The ISL, launched in 2014 with the backing of Reliance Industries, one of India’s biggest conglomerates, tried to change that with limited success.

In 2025, the AIFF and Reliance did not renew their partnership as negotiations stalled amid a Supreme Court case to implement a new constitution for the federation.

This year, under new management led by clubs, the ISL is yet to finalise a broadcaster and announce fixtures.

NorthEast United CEO Mandar Tamhane, who previously led Bengaluru FC, said clubs alone cannot fix Indian football.

“You’re talking about the government, corporate India… it has to be a collective effort,” he said.

“The federation has to make sure the clubs, state associations, the corporates and other stakeholders all work together.”

AIFF executive committee member and Mizoram’s sports minister Lalnghinglova Hmar said the government can help with infrastructure, but for Indian football to improve, the country’s youth development system needs a drastic overhaul.

“In South Korea and Japan, kids play over 40 competitive matches per season. This is missing in India,” he said.

“We start developing players too late. Most under-15 players get only 12 to 15 competitive games yearly. Some get called up to the youth national camp after playing less than 20 competitive games.

“We’re short on qualified coaches. Many states don’t even have a youth league… we just can’t compete like that.”

But India’s size, the very thing that makes it an attractive sports market and led to the huge success of cricket’s Indian Premier League, also makes it difficult for the AIFF to implement widespread reforms.

“If even half the states were doing a proper job at grassroots, things would grow,” Hmar added.

The uncertainty over the ISL, which forced some teams to suspend player salaries last year, also dealt a blow to the clubs’ development programmes.

“If you can provide stability, gradually the investment will increase,” Puskur said.

With India bidding to host the 2036 Olympics, the government is considering the launch of a “sports passport” that allows Indian-origin athletes to represent the country.

The AIFF leadership has backed the initiative, believing it will help improve the national team’s performances. But the proposal is still far from becoming law, and Hmar said Indian football needs to act fast.

“The other nations aren’t sitting idle… if we don’t match them, even if we improve, we will remain where we are,” he said.

While Indian football hangs in limbo, fans like Roy can only live in hope.

“They are talking about a 64-team World Cup,” he said. “It won’t gift us anything, but more places mean more hope.”

articles.title: New audio undercuts Dems who defended Biden, slammed Hur after classified docs report revealed memory loss
articles.excerpt: New recordings between Joe Biden and memoir ghostwriter Mark Zwonitzer have been released. In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall two economic advisers. (Credit: The Oversight P...
articles.body_text:
New recordings between Joe Biden and memoir ghostwriter Mark Zwonitzer have been released. In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall two economic advisers. (Credit: The Oversight Project)

After special counsel Robert Hur’s 2023 investigation and the subsequent report into former President Joe Biden’s retention of classified documents, Democrats rushed to defend the 46th president from his characterization that Biden was an "elderly man with a poor memory."

The left-wing's narrative surrounding Biden's mental cognition — especially as he was running for re-election against President Donald Trump — is now crumbling after audio tapes from the investigation were revealed Monday night.

Prominent Democrats lined up to defend Biden when the initial report was released in 2024, many using the same line that Hur's report was "gratuitous." Then-Vice President Kamala Harris was chief among the chorus of defenders, saying that the report was "inaccurate and inappropriate."

"The way that the president’s demeanor in that report was characterized could not be more wrong on the facts," she told reporters at an event in Washington at the time. She also said the report was "clearly politically motivated, gratuitous." Months later, Biden dropped out of the presidential race and was replaced on the ticket by his No. 2 without a primary election to decide his replacement.

President Joe Biden pauses as he concludes his address to the nation from the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, Wednesday, July 24, 2024, about his decision to drop his Democratic presidential re-election bid. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, Pool)

BIDEN'S HUR INTERVIEW TAPES COULD NOW GO PUBLIC AFTER HIS ATTORNEYS WAVE WHITE FLAG

"What everyone will soon realize is that this is a Republican special counsel who completely went out of his way to editorialize, to include material in his report that is unnecessary and irrelevant to what he was tasked with doing," Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., piled on in comments to ABC at the time.

In 2023, Hur was investigating Biden for retaining classified information. At the center of the investigation were audio tapes of Biden from interviews with his "Promise Me, Dad" memoir ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, from 2016 and 2017.

Hur's report concluded that Biden did, in fact, retain classified documents, but that prosecuting him might not lead to a conviction, because he could be viewed "as a sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory."

"Mr. Biden's memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017 and in his interview with our office in 2023," the report said.

Former special counsel Robert Hur returns from a short break to resume his testimony before the House Judiciary Committee in the Rayburn House Office Building on Capitol Hill on March 12, 2024, in Washington, D.C. Hur investigated President Joe Biden's mishandling of classified documents and published a final report with contentious conclusions about Biden's memory. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

BIDEN’S FIGHT TO KEEP HUR INTERVIEW TAPES UNDER WRAPS SUFFERS FRESH COURT BLOW

After a prolonged legal battle during which Biden sought to keep the audio tapes private, a nonprofit called the Oversight Project obtained them via public records requests. The damning tapes reveal Biden's inability to remember basic names and dates.

In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall the names of two economic advisers.

"I’ll think of his name," said Biden, who at the time was a private citizen and former vice president. "I should write the names down because I keep forgetting them."

There was then a long pause before Zwonitzer prompted Biden by saying Alan Krueger’s name.

Vice President Kamala Harris spoke at the American Federation of Teachers’ 88th National Convention on July 25, 2024, in Houston, Texas. (Montinique Monroe/Getty Images)

BIDEN SCORES TEMPORARY COURT VICTORY AS TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE DELAYS RELEASE OF HUR INVESTIGATION MATERIALS

In another instance, when trying to recall a memorial he attended for a fallen service member, Biden forgot the date of the service and name of the deceased.

"I think I went to that memorial service in Wilmington. It says [REDACTED] December the 4th, but I don't -- I know what this means. Memorial service -- [REDACTED] gets names really f---ed up," said Biden.

"So it says memorial service for [REDACTED]. I don't think her name was [REDACTED]. Or I forget [REDACTED]."

The interviews were marked by consistent lapses in memory.

But in 2024, that didn't stop Democrats from accusing Hur of being a partisan activist who intentionally tried to tarnish Biden and his chances in a rematch against Trump.

Andrew Weissman, a former general counsel to the FBI, cried foul on MSNBC.

"That is not the role of the Department of Justice ... to talk about your memory today — irrelevant, it is gratuitous," he reportedly said. "And it is also exactly what you're not supposed to do, which is putting your thumb on the scale that could have political repercussions."

Andrew Weissman, the top prosecutor from the Russia investigation, confessed he has a "man crush" on the judge overseeing Trump's hush money trial. (MSNBC)

Ian Sams, a spokesperson for Biden's general counsel, said at the time that the report was "gratuitous."

"When you are the first special counsel in history not to indict anybody, there is pressure to criticize and to make, you know, statements that maybe in otherwise you wouldn't make," Sams reportedly said.

"I think this issue of age is already out there, and when November comes, it’s going to be a choice between two people," said Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., told POLITICO. "I was with a congressional leadership about two weeks ago, and no one walked out of that meeting, saying, ‘Oh, my God, it was like he wasn’t in charge.’"

Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., who at the time had just spent a day traveling with Biden, insisted that he was, "at the very top of his game, all the way through it, both in private and in person."

Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI) listens as U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell testifies at a Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee hearing on the Fed's "Semiannual Monetary Policy Report to the Congress," on Capitol Hill on March 3, 2022, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Williams-Pool/Getty Images)

Later in 2024, Biden was yanked from the top of the presidential ticket after an embarrassing debate performance against then-candidate Donald Trump, which showcased his apparent mental decline.

Harris, serving as vice president at the time, was then coronated as the party's presidential nominee despite never winning a primary. When she ran in 2020, Harris never made it to the primaries, dropping out on December 3, 2019, months before the first elections took place.

A Biden spokesperson ducked the former president's memory in a statement to CBS.

"President Biden's conversations for a book a decade ago that discussed his late son are private, and were provided to the Department of Justice on the express condition they stay that way," TJ Ducklo told the outlet. "Reversing course and making them public is just the latest example of this Administration weaponizing the DOJ for political retribution."

"It's wrong, and while President Biden disagrees with today's decision, he also respects the courts and the vital role an independent judiciary plays in a healthy democracy."

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: SEN RAND PAUL: The COVID cover-up had layers. I’m peeling them back one at a time
articles.excerpt:
Laura Ingraham criticizes Dr. Anthony Fauci, suggesting his refusal to be questioned stems from insecurity.

For years, Americans were told the lab-leak theory was dismissed by science itself, settled...
articles.body_text:
Laura Ingraham criticizes Dr. Anthony Fauci, suggesting his refusal to be questioned stems from insecurity.

For years, Americans were told the lab-leak theory was dismissed by science itself, settled by "The Proximal Origin of SARS-CoV-2," the March 2020 paper cited by every fact-checker and health official who wanted the question closed for good. My investigation has now shown, document by document, that the people who peddled that certainty never believed it themselves.

Start with the authors. Newly released Slack messages show Kristian Andersen privately put the odds of a lab origin at 30%. Eddie Holmes said 20, then walked it back to 10. Andersen told colleagues about the "smoking(ish) guns" that left him "not comfortable" with his own conclusions. These scientists publicly ruled out a lab leak, but behind closed doors manipulated the narrative, hoping to stop the evidence building against their public assertions.

They weren't managing it alone. The same authors were in direct contact with the intelligence community and NIH leadership throughout the pandemic. Andersen expected to "have a handler" from within the intelligence community. Holmes cited a source in China he called "my spy." articles.title: Trump administration needs to stop ‘public harassment’ of Fauci and scientists, open letter says
articles.excerpt:
Letter, published before Anthony Fauci will appear before Congress, accuses Republicans of ‘waging a war on individual scientists’

More than 155 scientists, physicians and public health advocates hav...
articles.body_text:
Letter, published before Anthony Fauci will appear before Congress, accuses Republicans of ‘waging a war on individual scientists’

More than 155 scientists, physicians and public health advocates have called for an end to what they describe as the “vilification and harassment of many American scientists” by the Trump administration and its allies.

In an open letter published one day before Anthony Fauci, the former top US government science adviser, is scheduled to appear at a high-profile hearing in US Congress, after the Republican-controlled Senate homeland security and governmental affairs committee compelled him to testify, the scientists and physicians dismissed allegations against the ex-National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (Niaid) director as “baseless”.

Fauci, 85, who helped guide the country’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic as director of the Niaid, is set to testify under subpoena before the committee on Wednesday as a part of its investigation into the origins of the virus and whether US federal officials, including Fauci, misled the public and Congress about the source of the outbreak, a claim that has been made by Senator Rand Paul, a Republican of Kentucky who chairs the committee, for years.

The letter signed by the group of scientists and public health advocates alleges that the Trump administration and its congressional allies are “waging a war on individual scientists, through public harassment, arrests, criminal indictment and ongoing threats of prosecution”.

The letter states that several scientists have come under scrutiny under this administration, but the signatories argue that “the most prominent target of the administration and its allies” is Fauci, who left the federal government in 2022 after leading the Niaid for 38 years.

“The charges against Dr Fauci are baseless, suggesting he covered up the origins of Covid, that he bribed or persuaded other scientists to join his cover-up, that Niaid-funded research sparked the pandemic, that he personally holds patents on the virus, and that he’s working with intelligence agencies to suppress the true story of the pandemic,” the letter states. “No credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges.”

The letter adds that the allegations and accusations about Fauci have led to “five-year period of harassment and threats of violence directed at Dr Fauci and his family”.

“Now, this month, he is being subpoenaed by Congress once again,” it continues. “In over 60 years of public service, Dr Fauci has led the United States through epidemics of HIV and Covid, through outbreaks of Ebola and Sars 1, and through the 2001 anthrax attacks. He has worked tirelessly to advance science and protect the public’s health.

“As the congressional hearings targeting Dr Fauci approach, we are urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts and support good public health and scientific practices so that America’s leadership in innovation remains secure,” the letter concludes.

Ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, Paul, the Republican who chairs the committee, released thousands of pages of Fauci’s diary entries from during the Covid-19 pandemic, which showed Fauci’s efforts to manage and address the pandemic, navigate his relationship with Donald Trump, and reflect on his public profile and media image.

Fauci left the government at the end of 2022 and has said over the years that research has “strongly suggested” that coronavirus most likely emerged through natural origins, probably from animal-to-human transmission.

But he has insisted he keeps a “completely open mind” about other possibilities, including the theory that the virus may have leaked from a lab in China in 2019, and has denied allegations by some Republican lawmakers, including Paul, that he sought to suppress that theory.

Before Trump returned to office last year, Joe Biden issued a pre-emptive pardon to Fauci and other senior officials. But despite the pardon, Paul has referred Fauci to the Department of Justice for “potential criminal prosecution”.
