articles.title: Potential for first Australian oil refinery in 60 years as treasurer braces for inflation from Middle East war
articles.excerpt:
Commonwealth and Western Australia to fund study into construction of large-scale petrol refinery as buffer against fuel vulnerability

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Aus...
articles.body_text:
Commonwealth and Western Australia to fund study into construction of large-scale petrol refinery as buffer against fuel vulnerability

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s first new oil refinery in 60 years could be built in Western Australia under the Albanese government’s long-term strategy to shield the country from future global oil shocks.

The commonwealth and the WA government will fund a $4m early-stage feasibility study into construction of what would be the country’s third large-scale petrol refinery.

A series of refinery closures over the past 25 years means Australia now imports about 90% of its liquid fuels, a vulnerability exposed by the international oil crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

The announcement comes as Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, warned the recent escalation of the Middle East conflict posed “a substantial threat to global inflation”.

Treasury officials in a special weekend government briefing warned the collapse of the ceasefire meant oil prices were likely to remain high in the near future.

“The oil market is now more vulnerable, with weaker buffers against future supply shocks,” the officials said.

With petrol and diesel prices up by 25 cents and 50 cents a litre this month, respectively, the rekindling of the conflict has also boosted expectations that central banks will need to do more to bring inflation back under control – piling more pressure on households.

“The longer this drags out the more serious the consequences for inflation and growth here and around the world,” Chalmers said.

Financial markets were pricing a one-in-three chance of a Reserve Bank rate hike on 11 August. That was down from an even chance on Friday after Brent crude, the oil benchmark, tumbled more than US$10 a barrel on Monday to about US$87 after a pause in fighting over the weekend.

Australia’s oil refining industry has struggled to compete with cheaper overseas providers.

There are just two local refineries in operation: Ampol’s Lytton refinery in Brisbane and Viva Energy’s facility in Geelong.

Building a new refinery would cost billions of dollars, and would probably require ongoing government support to stay competitive.

The proposed WA project, were it to go ahead, would be constructed by Perdaman, the large multinational behind a $4.5bn fertiliser plant in the Pilbara. Perdaman would privately fund the project but could be eligible for taxpayer-funded assistance, such as concessional loans.

BP closed an oil refinery in Fremantle, just south of Perth, in 2021.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and WA premier, Roger Cook, will announce funding for the scoping study after visiting Perdaman’s urea plant in Karratha.

“The longer war in the Middle East goes on the greater the impact on Australia will be, and my government will continue to do everything we can to shield Australia from the worst effects – and set us up for the future,” Albanese said in a statement.

The federal government’s $10.7bn fuel security package, announced in May, included $10m to support feasibility studies into potential projects.

The package also funded a $7.5bn facility to secure extra fuel and fertiliser shipments during the Middle East conflict, and $3.2bn to build an extra 1 billion-litre reserve of diesel and jet fuel.

Chris Bowen, the energy minister, described plans to boost domestic refining capacity as “a sensible and prudent response to secure our energy security”.

But the early-stage support for a new oil refinery will probably face push-back from environmentalists, who have criticised the federal government for doubling down on petrol and diesel rather than using the oil shock to reduce Australia’s reliance on fossil fuels.

articles.title: 'Dr Death', Body Worlds creator Gunther von Hagens, dies at 81
articles.excerpt:
Von Hagens has suffered from Parkinson's Disease for many years

Gunther von Hagens, the creator of the controversial "Body Worlds" exhibitions where dissected human and animal bodies were displayed, ...
articles.body_text:
Von Hagens has suffered from Parkinson's Disease for many years

Gunther von Hagens, the creator of the controversial "Body Worlds" exhibitions where dissected human and animal bodies were displayed, has died at the age of 81, according to his family.

Sometimes known as "Doctor Death", he became famous for developing a technique called plastination, by which fluids and fatty tissue in corpses are replaced by rubber and polymers.

His family said in a statement that he had asked for his body to be made available for plastination and that they intended to carry out his wish.

More than 58 million people worldwide have viewed his exhibitions, the statement said. However, religious groups and others have frequently objected to his display of human remains.

His family's statement said von Hagens died on Friday, a day after being admitted to a clinic in Heidelberg, Germany, with a brain haemorrhage. He had suffered from Parkinson's Disease for nearly two decades.

"It was Gunther von Hagens' own wish to make his body available for plastination after his death," the statement reads. "His family will respect and carry out this wish."

Born in Nazi-occupied Poland in the last months of World War Two, von Hagens grew up in communist East Germany before fleeing to the West in 1970.

In the next few years he developed the plastination process. Specimens came to be used as teaching aids at universities or by research institutes.

But it was not until the late 1990s that he began taking his Body Worlds exhibitions around the world.

Colleagues paid tribute to a "pioneer, a researcher, an inventor" who made "anatomy accessible to the general public", but critics have accused him of voyeurism and profiting commercially from death.

In 2002 he caused further controversy by performing the first public autopsy in London for 170 years on camera. Authorities had warned the event could be illegal but no charges were brought.

'Real bodies' show in Australia controversy

articles.title: Chinese chipmaker shares surge nearly 470% in blockbuster stock market debut
articles.excerpt:
Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker have soared by nearly 470% as they made their debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's tech-heavy Star Market.

The surge has pushed ChangXin Memory Technolog...
articles.body_text:
Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker have soared by nearly 470% as they made their debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's tech-heavy Star Market.

The surge has pushed ChangXin Memory Technologies' (CXMT) stock market valuation to around 3.3 trillion yuan ($487bn; £365bn), making it the most valuable listed company in mainland China.

The spectacular debut comes despite a sharp sell-off in technology stocks around the world this month.

CXMT manufactures dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips that power AI data centres, mobile phones, PCs, tablets and other devices.

The firm, which was founded in 2016 by Chairman Zhu Yiming, is headquartered in Hefei, Anhui Province in eastern China.

The company has said it plans to use most of the proceeds from the initial public offering (IPO) to boost production of memory chips and carry out more research and developments.

The stellar performance of its IPO will offer some comfort to Chinese financial officials, who have been rolling out measures to help curb a stock market slump that wiped out more than $1.5tn in recent weeks.

Analysts said the jump was also being driven by demand for the shares far outstripping supply.

"The reason for the extraordinary bounce this morning is that only 7% of the shares are available for trading," Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at Hargreaves Lansdown told the BBC's Today programme.

It also highlights Chinese investors' strong appetite for a homegrown chipmaker, as the government in Beijing pushes ahead with plans to make its technology industry self-reliant.

South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix and US-based Micron dominate the Dram market, with the three companies accounting for around 90% of global production.

Earlier this month, SK Hynix raised $26.5bn (£19.8bn) in its New York share offering, marking the largest ever listing by a foreign firm in the US.

The company, a key supplier to AI chip giant Nvidia, said it had sold 177.9 million American depositary shares for $149 each.

The shares surged as much as 17% on Friday in their first day of trading on the Nasdaq but have since given up some of that gain.

SK Hynix saw its market value top $1tn in its home country in May, lifted by the boom in demand for AI chips.

Once an affordable component used to build devices, memory prices have more than doubled in recent months - and are still rising.

Some big tech firms have hiked the price of popular gadgets, such as tablets and video game consoles, to cope with rising component costs.

Ellie Wong, an analyst at technology research firm TrendForce, told Reuters, external such price increases were expected to continue until the end of 2027.

"Amid persistent supply shortages, many customers are seeking to diversify their memory supplier base, which should significantly benefit CXMT and create more business opportunities," she said.

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky argued Sunday that the war with Iran has "weakened" the United States.

"The U.S. has been significantly weakened by the war with Iran," the congressman wrote in a Sunday post on X.

"This administration depleted our missile defenses, drained our oil reserves, sacrificed our men & women, inflated the price of consumer goods, increased our debt, and neglected our domestic needs…" he continued, adding, "all for Israel."

Some parts of Massie’s criticism align with publicly reported effects of the conflict. The Energy Department authorized the release of 172 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, while news reports and congressional spending measures have pointed to heavy demand for U.S. missile-defense systems and billions of dollars in additional defense funding. His broader assertion that the United States has been "significantly weakened" is a political judgment.

HOUSE REPUBLICAN THOMAS MASSIE SUGGESTS OBAMACARE COULD NOW BE LABELED 'TRUMPCARE'

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House early on Monday morning to request a comment.

Massie, who has served in the U.S. House of Representatives for more than 13 years, lost the May Republican primary in Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to President Donald Trump-backed challenger, retired Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein.

MASSIE LASHES OUT WHEN PRESSED ON EX-GIRLFRIEND'S ALLEGATIONS OF AFFAIR WITH GOP FIREBRAND

In a Friday post on X, Massie accused Trump of shifting toward a neoconservative foreign policy, writing, "Why did he flip to neocon?"

Former National Counterterrorism Center Director Joe Kent, who quit earlier this year due to his opposition to the Iran war, has been calling for President Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from the region.

EX-COUNTERTERRORISM OFFICIAL JOE KENT CONTINUES CALLING FOR US MILITARY WITHDRAWAL FROM MIDDLE EAST

U.S. President Donald Trump motions to reporters after getting off Air Force One on July 22, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"The Israelis know they can’t fight this war without the U.S., so their goal is to get us on board with more strikes, ground troops, etc., in the hopes that American causalities will sway public opinion enough to escalate into a chaotic, drawn-out war," Kent wrote in part of a Sunday post on X. "Our only viable option is to leave now—President Trump should use this pause in fighting to get our troops out & use quiet economic diplomacy to reopen the SOH & BAM."

The Trump administration has defended the military campaign as necessary to destroy Iran’s missile capabilities, cripple its navy, sever its support for terrorist proxies and prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapon. The White House has also credited what it called "decisive American strength" with producing an agreement intended to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Burnham says there are ‘big decisions’ ahead on making council tax fairer – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Labour’s 2024 manifesto did not include any specific commitments on council tax but two models are being floated

Andy Burnham has said there are “big decisions” ahead of his government on council tax...
articles.body_text:
Labour’s 2024 manifesto did not include any specific commitments on council tax but two models are being floated

Andy Burnham has said there are “big decisions” ahead of his government on council tax, as he criticised the unfairness of the current system for making some people pay higher rates than are levied on more expensive homes in London.

In his interview with Laura Kuenssberg for the BBC’s Panorama programme, Burnham said:

double quotation markThere are people here in Greater Manchester who pay a much higher council tax than people living in much larger homes in London.

So the chancellor before, Rachel Reeves, was right to start to reform council tax to create some fairness there in relation to people in homes that are of much greater value, who haven’t seen their council tax go up over the years because of the failure to revalue the banding.

That’s an example of something that I think was right and fair.

double quotation markWe need to honour the manifesto upon which Labour was elected, and if I was to bring forward any changes, obviously people would rightly say, well, is this consistent with that manifesto? So there are big decisions ahead, you are right about that.

Labour’s 2024 manifesto did not include any specific pledges on council tax. But during the election campaign Labour ruled out changing council tax bands. This did not stop Rachel Reeves last year announcing a council tax surcharge on homes worth more than £2m – a policy that could be seen as a breach of those campaign promises.

In a story for the i today, Eleanor Langford says Burnham is considering options to replace council tax and stamp duty. She says:

double quotation markTwo models are competing for support: a proportional property tax, which would replace both council tax and stamp duty with a flat 0.48 per cent annual charge on a home’s current value; or a land value tax – an annual charge based on the value of the land a property sits on, rather than the building.

Government sources have played down this report. We should get a more formal response at the lobby briefing later.

Keir Starmer resisting calls to stand down was “selfish and stubborn”, according to the current sole Scottish Labour leadership contender, Monica Lennon.

As the Press Association reports, the earliest high profile call for Starmer to quit came from former Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar, who broke cover in February. Sarwar is now leaving Holyrood having been given a seat in the Lords and a job as a business minister by Andy Burnham.

Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland this morning, Lennon – a former MSP who will return to Holyrood to replace Sarwar under the regional list system – said Starmer was one of the main reasons why Scottish Labour won just 17 seats in the Holyrood election in May. She said:

double quotation markClearly, the focus is the May election and what’s happened in Scotland.

The party has had its worst election result ever in the history of the Scottish parliament – in fact we’ve been losing seats and votes since 1999, so there’s a downward trend that cannot be ignored.

There’s lots of reasons, but I think the primary reason was Keir Starmer.

We couldn’t get a proper hearing on the doorsteps or around the country because that was the first thing that was brought up.

People felt they saw Keir Starmer and his words and actions didn’t match – there was a deep disappointment.

double quotation markI think, on reflection, Keir Starmer should have read the room, I think he was selfish and stubborn and I think that’s been a big part of our problem.

That has contaminated people’s view of Scottish Labour.

While the party is at its lowest ebb since the creation of the Scottish Parliament in terms of MSPs, Lennon warned: “It can get worse”.

The soon-to-be Glasgow MSP is the first to throw her hat in the ring to replace Sarwar, but has encouraged others to do so. She said:

double quotation markScottish Labour’s got some serious decisions to make, and it’s really important that our members have their say, that they’re heard.

I hope that other colleagues do come forward because I would welcome a debate, a discussion and a contest, because I think we really need to have that.

Denis Campbell is the Guardian’s health policy editor.

Andy Burnham must convince voters of the “moral” and “positive” case for reforming social care, not just that it will help the NHS, health thinktanks said today.

The practical benefits that an overhaul of the system would bring for millions of older and disabled people and their families are also a strong argument the prime minister should make, not just less pressure on overcrowded hospitals, they believe.

Natasha Curry, the Nuffield Trust’s deputy director of policy, said:

double quotation markIt is right to recognise that the NHS and social care are deeply interconnected but the case for fixing social care extends far beyond protecting the NHS. There is a moral imperative to ensure older and disabled people can live independently with dignity and a compelling economic case too.

Millions of people have unmet care needs, while unpaid carers and disabled adults are too often prevented from working, participating in their communities and planning for their futures because the support they need simply isn’t there.

While it would help, reducing the number of people who get stuck in hospital despite being medically fit to leave – delayed discharges - won’t on its own get the NHS back to functioning smoothly, she added.

double quotation markBetter social care would undoubtedly help some patients leave hospital more quickly but we should avoid suggesting that fixing social care alone will fix the NHS.

Sarah Woolnough, the chief executive of the King’s Fund, welcomed Burnham’s determination to transform social care after successive governments “consigned [it] to the politically ‘too difficult’ box”.

His efforts to build public support for radical change must go beyond rhetoric about the NHS, she said.

double quotation markDebates about social care are too often haunted by ‘death tax’ rhetoric and the costs of improving the system rather than focussed on the tangible benefits reform could bring for people and families.

If the prime minister wants to succeed where previous governments have failed, he must make a positive case for reform and build a shared understanding of why change matters.

The Casey commission’s already-planned engagement with the public is an “opportunity to build understanding of social care and what reform could mean for people and their families”, added Woolnough.

As I explained earlier this month, we are no longer having comments open regularly below the line (BTL) on this blog. We are sorry about that, and the views of readers who complained about this BTL last week were noted.

I was away for most of last week, but I was reading the blog and the comments and I am grateful to everyone who made a point of saying how much they appreciated the blog. And I particularly enjoyed the poetry tributes, like the My Way version from Hesfalleninthewater and the Cole Porter one from AverageObserver, which was so lovely I’m tempted to quote it on my CV. Thank you.

The fact that we are closing comments does not mean we want to stop hearing from you.

From today, if you want to contact me, or anyone else writing the blog when I am not here, please email politics.live@theguardian.com.

You can email about anything but I am hoping that readers will use this email address for four things in particular.

1) Corrections. If I make a mistake, please flag it up and I will correct it. Blog posts are written and published quickly, and some errors do get through. It is even helpful to have typos pointed out; no mistake is too small to correct.

2) Comments (for publication). When we announced that we were closing comments BTL, many of you said you greatly value hearing what other readers think about the politics stories of the day. I would like to let this carry on by using some comments ATL. In particular, I would welcome comments that: contain new information about a story being covered ATL (ideally with links); contain comments or arguments about those stories that readers may find original and interesting; or signpost readers to other stories or articles they may find interesting (again, with links please).

It may take a while before I work out how best to mix comments with all the other material used ATL. I’m sure I will end up only using some of the comments submitted. But it is important and helpful to me to know what you think about what is in the news, so do please send in your thoughts anyway.

When I do include comments, I am less likely to quote in full anything longer than about 150 words.

And I will assume that readers are happy to be quoted by name unless they say otherwise.

3) Questions. If you have a question, do email. If I think readers generally may be interested in the answer, I will post the Q&A ATL (as I used to do when comments were open BTL.)

4) Complaints. If you don’t like the way I am covering anything, or not covering something, do say. I don’t have any control over other aspects of the Guardian’s reporting, but I always want to know if people have concerns about what I am writing.

All emails will get read, and I will try to reply to most or all of them too. But it is hard to know how many will come in.

If you want to contact me very quickly, I will probably see your message sooner if you use social media. You can reach me on Bluesky at @andrewsparrowgdn.bsky.social or, if you still use X, at @AndrewSparrow.

Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, has said that he hopes MPs can find “a real and lasting consensus” on social care.

In a statement issued in response to Andy Burnham’s comments on the topic (see 9.03am), Davey said:

double quotation markI know for a fact this morning that carers I know will feel a sense of hope that politicians may finally do something serious to fix care in our country.

I am ready to roll up my sleeves and do whatever I can to find a real and lasting consensus on social care.

Family carers must be at the heart of any new system, everyone must get the care they need and no one should lose their home as a result.

Good morning. Yesterday Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told Sky News that, while Andy Burnham spent his first week as PM focusing on cost of living issues, this week the public would see “a prime minister that runs towards big and difficult issues rather than runs away from [them]”. Those challenges include reforming social care and, as Peter Walker reports, Burnham has pledged to use “whatever political capital I have” to finally fix the crumbling social care system in England, saying that without rapid action the NHS could effectively collapse.

Burnham was speaking in a 30-minute interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg going out on Panorama tonight. The BBC put the full interview on iPlayer at 6am this morning, and there is a write-up on the BBC’s website here.

Burnham is due to give a speech on social care on Wednesday, but he is due to be addressing other problem issues this week as well. According to Andrew McDonald and Megan McElroy in their London Playbook briefing for Politico, tomorrow we are getting some announcement on getting young people back to work, on Thursday a defence-related announcement is due, and on Friday Burnham is expected to unveil plans (first reported in the Sunday Times) to give more control over how government money gets spent in their areas.

In his interview with Kuenssberg, Burnham was asked if he would put a new social care system in place before the next election. He did not make that commitment; he has only got three years at best, and full reform could take the best part of a decade. But he did say that he wanted to go “as quickly as I can on the reform” and that there were “major changes you can make before the next election”.

Burnham does not need Tory votes to pass legislation to reform social care in the Commons because he has a working majority of 166. But Burnham’s plans won’t survive if the next election results in Labour being replaced by a government committed to ripping them up. Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, has indicated that he hopes Burnham will produce plans that the Liberal Democrats can support. But Reform UK and the Conservatives have both signalled that they might use their opposition to the Burnham plan. When Burnham was health secretary before the 2010 general election, he floated a proposal to fund better social care through a levy on inheritance. The Tories immediately labelled this a death tax, it became hugely unpopular, and Labour had largely dropped the idea even before they lost the election.

We don’t know what Burnham will propose this time; the veteran Whitehall fixer Louise Casey is leading a review, and Burnham is expected to ask her to produce a final report soon, instead of waiting until 2028 as originally planned. But Burnham has talked about the case for a “care levy”.

In an article for the Sunday Telegraph yesterday, Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson, said his party would oppose anything that amounted to a “radical tax grab”. He said voters “rightly want meaningful efficiency savings, not another tax assault”, and he challenged Burnham to hold an election on this issue. He has been repeating this message on GB News.

This morning, in an open letter to Burnham, Kemi Badenoch has implied that she is willing to work with Labour on this. “The Conservatives are happy to work with you and other parties on reforming social care,” she says. But she also makes it clear that she will fight like fury any plan Burnham is realistically likely to propose.

double quotation markBut we will only support a solution that abides by two core principles.

First, any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives.

Second, the money must be found by reducing current spending. You must rule out any tax rises, or increased borrowing that will ultimately fall on the next generation to pay for.

Compared to the last Conservative government’s budget plans, spending in 2028/29 alone will be £152bn higher (that’s 11% above what was planned in that year under the Conservatives). As a result, taxes will be £105bn higher (up 8%) and borrowing will be £47bn higher (more than double previous plans).

The tax burden has risen to a record high under Labour, and there is already speculation that you will increase taxes further at the budget this autumn in order to pay for all the things you have announced in your first week, plus the outstanding gaps in funding for the defence investment plan.

(Labour is spending a lot more than the last Conservative government budgeted for the second half of this decade. But the Tory long-term spending projections were widely criticised at the time by economists as unrealistically low.)

I will post more on Burnham’s BBC interview soon.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Afternoon: Andy Burnham meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, at a naval base in the UK.

As I explained earlier this month, we are no longer going to have comments open below the line on this blog. From today, if you want to contact me, or anyone else writing the blog when I am not here, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. I will post a bit more on how we hope to use this email system a bit later.

articles.title: Prince William likely 'livid' over Meghan Markle's 'tasteless' photos at Princess Diana's home: expert
articles.excerpt:
Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," recounts how Kate Middleton rebounded after her 2007 breakup with Prince William before the couple reunited.

Meghan Markle shared photos of her children, Prin...
articles.body_text:
Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," recounts how Kate Middleton rebounded after her 2007 breakup with Prince William before the couple reunited.

Meghan Markle shared photos of her children, Princess Lilibet and Prince Archie, frolicking around the late Princess Diana's childhood home and experts are calling Markle's move "tasteless."

This week, Markle crafted an Instagram post from the family's recent U.K. visit. She captioned her post, "Summer Holiday," and one of the images shows Prince Harry with his kids walking on a grassy path with hedges and large trees. The photo is believed to be taken at Althorp, the Spencer family’s ancestral estate.

In the photo, Archie and Harry are carrying bouquets, which seemingly suggest that they visited Diana's burial site, which is on an island in the middle of her family's estate.

A royal expert says Prince William is likely "livid" that Meghan Markle shared photos from Princess Diana's ancestral estate. (Getty Images)

Hilary Fordwich, British royals expert, told Fox News Digital that Prince Harry's oldest brother, Prince William, is likely "livid" by Markle's photos.

KING CHARLES KEPT PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON IN THE DARK ABOUT SECRET HARRY AND MEGHAN REUNION: REPORT

"Not only is Prince William likely to be livid regarding such commercialization of Althorp in such a tacky tasteless media post, it’ll fuel his disgust so he shall thwart any major re-entry," she began. "Likewise,  Camilla, courtiers, palace aides, security officials & other institutional gatekeepers who are duty bound to protect the monarchy, will all do their utmost to thwart MM & H’s attempts."

"Not only is Prince William likely to be livid regarding such commercialization of Althorp in such a tacky tasteless media post, it’ll fuel his disgust so he shall thwart any major re-entry."

Richard Fitzwilliams, royal expert, pointed out that the Spencer's must have given the Duke and Duchess of Sussex permission to visit Althorp, therefore her post is "permissible."

PRINCE HARRY LONGS FOR HIS OLD ROYAL LIFE AS AMERICA ISN'T WHAT HE EXPECTED, EXPERTS SAY

"Meghan shared pictures of their children on what is assumed is Althorp, home of the Spencer family. That would have been allowed by the Spencer's and is therefore permissible," he told Fox News Digital.

Fitzwilliams continued, "What is important is the silence Harry and Meghan have somehow managed to maintain after seeing King Charles and Queen Camilla in contrast to what has happened previously. It will have been made clear that there would be no future meetings if they had talked to any of the media."

An aerial view shows the burial site of Diana, Princess of Wales, at the Althorp Estate in Althorp, United Kingdom. (David Goddard/Getty Images)

Helena Chard, British broadcaster and photographer, called Markle's decision of sharing a private family moment publicly "predictable."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"As for Meghan posting photos of the children at Diana’s family home. It is a predictable move. It ties them to history without using a title. However it also shows a slight tension, wanting the Royal story when it helps, while keeping distance when it doesn’t," Chard said.

"The public understands Peace in Private but basically the Crown has to come first," she concluded.

A photo of Kate Middleton, Prince William, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Chris Jackson/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

On Harry and Meghan's recent trip to the U.K., they were reportedly reunited with King Charles and Queen Camilla. Charles had not seen his grandchildren since 2022.

"No doubt KCIII wants his 'dear boy' H back within the royal fold with limited family contact & a controlled private reconciliation. But given the stance of Prince William there will not be a return to any significant working-royal role," Fordwich told Fox News Digital.

Harry, Meghan and their kids reportedly reunited with King Charles and Queen Camilla during their recent U.K. trip. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"The entire family is most wary of the institutional risk H & MM are likely to cause at any given moment via leaks to the media. MM sharing photos which appear to be taken at Althorp of her children is a ghastly exploitative move & precisely why the couple aren’t trusted," the royal expert continued.

"She is being predictably provocative & tasteless since Princess Diana’s resting place is purposely at Althorp, a most private family mourning location & deeply symbolic being Princess Diana’s ancestral home."

Princess Diana died in 1997. She was photographed here in 1983. (Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images)

Chard is highly doubtful that Charles' visit with his estranged son means Harry will be accepted back into the "royal arena."

"I doubt Charles will just let the Sussexes back into the Royal arena, especially as there has been no genuine contrition. A family reunion is one thing. A return to royal life is another," she said. "Harry and Meghan would need to take responsibility and offer a proper apology to the King and to the country. Hasn’t happened so far and without it, moving forward is impossible."

Janelle Ash is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital covering Hollywood, celebrity culture and breaking entertainment news through exclusive reporting, interviews and in-depth storytelling.

articles.title: Heated Lindsay Clancy courtroom exchange over 911 call, crime scene photos sets stage for mom’s murder trial
articles.excerpt: A jury has been seated in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial as legal analyst Donna Rotunno explains how the defense's postpartum psychosis argument could shape one of the most closely watched criminal c...
articles.body_text:
A jury has been seated in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial as legal analyst Donna Rotunno explains how the defense's postpartum psychosis argument could shape one of the most closely watched criminal cases in Massachusetts.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A jury has been seated in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three young children inside the family’s home while suffering from what her attorneys say was severe postpartum psychosis.

The panel of 12 women and six men was finalized Thursday in Plymouth Superior Court, clearing the way for opening statements Monday. The trial is expected to center not on whether Clancy, 32, caused the children’s deaths, but whether she was legally responsible for her actions.

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at at the prestigious Mass General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN

Lindsay Clancy was indicted on three counts each of murder in the 2023 deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson and 7-month-old son Callan. She pleaded not guilty to the charges. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

Her attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children but plan to argue that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and lacked criminal responsibility. Prosecutors allege the killings were intentional and carefully planned.

"It is usually a hard battle to win," criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno told Fox News Digital of the defense's insanity bid. "But given the fact that she has such a documented history of treatment and going to doctors and being diagnosed and seeking out more treatment when she wasn’t doing well, I think she can lay the groundwork for it."

Rotunno said Clancy’s attorneys are likely to emphasize that her condition allegedly continued to deteriorate even as she sought medical help.

"She continued to get worse. She continued to seek treatment," Rotunno said, pointing to reports that Clancy discussed hearing voices and was prescribed several medications before the children’s deaths.

Clancy’s prior work as a nurse could cut both ways at trial. Prosecutors may argue that her medical background made her more capable of understanding her treatment and actions, but Rotunno said the defense could use the same fact to demonstrate the severity of her alleged psychosis.

"She was a nurse and still so out of it that she didn’t know she shouldn’t be taking all this stuff," Rotunno said. "That, to me, doesn’t play into the intention on this. It’s the total opposite."

Lindsay Clancy with two of her three children in this undated photo. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/ Facebook)

Authorities said Patrick Clancy left the family’s Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023, to pick up takeout food and an item from a pharmacy.

While he was gone, prosecutors allege, Lindsay Clancy used exercise bands to strangle the children before jumping from a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

FLORIDA AG SEEKS JUDGE'S IMPEACHMENT AFTER BABY DROWNING COVID INSANITY ACQUITTAL

The fall left her paralyzed, and she now uses a wheelchair.

Cora and Dawson were pronounced dead after being taken to a Plymouth hospital. Callan was flown to Boston Children’s Hospital and died several days later. The medical examiner determined that Cora and Dawson died from asphyxia and that Callan died from complications of asphyxia.

Exterior view of the home of Patrick and Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, MA on Wednesday, Feb. 15, 2023. Lindsay Clancy, 32, allegedly killed their three children here before attempting to take her own life on Jan. 24, 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Clancy’s mental condition in the months and weeks before the killings are expected to become the central battleground at trial.

LUIGI MANGIONE OVERRULED HIS OWN LAWYERS WITH A 'CHANGE OF HEART' ON PSYCH DEFENSE, LEGAL EXPERT SAYS

Her attorneys say she sought help repeatedly as she struggled with depression, sleeplessness, suicidal thoughts and voices urging her to harm herself and the children.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

She was admitted to a psychiatric hospital weeks before the deaths and was prescribed several medications as providers attempted to treat her worsening symptoms.

According to lawsuits filed by Lindsay and Patrick Clancy against her medical providers, she heard a voice on the day of the killings telling her it was her "last chance" to kill the children and herself.

The lawsuits accuse her providers of failing to properly diagnose, treat and monitor a severe postpartum psychiatric condition.

The defense is expected to argue Clancy lacks criminal responsibility because she suffered from postpartum psychosis and was overmedicated. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan ruled Friday that the media and public may not record, display, reproduce or distribute Patrick Clancy’s initial 911 call or autopsy photographs of the children.

The ruling came after Patrick requested that the evidence be shielded by media dissemination.

Reporters may also describe what is heard or shown in court but cannot broadcast or publish the recording or images themselves, according to the two-page order.

Exterior view of the home of Patrick and Lindsay Clancy in Duxbury, MA on Wednesday, Feb. 15, 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

The privacy dispute produced a heated courtroom exchange Thursday after the jury was seated.

Patrick Clancy asked Sullivan to limit the public and media’s ability to record, broadcast or distribute his initial 911 call, family and crime-scene photographs of the children, autopsy images and the clothing the children were wearing.

His attorney, David Meier, said the request was not intended to close the courtroom, prevent jurors from seeing the evidence or interfere with either side’s case. Instead, he argued that allowing the materials to circulate online would cause lasting emotional harm to Patrick Clancy.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is expected to last six to eight weeks, and the witness list contains more than 200 names. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Lindsay Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, supported Patrick’s request and accused prosecutors of planning to present the evidence in a manner designed to "inflame" the jury.

"Even though we’re in a court, let’s talk a little bit about humanity," Reddington said. "Let’s talk a little bit about how we should try this case."

Reddington said Patrick had suffered "one of the worst tragedies that anyone could ever suffer" and was attempting to rebuild his life.

"How that guy is still not an emotional basket case is beyond me. But nevertheless, he is trying hard to move on with his life. He has, as the court is aware, divorced. He’s remarried. He has a family. He has his extended family," he said.

Lindsay and Patrick Clancy with two of their three children in this undated photo. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/ Facebook)

Reddington accused the prosecution of trying "to put a circus in front of this jury" and later called its approach "reprehensible."

"The district attorney wants to put that guy on the witness stand and show little onesies with bodily fluid of his child?" he said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Sullivan interrupted and reminded Reddington that the issue before the court was whether the media could record or distribute the evidence, rather than whether prosecutors could introduce it at trial.

Sprague began responding that the defense wanted to "rush past what happened to these children" and "whitewash away what happened," but Sullivan cut off the exchange.

Superior Court Judge William Sullivan presides over day three of jury selection Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in the triple murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of murdering her three young children in 2023 in their Duxbury, Massachusetts home.  (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

Reddington argued that calling one first responder after another would produce cumulative testimony intended primarily to stir jurors’ emotions.

"The Commonwealth did not choose the number of victims. The defendant did," Sprague responded. "The Commonwealth did not choose the ages of the victims. The defendant did."

Opening statements are scheduled for Monday morning at 9 a.m.

Sarah Rumpf-Whitten is a U.S. Writer at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to sarah.rumpf@fox.com and on X @s_rumpfwhitten

articles.title: Blanche-led DoJ likely to derail Epstein survivors’ pursuit of justice, experts say
articles.excerpt:
Lawyers predict ‘more suppression and no active investigations’ but victims’ groups determined to continue fight

As Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer Todd Blanche appears poised for confirmation a...
articles.body_text:
Lawyers predict ‘more suppression and no active investigations’ but victims’ groups determined to continue fight

As Donald Trump’s former defense lawyer Todd Blanche appears poised for confirmation as attorney general, numerous Jeffrey Epstein survivors have sounded the alarm that a US justice department helmed by him would derail their pursuit of justice.

In a letter urging Republican senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn to reject his nomination, these survivors said that Blanche’s handling of the Epstein case as acting attorney general was characterized by misstep after misstep.

Blanche, who reportedly led the disclosure of documents as required by the bipartisan Epstein Files Transparency Act, allowed the disclosure of survivors’ names, photos and identifying information – but omitted the names of accused abusers and enablers, they said.

While more than 1,000 teenage girls and women were abused, not a single person other than Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell faced charges, they noted. And in a recent sit-down with survivors at Tillis’s urging, survivors “received an hour of deflection, interruption and gaslighting”, they said.

These survivors’ concerns about Blanche by no means exist in a vacuum, and have only fanned the flames of a controversy that has dogged Trump since he again took office. While campaigning, Trump promised to release all Epstein files – playing into his supporters’ belief that there was a global sex-trafficking cabal involving high-profile business and political figures.

But Trump’s justice department only released dribs and drabs of information until Congress forced its hand following a series of embarrassing disclosures that renewed attention on Trump’s former friendship with Epstein. Trump has denied all wrongdoing including in relation to Epstein.

Blanche’s meeting with Maxwell in prison last summer, which was followed by her transfer to a lower-security facility, further heightened outrage over the DoJ’s underwhelming disclosures. The constellation of circumstances has raised the question: what would a Blanche-directed justice department mean for Epstein survivors’ search for justice?

Legal veterans told the Guardian that a Blanche-led DoJ would likely derail survivors’ efforts for accountability. Several survivors’ advocates said that all hope was not lost, noting that roadblocks likely under Blanche did not portend a permanent impediment to justice.

Bryan Sullivan, a partner with Early Sullivan Wright Gizer & McRae, said that based on what he has read and seen in Blanche’s testimony before the judiciary committee, he thinks a confirmation would mean “more suppression and no active investigations” into Epstein’s sex-trafficking.

“I think it’s because that’s what Trump wants. He wants this to go away,” Sullivan said. “And that’s one of the reasons he fired [former attorney general Pam] Bondi, because she didn’t make it go away, in my opinion.”

Ron Kuby, a renowned defense lawyer with a focus on civil rights, voiced similar sentiments about a Blanche confirmation.

“It means that no other perpetrators will be held criminally liable for their misconduct,” he said. “That’s no different from the way it’s been throughout the Trump administration and the Biden administration.”

“All the millionaires and billionaires and hangers-on and others in Epstein’s orbit who, you know, enabled him have not been brought to justice,” Kuby said. “And they’re not going to be.”

Carl Tobias, the Williams chair in law at the University of Richmond School of Law, said that even if Blanche were not confirmed, he could serve as acting attorney general for the rest of Trump’s term, meaning he would have continued control over the Epstein case.

“He’ll have more power, of course, if he’s formally confirmed by the Senate … but he’ll have plenty of power even if he’s not,” Tobias said. “So I can’t be very optimistic about what he might do – if anything – about the Epstein files, or to give much comfort to the survivors.”

While there are some legal avenues for survivors to seek justice outside an allegedly recalcitrant DoJ, attorneys cautioned that success would be an uphill battle.

“You could bombard them with [public records] requests, and then file a lawsuit for them not providing responses to the Foia [Freedom of Information Act] requests, but that alone is a long process,” Sullivan said. “Bluntly, the problem with all of this is [that] all of it takes time.”

“Courts are grossly underfunded [and] understaffed,” he said. “It will take quite a while to go through that sort of legal process.”

There has been litigation against federal authorities over their handling of the Epstein investigation, alleging that their failure to act years ago enabled more abuse. Those kinds of cases “are exceptionally difficult to win”, Kuby said.

“It’s always true that had the government done something differently, a different outcome would have ensued,” Kuby explained of the legal intricacies. “There’s no generalized duty to protect specific individuals outside of a special relationship with the victims.”

“I’m certainly sympathetic to those claims, but the government historically is not.”

Tobias similarly described the possibility of winning litigation against the DoJ as “difficult”.

Neither reps for Tillis or Cornyn responded to requests for comment.

Asked for comment on survivors’ concerns, White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson said: “Todd Blanche has done an excellent job as acting attorney general and will continue doing so as attorney general.”

A justice department spokesperson said in a statement that Blanche, senior DoJ officials, FBI agents and victims services representatives “met with Epstein victims last week and had a productive, initial discussion”.

The spokesperson said Blanche “answered questions and walked through what is needed for investigations to proceed”.

“While some victims said that they had not reached out to the FBI under this administration, he encouraged victims to meet with FBI investigators as the next step, and attendees spoke with agents after the meeting about scheduling interviews. The justice department is determined to bring justice for all victims of human trafficking and sex crimes.”

Gretchen Carlson and Julie Roginsky, who filed sexual harassment lawsuits against former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and co-launched the non-profit survivors advocacy organization Lift Our Voices, expressed hope that survivors could still find justice one day even if faced with more setbacks.

Carlson said she was disappointed in Republicans poised to let Blanche’s nomination go through, noting that Trump went on the attack against Cornyn and Tillis.

“They have the ability not to allow this,” Carlson said, explaining that not everything should be on their shoulders, as “everyone should have questions about Todd Blanche being attorney general, just about the Epstein issues”.

That said, there is a midterm election coming up. “I’ve learned, in all the work I’ve done on the Hill in trying to get bills passed, that you never know who you might get, first of all, to be on your side,” Carlson said. “So you never judge it before you actually try.”

“I feel the same way about this,” she said. “We don’t know who’s going to potentially step up to the plate and say, ‘You know what, I’m going to take over the work that [Republican congressman] Tom Massie was doing on this.

“We can’t do this work with any kind of a negative lens. And although it feels like we’re in a little bit of a setback if Todd Blanche is confirmed, I think there’s always a way to find victory.”

Roginsky expressed similar views. While a possible Blanche confirmation represented a “slap in the face to anybody who’s ever fought … a system that is already rigged very much against survivors”, she advised survivors and advocates to keep pushing for justice.

“If you think about how far our movement has come just in the last decade, we’ve seen tremendous advances,” Roginsky said of Lift Our Voices’ successful advocacy for federal legislation against non-disclosure agreements and forced arbitration related to workplace sexual misconduct.

“We’ve seen some setbacks, but ultimately the advances will always outweigh the setbacks.”

articles.title: Cracker Barrel comeback gains steam as loyal customer says return visit 'felt like coming home'
articles.excerpt: Rachel Love, a 38-year-old Tennessee woman whose viral video of Cracker Barrel's changes sparked outrage, told Fox News Digital that she's "super excited" for the restaurant chain's future now that th...
articles.body_text:
Rachel Love, a 38-year-old Tennessee woman whose viral video of Cracker Barrel's changes sparked outrage, told Fox News Digital that she's "super excited" for the restaurant chain's future now that the remodels have been suspended.

After months of backlash over a controversial rebranding that alienated many longtime customers, Cracker Barrel Old Country Store is betting its future on returning to its roots, selling off secondary assets, cutting debt and focusing entirely on the iconic country restaurant chain.

The Tennessee-based restaurant chain announced last week that it has completed two major strategic moves designed to strengthen its core business, while raising its profitability outlook for fiscal year 2026.

The company completed a sale-leaseback transaction involving 26 company-owned restaurant locations, generating about $77 million in proceeds that it plans to use to reduce debt. It also sold most of its Maple Street Biscuit Company business to Biscuit Belly and said it will close the remaining 16 Maple Street locations, allowing the company to focus more heavily on the Cracker Barrel brand.

CRACKER BARREL SELLS MAPLE STREET BISCUIT COMPANY, CLOSES 16 LOCATIONS

"Our sale-leaseback transaction will allow us to opportunistically reduce debt while monetizing a portion of our owned real estate at an attractive valuation," President and CEO Julie Masino said in a statement. "Divesting Maple Street sharpens our focus on the core Cracker Barrel brand and is expected to improve profitability."

The moves come after a challenging stretch for the country-themed chain.

Cracker Barrel sold most of its Maple Street Biscuit Company restaurants and is closing the remaining 16 locations. (iStock)

Last summer, Cracker Barrel faced vocal backlash over updates to its logo and restaurant remodels, with longtime customers arguing the company was abandoning the nostalgic look that had defined the brand for decades.

The criticism coincided with weaker sales and backlash that prompted company leaders to restore the chain's signature "Old Timer" logo and interior.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Among the chain's most outspoken critics was Tennessee resident Rachel Love, who previously told Fox News Digital she was disappointed by the changes. After recently visiting a restored Cracker Barrel that had undergone a remodel, however, she said the experience left her optimistic about the brand's direction.

"Going back to Cracker Barrel felt like coming home," Love told Fox News Digital. "Seeing the building returned to its original look honestly brought tears to my eyes before I even walked inside."

A longtime Cracker Barrel customer said visiting a formerly remodeled restaurant in Tennessee that had been restored "felt like coming home" and brought tears to her eyes.  (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Love said the familiar brown exterior, welcoming Old Country Store and her favorite meatloaf meal made it feel as though the company had rediscovered what longtime customers valued.

"What has impressed me the most is that this turnaround feels like more than just cosmetic changes," she said. "It feels like Cracker Barrel listened to the people who have supported the brand for generations."

Love added that she is "genuinely hopeful about where the company is headed."

Cracker Barrel is projecting a better fiscal year after a difficult 2025. One loyal customer told Fox News Digital that she's "genuinely hopeful about where the company is headed." (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Restaurant industry publication Nation's Restaurant News recently reported that Cracker Barrel's comeback "continues to gain steam," noting that the company believes it could exceed its financial outlook for the year despite restaurant sales remaining slightly below last year's levels.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Cracker Barrel now expects to meet or exceed the high end of its previously issued revenue guidance and surpass its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) forecast for the fiscal year.

The company declined to comment when contacted by Fox News Digital.

Peter Burke is a lifestyle editor with Fox News Digital. He covers various lifestyle topics, with an emphasis on food and drink.

articles.title: Oil price slides as US and Iran pause fire; cancer treatments help AstraZeneca beat profit forecasts – business live
articles.excerpt:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Oil prices have fallen more tha...
articles.body_text:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Oil prices have fallen more than 5% this morning as the US paused strikes on Iran for the second night in a row, with military officials advising Donald Trump to stop his bombing campaign.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is now down 5.3% to $91.68 a barrel, after it hit $100 last week.

Trum is believed to be considering diplomatic and military options in the conflict with Iran, while the Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to visit the White House on Tuesday.

Iran said on Sunday that it would pause “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region.

Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, says that while the pause is not a formal ceasefire, both sides have presented it as “an opportunity for diplomacy”.

double quotation markUS officials, including UN ambassador Mike Waltz, have stressed that all military options remain on the table and that President Trump is simply giving negotiations more space. However, reports from the New York Times and Axios suggest an active debate within the administration over both the effectiveness and costs of further strikes, with some military officials reportedly arguing that key objectives have largely been achieved. For now, the market is treating the lull as a positive development, although the situation remains highly fluid.

The main market risk remains the energy and shipping front. Traffic through Hormuz remains severely disrupted, while the conflict has broadened into the Red Sea, where Iran-backed Houthi forces reportedly launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure around Jizan and Yanbu over the weekend, prompting retaliatory Saudi strikes. This raises the prospect of simultaneous disruption to both Gulf and Red Sea export routes. So a welcome pause from the main actors but a fragile one, especially with side battles still ongoing.

Elsewhere this morning, AstraZeneca reported better than expected profits for its second quarter, driven by strong growth in its cancer treatment sales.

Its earnings for the three months ended in June rose 18% to $2.63 (£1.97) a share, while its overall revenue rose by 5% to $15.38bn at constant currency.

While European wholesale gas prices are falling today, analysts are warning that low levels of supply and strong demand in Asia mean prices could ramp up this winter.

European gas stockpiles are at a “historic low” for July, at just above 50% capacity, according to the energy cosultancy Wood Mackenzie.

Analysts warned that European gas storage is on track for 75% capacity “at best” by 1 November, compared with a five-year average of 90%. They wrote:

double quotation markShould the strait [of Hormuz] remain closed for a further two months, storage will end up lower than 70%. Prices would rise further and some emerging Asian economies, already strained by high LNG costs, face demand destruction.

Massimo Di Odoardo, vice president of gas and LNG research at Wood Mackenzie, said:

double quotation markLow European inventories, strong Asian demand and limited new LNG supply growth almost guarantee elevated prices through this winter and into 2027.

Russ Mould, investment director at the broker AJ Bell, adds that the upbeat mood in stock markets today has been helped by the debut of the Chinese silicon chip maker CXMT. He said:

double quotation markIts near five-fold surge may help to soothe concerns about the AI trade after slumps in SpaceX and Korea’s SK Hynix after their recent offerings.

The Chinese chipmaker listed in Shanghai today, with its shares surging by more than 400% – making it the country’s biggest onshore-listed company, overtaking the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC).

The UK’s financial watchdog has launched a £2m advertising campaign aimed at curbing use of claims management companies (CMCs), and encouraging drivers hit by the car finance scandal to file their own complaints.

The Financial Conduct Authority’s 30-second video advert features a series of pedestrians jumping over car bonnets in slow-motion, action film style, while text flashes across the screen to encourage their peers to “Feel Claim Confident.”

The multi-million pound campaign will run until 6 September, across outdoor billboards, national radio slots, print and social media, including Facebook, Instagram and Tiktok, and direct people to a self-fill form on the FCA website.

The FCA has been trying to steer consumers away from CMCs who lenders say have been targeted victims of the scandal, and can end up charging fees worth up to 33% of the final payouts. The FCA and lenders have advised consumers not to use these firms as the regulator’s scheme is free to use.

It comes as the FCA tries to push ahead with a portion of a £9.1bn compensation scheme which isn’t being challenged in the courts. The FCA is trying to draw a line under a long-running scandal in which borrowers were overcharged due to lenders paying commission to car dealerships between 2007 and 2024.

Commenting on the ad campaign, one of the FCA’s executive directors Sheree Howard said:

double quotation markMany people who may be owed compensation aren’t sure where to start or don’t realise they don’t have to pay someone to make a complaint. Our free tools are there to help people feel claim confident – so they can get any money owed back without it costing them a penny.”

Shares in European airlines are also rising strongly this morning – Ryanair is up 2.6%, while British Airways owner International Consolidated Airlines Group is up about 3%. Budget airline Wizz Air is also up by 3.2%.

US stocks are poised to join the global market rally later this afternoon – futures for the blue chip S&P 500 index are pointing to a 0.9% rise, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq is poised to rise 1.5%. US airlines are also set to rise, with Delta and American up 2.6% and 3% in pre-market trading. Cruise operators Royal Caribbean and Carnival are also up by about 3% each.

European wholesale gas prices are also falling this morning, as a pause in US and Iranian strikes over the weekend lifts hopes that traffic through the strait of Hormuz could continue.

The European benchmark, the Dutch front-month contract, fell by 6.8% to €59.22 per megawatt hour (MWh). The British month ahead contract dropped by 6.8% to 143.93p per therm.

Energy companies BP and Shell are unsurprisingly the worst performers across the FTSE 100 this morning, with their shares down by 3.8% and 2% respectively thanks to the weaker oil price. Overall the energy sector is down by about 2.6%.

JD Sports is the best performer, with shares in the fashion retailer up 3.6%. Vodafone is second, with its shares up 3% after an upbeat quarterly update this morning.

European stocks are rallying this morning as investors rejoice at a sharp drop in oil prices, after the US paused its nearly two-week long run of strikes against Iran.

The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, is up by 0.9%. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 is up 0.5%, while the French Cac 40 is up 1.1% and the German Dax is up 1.5%.

The oil price has dipped below $90 a barrel, as investors weighed the pause in fire between the US and Iran.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell by 7.1% to $89.94 a barrel. It rose above $100 last week, when the US carried out several consecutive nights of strikes against Iran, and the Yemeni Houthi movement threatened to carry out a naval blockade of Saudi Arabian ports.

However prices are falling today as the US paused strikes on Iran for the second night in a row, and as military officials advised Donald Trump to stop his bombing campaign.

In Europe, bond yields are slipping on lower oil prices – Eurozone 10-year yields are down by about 3 basis points, while in the UK the 10-year gilt yield is down by about 5 basis points to 4.98%.

The drop in the UK gilt yield also came after Andy Burnham said over the weekend that the UK needed to bring the welfare bill down.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said the lower gillt yield eased some of the pressure off Burnham’s new government.

double quotation markThis will be welcome given focus has switched firmly to the spending challenges facing the new government, with warnings from the prime minister that social care needs desperate reform to help save the NHS while also accepting that the benefits bill needs to be brought down. There is still a distinct lack of detail on how he and his ministers will go about tackling the huge costs of welfare, and so investors in government debt look set to stay wary while there’s so much talk but so little action on lowering government spending costs.

Elsewhere on the corporate front this morning, Vodafone has reported a 9.7% rise in revenue in its first quarter to €10.3bn.

Service revenue rose 5% in the quarter ended in June, compared with investor expectations of a 4.6% gain. Management now expects that its adjusted earnings will reach somewhere between €13bn to €13.3bn for the full year ending in March.

In recent years, Vodafone has restructured its business – including selling its Italian and Spanish operations and its 50% stake in its Dutch joint venture – as well as merging with Three to create the UK’s largest mobile operator.

Earlier this month the French telecoms billionaire Xavier Niel became Vodafone’s largest shareholder after buying a 16% stake for £4.4bn.

The company has also been fighting allegations, first published in the Guardian, that it “unjustly enriched” itself at the expense of scores of vulnerable small business owners by slashing commissions to franchisees running the mobile phone group’s high street stores.

Yet another company has been picked off London’s stock exchange this morning: DCC Energy has agreed to a £5.75bn takeover by private equity investors KKR and Energy Capital Partners.

Shareholders in the FTSE 100 energy distributor will receive £65.25 per share ‌in cash, a proposed ‌final dividend of 147.22p per share, and a potential payment of up ‌to £1.25 per share if DCC can sell its technology unit for at least $800 million.

The deal represents a 24% premium to DCC’s share price in late April, before it received the consortium’s first bid.

DCC ‌chair Mark Breuer said in a statement:

double quotation markWhilst the DCC Energy Board remains confident in the energy strategy and associated 2030 Ambition announced in 2022, the Board believes the Consortium’s offer represents a compelling opportunity for shareholders to crystallise value in cash at an attractive premium to DCC Energy’s historical trading price.

We are confident that the Consortium will be strong stewards of DCC Energy’s 50-year heritage and support the business during its next phase of growth.”

It is the latest in a long string of takeovers in London’s stock market – Mitie, Intertek, easyJet, Beazley and Schroders have all agreed to takeovers this year.

The Chinese fast fashion giant Shein reported a $99m (£74.1m) net loss in its first quarter, after the removal of an import duty exemption in the US on small packages triggered a slowdown in sales.

The figures were released as part of the company’s pre-IPO paperwork, as it prepares to list on Hong Kong’s stock exchange.

It showed that the business made a $99m loss in the first quarter of 2026, compared with net income of $395m a year earlier.

The US scrapped its tariff exemption for small packages in May. Shein said in its filing that it was “pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs”.

The European Union has also this month imposed a €3 fee on low-value e-commerce imports, in a move designed to defend European businesses from what the union calls “unfair competition” from China.

Shein has seen a sharp drop in its valuation in recent years, as the pandemic-era boom in online shopping has ended. The company is now reportedly seeking a valuation of $40bn to $50bn, compared with reports of a potential valuation of $100bn in 2022.

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Oil prices have fallen more than 5% this morning as the US paused strikes on Iran for the second night in a row, with military officials advising Donald Trump to stop his bombing campaign.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is now down 5.3% to $91.68 a barrel, after it hit $100 last week.

Trum is believed to be considering diplomatic and military options in the conflict with Iran, while the Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to visit the White House on Tuesday.

Iran said on Sunday that it would pause “retaliatory” attacks against US allies in the region.

Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, says that while the pause is not a formal ceasefire, both sides have presented it as “an opportunity for diplomacy”.

double quotation markUS officials, including UN ambassador Mike Waltz, have stressed that all military options remain on the table and that President Trump is simply giving negotiations more space. However, reports from the New York Times and Axios suggest an active debate within the administration over both the effectiveness and costs of further strikes, with some military officials reportedly arguing that key objectives have largely been achieved. For now, the market is treating the lull as a positive development, although the situation remains highly fluid.

The main market risk remains the energy and shipping front. Traffic through Hormuz remains severely disrupted, while the conflict has broadened into the Red Sea, where Iran-backed Houthi forces reportedly launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure around Jizan and Yanbu over the weekend, prompting retaliatory Saudi strikes. This raises the prospect of simultaneous disruption to both Gulf and Red Sea export routes. So a welcome pause from the main actors but a fragile one, especially with side battles still ongoing.

Elsewhere this morning, AstraZeneca reported better than expected profits for its second quarter, driven by strong growth in its cancer treatment sales.

Its earnings for the three months ended in June rose 18% to $2.63 (£1.97) a share, while its overall revenue rose by 5% to $15.38bn at constant currency.

articles.title: Father of boy on life support calls for safety review at Essex beach where two died
articles.excerpt:
Shalina Rahman, 42, and daughter Sameeha, 15, were on holiday in West Mersea and boy is believed to be family member

The teenage girl and woman who died in the waters off an Essex beach were trying t...
articles.body_text:
Shalina Rahman, 42, and daughter Sameeha, 15, were on holiday in West Mersea and boy is believed to be family member

The teenage girl and woman who died in the waters off an Essex beach were trying to help a seven-year-old boy who had got into difficulty, police believe.

Family members identified the pair as Shalina Rahman, a 42-year-old British-Bangladeshi teacher who is married to a Bangladeshi politician, and her 15-year-old daughter, Sameeha. The boy, who police say was a relative, is on life support in a hospital in London.

Shalina Rahman’s husband is Mansur Rahman, the leader of Jubo Dal UK, the overseas youth wing of the Bangladesh Nationalist party in Britain. Her father is Mujibur Rahman, the former vice-president of the party in Britain.

The family are understood to have been on a summer holiday trip in West Mersea, where they may have got into difficulty after a heavy incoming tide caused the sand beneath their feet to give way, sweeping them into the water.

Essex police were called by the ambulance service at 5.35pm on Wednesday after reports of the incident near Seaview Avenue in West Mersea.

DCI Al Pitcher confirmed that a mother and daughter had died, saying: “My thoughts, and those of my team, are with the friends and family of the woman and girl who died yesterday. We can now confirm they were a mother and daughter from London and we are supporting their family in what is an unimaginable time.

“Since yesterday we have been working to establish the circumstances which led up to this incident. At this stage we believe they were trying to help a seven-year-old boy who had got into difficulties.

“The boy was taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical condition, but the woman and teenage girl, sadly, died. All the people involved in this incident are related to each other.

“As part of our investigation we are working through speaking to dozens of witnesses and taking their accounts, and we are building a picture of what happened.”

Mishba Uddin, a family friend, said he believed the mother and teenage girl “were not very good swimmers”. He said that those involved came from east London, with one family based in Barking.

Matiur Rahman, the brother-in-law of Shalina Rahman, told the BBC: “We all feel very bad, my four brothers, my sister … My whole family – we are speechless. We are very shocked.”

Rahman was told in a phone call from his brother about the tragedy. “They went in Colchester, [to the] seaside, and they were near water and playing with them, then suddenly a big wave came,” he said, adding that about 10 family members were on the day out.

Carl Powling, of Colchester council, said his daughter was one of three teenage waitresses at a local cafe who had tried to help. “Members of the public witnessed it, called the emergency services, helped starting to pull people out, then they went into the Seaview cafe to ask for assistance,” he said.

A woman, who did not give her name, told PA Media that the incident had happened at high tide, which caught the small group on a sandbank.

“It comes in very quickly and you have to be careful,” she said, adding that there was “quite a commotion” and “just total panic”. She said helicopters were deployed and the air was filled with the sound of sirens.

“That was quite alarming, for a small place like this, I think that’s why so many people are shocked,” she said. “The beach was packed with people, they were coming down to see what was going on.”

The woman said the emergency services “worked diligently” to deal with an “absolutely tragic” incident.

There have been at least 29 accidental deaths in open water across the UK since the middle of May, according to the National Water Safety Forum.

The area in Essex is known for its strong currents, though the local MP, Bernard Jenkin, told the BBC that “we don’t think of West Mersea beach as a dangerous beach”.

Anyone who was in the area at the time and has information or footage that may assist the investigation is asked to contact the police on 101 and quote incident 1090.

articles.title: Musk takes 'crusade' to Europe with Armie Hammer film
articles.excerpt: An American vigilante tears across an unnamed European country, killing dozens of police officers and judges, slaughtering a gang of rapists, and killing a refugee family and a random civilian – all i...
articles.body_text:
An American vigilante tears across an unnamed European country, killing dozens of police officers and judges, slaughtering a gang of rapists, and killing a refugee family and a random civilian – all in the name of a crusade against Muslim migrants and "woke" government officials.

Citizen Vigilante, a film from German director Uwe Boll and starring actor Armie Hammer, is violent – and very schlocky – stuff.

Initially denied a rating by German's film regulator, it would likely have garnered very little attention, had it not caught the eye of the world's richest person.

Listen to The Global Story: Citizen Vigilante and Elon Musk's war on 'woke' films

Elon Musk made the film free to view via his social media platform X for 48 hours in late June, and the subsequent attention briefly pushed the movie into the top of the charts of several streaming providers including Apple and Amazon.

At one point he reposted a message about the film that described vigilante murder as the "moderate response" to violent crimes committed by immigrants.

It's just one of many recent examples of the tech titan's increasing interest in extreme ideas and activists, and in particular his support of political parties and politicians on the right in Europe.

Musk left the Trump administration more than a year ago and his Doge project, which aimed to slash the size of the US federal government, has since been wound down.

But he has recently sought to conquer other political territory.

"This is a crusade," says Georgios Samaras, an assistant professor of public policy at King's College London who studies the European and US far right. "Musk uses the power he has to amplify the ideas that he thinks should dominate society. He knows he has the money and he knows he has the influence."

Much of that influence comes via X, formerly Twitter, the social media platform that Musk bought outright in 2022. Since stripping away many of the old Twitter's content moderation rules - derided as censorship by Musk and others - the network has become a haven for far-right beliefs and conspiracy theories.

Although it's difficult to glean a cohesive worldview from social media fragments - Musk did not respond to requests for comment for this story - his output has demonstrated a growing obsession with race and white people in particular.

He has posted and reposted a slew of messages - often from white nationalist and far-right activists - portraying white people as under threat, including messages like "Whites are a rapidly dying minority" and "If White men become a minority, we will be slaughtered".

He has endorsed the leader of France's hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen. "She is France's last hope," he wrote.
